Streamflow validation

To validate streamflow estimates, AnnAGNPS-simulated monthly discharge was compared to measured discharge at four stations within the watershed: three upstream stations (stations 5, 11, and 14) and the watershed outlet (station 1; Fig. 1). Station 5 is located in the main reach and measures flow for 419 ha in the upper portion of the watershed, while stations 11 and 14 are located on secondary reaches and represent

</page>

<page number="5">

mixed land uses; sub-basin 11 is about 26 ha and sub-basin 14 is 166 ha. The area represented at station 1 is 2132 ha. These reaches were selected for comparison with simulated results a priori, as they represent a variety of sub-basin sizes and contain a varying number of ponds. A manual baseflow filtering approach was applied to the streamflow record to remove baseflow before comparison with AnnAGNPS, as baseflow is not simulated in the model (Bingner 1998). The Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), correlation coefficient (r), percent bias (PBIAS), and root mean square error -observations standard deviation ratio (RSR) were used to evaluate model results (Moriasi et al. 2007, 2015).

Results and discussion

Characterization of ponds

The AgWET GIS tools were able to delineate ponds with fairly good accuracy. Comparison of manually digitized and AgWET-generated pond shapes and extents (Fig. 2) and surface areas (Fig. 3) indicates that there was a tendency to overestimate pond areas using AgWET, as compared to manually delineated areas, and there are several reasons why this may occur. First, it is important to note that the manually delineated areas may fluctuate through time due to wet or dry seasons and years. Second, the manually delineated ponds were developed using aerial imagery and areas that were vegetated surrounding the pond introduce uncertainty as to where the pond edge ends and the land begins; this was especially common where trees surround the pond edge. Third, AgWET was using the DEM and the barrier height to define the pond extent. The barrier height was determined from the DEM, but pond depth will typically be lower than the barrier height by a meter or more; therefore, the area determined by AgWET could be considered the maximum pond pool height considering the height of the barrier and the surrounding topography. Bearing in mind the uncertainties in the manually delineated areas, AgWET did a sufficient job in estimating pond area. AgWET was more accurate representing small ponds and there was greater error when estimating shapes and sizes of larger ponds (Figs 2 and 3). The smaller ponds tended to have shorter barrier heights than the larger ponds and this could contribute to this bias.

Watershed simulation validation

Streamflow was simulated with excellent agreement at the four examined gauges without calibration of flow parameters (Fig. 4). NSE values ranged between 0.91 and 0.94; r values were 0.96–0.97; PBIAS was between −0.32 and −16; and RSR scores were 0.24–0.30 (Table 1). The main difference between the simulated and observed time series was a slight underestimation of streamflow in some months with higher flow; these differences were more pronounced at station 14 and less visible at the watershed outlet (station 1). Generally, excellent results were achieved at both the smaller sub-basin scale, as well as the overall watershed scale, which provides confidence that AnnAGNPS was able to accurately simulate streamflow in this watershed. As the results were excellent after using model inputs based on previous studies and expert knowledge of this watershed, no calibration was performed.

The streamflow validations statistics were compared with and without ponds to determine if including the ponds increased the accuracy in streamflow estimates. In three of the four examined watersheds the addition of ponds improved NSE, PBIAS, and RSR statistics slightly, with the most noticeable changes in PBIAS. There was no change in the correlation coefficient (r). Station 14 was the only station that saw a decrease or no change in accuracy with the addition of ponds.

Impact of ponds on watershed hydrology

The ponds for the entire GCEW were only capturing drainage water from approximately 424 hectares or 20% of the watershed, and they were located mainly in the uplands and not near the main reach in the watershed; therefore, the effect of ponds on watershed-wide hydrology was limited. Upland areas of this watershed are typically pasture, forest, or residential land use; therefore, these ponds have varying

The impacts of ponds on watershed hydrology were evaluated at both the local reach scale and the overall watershed scale. At the overall watershed scale, flows were reduced on average by 46 515 m³, which is an overall 4.0% reduction in streamflow. The annual maximum peak flow was reduced by an average of 2.0 m³/s throughout the simulated time period, which is a 2% reduction in peak at the watershed outlet. While the effect of the ponds was fairly small at the watershed outlet, there was a slightly larger impact on streamflow at the sub-watershed scale, and a much greater impact on local streamflows directly downstream of the ponds. Sub-watershed 5, 11, and 14 had average reductions in monthly flow of 5, 8, and 6%, respectively, when considering the impact of ponds. Using data from the individual 67 ponds, local streamflow decreased downstream of the ponds by an average of 9300 m³, or an average decrease of 56% at all sites. The ponds varied in their influence with a spread of 860 to 67 000 m³ reduction in streamflow just below the dam structure, which corresponded to a 9 and 23% reduction in flow, respectively (Table 2). Six ponds captured 100% of the streamflow, reducing the localized flow by an average of 5300–10 500 m³ per year. Annual average peak flow rates were also reduced below the ponds by an average of 36% or a decrease of 0.165 m³/s, with a median decrease of 13% or 0.08 m³/s. The spatial variation in local pond streamflow reduction and percentage reduction is shown in Figure 5 at the full watershed scale and in an inset with sub-watershed 14 results.

Reductions in streamflow increased with larger pond areas, which is to be expected (\( y = -2.33x; R^2 = 0.89 \); \( x \) is pond area (m²), \( y \) is streamflow reduction (m³); \( p \)-value < 0.0001.). This relationship was not improved by considering total pond volume (\( y = -0.43x; R^2 = 0.68 \); \( x \) is pond volume (m³), \( y \) is streamflow reduction (m³); \( p \)-value < 0.0001). While smaller ponds typically had lower reductions in streamflow, they typically had higher percentage differences in streamflow (Fig. 5). While the actual water trapped is less, these smaller ponds may reduce 70–100% of the flow directly downstream.

Potential impacts on geochemical and physical processes

Ponds increase the residence time of water within the upstream hydrological network, which has an influence on sediment and nutrient loads transported downstream. Small ponds are highly effective at trapping sediment, with reported rates of 50–80% in arable landscapes (Mekonnen et al. 2014). Trapping efficiency can vary greatly between ponds, and sediment particle size will influence greatly if particles settle or are suspended

Field studies also have demonstrated a strong relationship between water trapping and nutrient trapping (Cooper and Knight 1990, Yin and Shan 2001, Fairchild and Velinsky 2006). Stream nutrient loads were not verified in these simulations, so estimates were not made with regard to reductions in nitrogen and phosphorus loads due to trapping in the pond. Also, as these ponds are located in the upland portions of the watershed and with very little agricultural land use, overall watershed loads of nitrogen and phosphorus are likely minimally reduced by the ponds. However, a study of Morris Pond (labeled in Fig. 5), one of the largest reservoirs within the Goodwin Creek watershed, demonstrated storm-event nutrient trapping efficiencies ranging from 54% for total phosphorus to 71% for nitrate-nitrogen (Cooper and Knight 1990). Ponds can be successful locations for nutrient trapping as they provide a space for the physical capture of dissolved and particulate sources of nutrients. Ponds also increase the residence time for nutrients, which encourages biological and chemical processing through uptake, denitrification, and sediment sorption (Wetzel 2001).

The ponds also showed that they immediately reduced peak flow below the pond to varying degrees. Overall watershed peak flows were decreased by 2%; however, some ponds reduced sub-watershed peak flow by 70–100%. Decreasing peak flow may help to decrease stream power, which may help to maintain

channel stability while decreasing sediment loads (Goff and Gentry 2006).

Broader implications for watershed assessment

In Mississippi it is estimated that farm ponds make up 3–4% of agricultural land due to high annual average precipitation, yet the location of these ponds may not be included in a publicly available database (Downing et al. 2006). Within the GCEW study watershed, only one of the approximately 70 ponds identified by aerial imagery was on the registered inventory of dams (National Inventory of Dams, 2017). However, there were 5114 dams listed in Mississippi on the national inventory. It is reasonable to assume that there are many additional small waterbodies in the state other than those listed, and that their influence on local and regional hydrology is largely overlooked. In general, studies across the United States demonstrate that SWBs are common landscape features with considerable influence on local and regional hydrology. Larger landscape-scale analyses in Mississippi would be helpful to determine the influence of these waterbodies on regional hydrology and to estimate the trapping potential for pollutants. Analysis of aerial and remotely sensed imagery can provide realistic estimates of size and location of waterbodies, and tools such as AgWET can help to characterize these SWBs to assess their impact on hydrology and water quality processes.

This study tested the capabilities of AgWET on constructed ponds with barriers bisecting a stream channel, as AgWET is currently limited to representation of ponds or wetlands within a simulated stream channel network. Future model development will expand AgWET’s capability to include water bodies receiving overland flow from the landscape that are intermittently connected to channelized flow. Correspondingly, future studies should explore the application of AgWET to natural water bodies. Another area of future model development is to improve the phosphorus and sediment routing and process representation within SWBs in AnnAGNPS in order to study the impact of ponds or wetlands on these pollutants.

Conclusions

Small water bodies (SWBs) are ubiquitous features of the landscape, yet their influence on local and regional hydrology is usually not considered in watershed modeling efforts. The AgWET wetland module, as part of the TOPAGNPS tool, provides topographic tools to represent SWBs. The AnnAGNPS model utilizes the associated AgWET information with internal algorithms to incorporate the influence of these water bodies on hydrology within watershed simulations. An assessment of Goodwin Creek Experimental Watershed in Mississippi found that AgWET was able to accurately represent the ponds within the watershed and streamflow estimates were improved by including the influence of these water bodies. Overall, the ponds decreased watershed flow by 4%, but demonstrated much greater decreases at the local scale. Peak flow was also decreased on average by 2%. By incorporating AgWET into modeling efforts, SWBs are accounted for and hydrological processes can be simulated with greater accuracy. This tool would be especially useful in areas with large numbers of constructed farm ponds, reservoirs, or wetlands.

CRYPTIC TROPHIC CASCADE ALONG A GRADIENT OF LAKE SIZE ALAN J. TESSIER1 AND PAMELA WOODRUFF W. K. Kellogg Biological Station and Department of Zoology, Michigan State University, Hickory Corners, Michigan 49060 USA Abstract. Lake size and depth mediate the strength of interaction between fish and zooplankton. We test whether this variation in zooplanktivory indirectly affects the phytoplankton by comparing 19 lakes that represent two food webs resulting from the absence of piscivores in small, partial-winterkill lakes. Lakes with piscivorous fish are further distinguished by thermal stratification, which provides a refuge for zooplankton to avoid fish predation. We contrasted phytoplankton abundance in these three categories of lakes over six years, using both direct measures of concentration and a growth bioassay that measures phytoplankton from the perspective of a standard grazer (Daphnia). Contrary to expectations, phytoplankton abundance was largely unaffected by trophic structure or the presence of a deep-water refuge. However, grazer growth differed dramatically among the three categories of lakes. Consistent with trophic cascade, increased fish planktivory resulted in more phytoplankton food as measured from the grazer’s perspective. This effect was independent of lake productivity or total abundance and size of phytoplankton. Instead, variation in food quality for grazers was associated with compositional differences in phytoplankton. These results indicate that persistent trophic cascades are more dramatic in the plankton than previously realized but primarily influence composition, rather than biomass. Although cryptic, such top-down effects create functional variation in grazer–resource coupling. Key words: Daphnia growth bioassay; indirect effects; phytoplankton; species sorting; trophic compensation; winterkill; zooplankton refuge. INTRODUCTION Changes at the top of food webs can have cascading effects, but what determines the magnitude and persistence of those effects is poorly understood. Addressing the issue demands that we first define what is meant by “effect” (Schmitz et al. 2000). Recently, Polis et al. (2000) argued for separation of species- and community-level effects of trophic cascade. They reasoned that effects on traits of individual species (e.g., leaf damage) do not hold the same significance for ecosystem processes as changes in community composition or biomass. While a primary concern with community change is reasonable, important differences in food web or trophic interactions need not involve shifts in the distribution of trophic biomass. Nor is it clear that species turnover will serve as a useful estimate of trophic cascade, given that most species are relatively rare. In short, the strength of trophic coupling and food web function may not be predictable from relative changes in biomass or species composition. We suggest a need for studies of trophic effects that quantify the functional consequences of changes in community composition. Of particular interest to trophic cascade theory is whether variation in predation changes the nature of prey–resource coupling. In a three-trophic-level food chain, increased predation weakens the coupling of prey with their resources and typically increases resource biomass. From the perspective of prey, this higher resource availability should increase individual growth and reproductive rates (a functional change). In real food webs, compensatory responses within either the prey or resource trophic levels might mask the cascade effect when measured in terms of biomass. But does compensation of biomass mean that the functional effects on trophic coupling are also diluted? We address this question by quantifying the indirect effect of predators (fish planktivores) on the resources (phytoplankton) of their prey (zooplankton grazers) from two perspectives: biomass and prey growth rate. We rely on prior work (Desmarais and Tessier 1999, Tessier et al. 2000) showing that the growth response of a standard Daphnia to different phytoplankton assemblages is broadly representative of growth and reproductive responses of other suspension feeders, the dominant grazers. This allows us to quantify resource availability from the perspective of the grazers in short-term growth bioassays and to compare that to traditional measures of phytoplankton biomass. Our bioassay approach provides a common currency with which to quantify the trophic significance of compositional changes within the phytoplankton. We apply this approach to a study of trophic cascade effects in lakes that naturally differ in intensity of fish planktivory. Fish planktivory is typically stronger in

Large Daphnia that are effective grazers (Mazumder 1994) exist in deep stratified lakes, while smaller grazers dominate in shallow lakes (Tessier and Welser 1991). The significance of zooplankton body size and especially of large Daphnia to grazing impact on phytoplankton is well documented (Carpenter and Kitchell 1993). Therefore, we predicted that at the same level of system productivity shallow lakes should display higher phytoplankton levels than deep lakes. METHODS Lake basins and trophic coupling We chose lakes located in southwestern Michigan, USA, on the basis of size, depth, and thermal stratification so as to achieve a representative sample of two different food webs and three different levels of zooplanktivory (Fig. 1, Table 1). Lakes in our first category have small surface area relative to depth, so they thermally stratify in summer. Consequently, the zooplankton of these “deep-refuge” lakes is dominated by large-bodied Daphnia species that vertically migrate to feed on phytoplankton in the surface waters at night, but refuge in deep waters during the day to avoid fish. Centrarchids are the dominant fish in this and the next category of lake; bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus) and pumpkinseed (L. gibbosus) sunfish are the main planktivores, and largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) is the major piscivore (Werner et al. 1977). Lakes in our second category have large surface area relative to their depth and do not thermally stratify in summer. These “shallow” lakes have no refuge for zooplankton to avoid daytime planktivory, so zooplankton suffer a greater risk of predation than in the deep lakes (Tessier et al. 1992, Leibold and Tessier 1998). While not measured in our lakes, biomass of fish (per cubic meter) is generally known to be greater in shallow than in deep lakes (Jeppesen et al. 1997). Consequently, the zooplankton of shallow lakes is composed of a lower biomass of smaller-sized taxa than the big Daphnia of deep lakes (Fig. 1). Lakes in our last category are both shallow and small in water volume. Low oxygen under the ice in winter is a recurring stress in these lakes and results in partial winterkills (Greenbank 1945), to which largemouth bass is particularly sensitive (Moore 1942). Hence, lakes in this category lack strong piscivory, and the fish community is composed of high densities of efficient planktivores (Tonn and Magnuson 1982). Reflecting this “high planktivory,” the grazer assemblage is dominated by the smallest of cladocerans and copepods, and rotifers dominate the zooplankton in these lakes (Hall and Ellinger 1989, Mittelbach et al. 1995; Fig. 1). Hence, the three categories of lakes represent a gradient of intensity of fish planktivory; lowest in the deep-refuge lakes, intermediate in the shallow lakes, and highest in the partial winterkill lakes. We examined seven deep-refuge lakes, six shallow lakes, and six high-planktivory lakes over a period of 6 yr (Table 1). Most lakes were sampled in multiple years (>2 yr per lake) and on multiple dates throughout the summer (June–September). We also sampled each lake during the spring turnover and collected pelagic water for determination of total phosphorus. Phytoplankton-eston abundance We collected water from the pelagic zone, ~0.5 m below the lake surface between 0900 and 1300. Sam- ples were screened through 62-μm Nitex (Tetko, Elmsford, New York, USA) and then filtered on GF/F glass fiber filters (Whatman, Clifton, New Jersey, USA) for analysis of chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate matter. Chlorophyll \( a \) was extracted overnight in cold, 95% ethanol and measured using narrow band fluorometry. Ash-free dry mass of the seston was determined after muffling at 500°C and converted to carbon using a calibration based on C analysis using a Carlo-Erba elemental analyzer (C. E. Instruments, Milan, Italy; A. J. Tessier, unpublished data). During summer of 1999 we sampled all lakes for a size-fractionation of chlorophyll \( a \) (<3, <15, <35, <62, <100 μm, and total) using Nitex screens except for the <3-μm fraction, which was achieved by filtration through Whatman GF/D glass fiber filters. Growth bioassay As a direct estimate of phytoplankton food value for zooplankton, we conducted growth rate bioassays on the same dates that we sampled chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate carbon. The bioassays measured juvenile specific growth rate of a clone of *D. pulex-pulicaria* fed seston from the lake but under standard laboratory conditions. Bioassay results are representative of growth and reproduction responses of all common daphniid species in our region (Desmarais and Tessier 1999, Tessier et al. 2000). Bioassays start with neonates (<24 h) born to mothers that were raised under a standard, high-food environment (Tessier et al. 2000). Each bioassay used a minimum of 10 neonates per lake-seston treatment, with an additional 15 harvested for initial dry mass. On each day, individual animals were changed to freshly collected lake water (screened through 80-μm Nitex to remove other zooplankton) in separate beakers until age 4 d, at which point animals were harvested for measurement of dry mass (see Desmarais and Tessier 1999 for detailed methods). Water was collected from the pelagic zone as described above. We expressed growth rate as the difference between the natural log of initial and final dry mass (measured to the nearest 0.1 μg) of the average individual, divided by 4 d (units are per day). The full range of growth rates expressed by our bioassay *Daphnia* is −0.10 (starvation) to 0.65 d\(^{-1}\). Statistical models We averaged all data collected in the same summer and lake to create a single value for chlorophyll \( a \), particulate carbon, and bioassay growth rate, per lake, per summer. These values constitute the lowest level of replication for comparison of lake categories. We used two different statistical models to compare phytoplankton-seston abundance and bioassay growth among the three categories of planktivory, using log\(_{10}\)-transformed seston and phosphorus values to satisfy the requirement of homogeneous variances. We first ran a nested ANOVA in which the three categories of planktivory were the top-level effect, lakes were nested within each category, and observations from different years were nested within each lake. We used restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML) in Proc Mixed (SAS 1999) to estimate variances and test for significance at each of the three sampling levels. Second, we ran an ANCOVA model, using total phosphorus in spring as a covariate, in order to compare categories of planktivory while controlling for productivity. To meet the assumption of equal slopes for the ANCOVA model, we restricted the range of lakes to those having <1 μmol/L total phosphorus (i.e., oligotrophic and mesotrophic lakes), which only meant removing 4 eutrophic observations (out of 46). We used repeated MANOVA (profile analysis) to compare size-fractionation of the chlorophyll \( a \) among the three categories of planktivory. Phytoplankton composition During the summer of 1998, we preserved phytoplankton from the pelagic zone (~0.5 m depth) of 11 lakes (5 deep-refuge, 3 shallow, and 3 high-planktivory) with acid Lugol’s solution, concentrated by settling, and counted abundance of each algae taxon. Taxonomic diversity was great, so to facilitate a comparison across levels of planktivory we lumped taxa into seven ecological groups based on morphology, taxonomy, and resistance to digestion. We then performed a multidimensional scaling of the correlation matrix for the 11 lake samples. The ordination was constrained to a single dimension to simplify visual comparison of categories of planktivory. RESULTS Chlorophyll \( a \) was tightly correlated with particulate carbon (<62 μm; \( r_p = 0.82, n = 43, P < 0.0001 \)), and both were correlated with total phosphorus (chlorophyll \( a \), \( r_p = 0.85, n = 43 \); particulate carbon, \( r_p = 0.63, n = 44 \); both \( P < 0.0001 \)). However, most variation in these parameters was distributed among lakes within the same level of planktivory (87% for chlorophyll \( a \) and 92% for particulate carbon). Differences among levels of planktivory were minor, explaining only 13% and 8% of the variation in chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate carbon, respectively. Moreover, ANCOVA (covariate = total phosphorus) revealed no difference among the three levels of planktivory for chlorophyll \( a \) (\( F = 0.97, \text{df} = 2, 34, P = 0.39 \)) or particulate carbon (\( F = 2.5, \text{df} = 2, 36, P = 0.09 \)). Hence, there was no evidence of a trophic cascade on phytoplankton biomass. In marked contrast, the bioassay growth rates revealed large differences among the three levels of planktivory (Fig. 2). Across the 6 yr of observations, 85% of the variation in *Daphnia* growth was explained by level of planktivory. The magnitude of this growth variation was dramatic; mean rates were 0.1453 ± 0.009 d\(^{-1}\) (mean ± 1 SE) for deep-refuge lakes, 0.343 Fig. 2. Values are based on single estimates for each lake, plotted separately for each year and level of planktivory. Additionally, controlling for variation in productivity did not change this pattern (ANCOVA: differences among the three planktivory categories using total phosphorus as a covariate, \( F = 93.4, \text{df} = 2, 36, P < 0.0001 \)). Hence, increasing fish planktivory resulted in richer food resources for grazers, as measured by growth rate, independent of lake productivity. Growth rate was only weakly associated with phytoplankton abundance (chlorophyll \( a \) or particulate carbon) or lake productivity (Fig. 3), except for a few eutrophic ponds having both high growth rates and high seston abundance. Over a range of productivity that encompassed oligotrophic and mesotrophic lakes, variation in grazer growth was only marginally correlated with chlorophyll \( a \) (\( r_p = 0.41, n = 38, P < 0.06 \)) and independent of particulate carbon (\( r_p = -0.21, n = 40, P = 0.69 \)). Further, concentrations of particulate carbon were typically >300 \( \mu \)g/L, which exceeds the satiation level for most grazers (Sterner and Schulz 1998), including the bioassay animals. Size fractionation of the chlorophyll \( a \) revealed no difference among the three categories of planktivory (Fig. 4). Small particles dominated; picoplankton (<3 \( \mu \)m) made up ~20% of the chlorophyll \( a \), 60% was <15 \( \mu \)m, and ~75% was <35 \( \mu \)m. Since neither biomass nor size of phytoplankton explained the higher growth rate of grazers with increased planktivory, we examined the composition of phytoplankton. A multidimensional scaling of samples from 11 of the lakes explained 94% of the variation in relative abundance of seven ecological groups of phytoplankton as a single axis that reflected a gradient in resistance of phytoplankton to grazing (Fig. 5). Digestion-resistant taxa (including numerous Chlorococcales distinguished by thick cell walls or gelatinous sheaths) were positively associated with this axis. In contrast, small flagellates and unicells were negatively correlated with this axis. Lakes sorted out along this axis on the basis of level of planktivory (ANOVA \( F = 25.4, \text{df} = 2, 8, P < 0.001 \)). Deep-refuge lakes had relatively low abundances of easily digested flagellates and unicells, but higher abundances of digestion-resistant forms. Fig. 3. Symbols and ellipses (means and 1 SD) indicate lakes of different levels of fish planktivory. DISCUSSION Based on differences in the strength of planktivory and the body size and biomass of grazers, we expected Fig. 4. Cumulative size-frequency distribution of chlorophyll \( a \) in lakes of different levels of fish planktivory. Values indicate means and among-lake SE for the proportion of total chlorophyll \( a \) smaller than various mesh sizes. Frequency profiles are not significantly different (\( F = 0.86, \) df = 2, 17, \( P = 0.44 \), size \( \times \) planktivory interaction Pillai Trace \( F = 0.54, \) df = 8, 30, \( P = 0.82 \)). to find more phytoplankton in the shallow and high-planktivory lakes than in the deep-refuge lakes. This was clearly not the case. However, a strong cascade effect on phytoplankton was apparent when measured in terms of growth rate of a representative grazer. The magnitude of this effect and its consistency across lakes and years is remarkable. Perhaps most surprising is that these large differences in grazer growth rates were fairly independent of phytoplankton biomass. Deep-refuge lakes varied in productivity (0.15–1.0 \( \mu \)mol/L total P) and in chlorophyll \( a \) and particulate carbon, but exhibited little variation in food resources for *Daphnia* across all six summers of observations. Typical concentrations of particulate carbon in these lakes were 300–700 \( \mu \)g/L, and three-fourths of that was able to pass a 35-\( \mu \)m screen. These concentrations of edible seston suggest that food quantity was not limiting to most grazers (Sterner and Schulz 1998). Grazers in our lakes were apparently limited by food quality. Our study demonstrates a positive link between the strength of top-down planktivory and the food quality of phytoplankton for grazers. We further show that this relationship between phytoplankton food quality and level of planktivory is associated with changes in the composition of the phytoplankton. When grouped ecologically on the basis of defenses against grazing, (size, cell wall thickness, gelatinous sheaths, etc.), the phytoplankton assemblages illustrate a gradient from well-defended forms that dominate in the deep-refuge lakes to highly vulnerable forms that dominate in the high-planktivory lakes. This compositional change in phytoplankton along a gradient of top-down planktivory suggests a reasonable explanation for the variation in growth rates observed in our *Daphnia* bioassays. We acknowledge that categorization of phytoplankton with respect to digestion resistance is somewhat subjective. However, we have conducted experiments in deep and shallow lakes to quantify phytoplankton vulnerability to a standard grazer and found large differences consistent with our interpretation of Fig. 5 (A. J. Tessier and E. V. Bizina, *unpublished data*). These findings indicate that while compensation within the grazer or phytoplankton assemblage may dissipate the magnitude of a trophic cascade on phytoplankton biomass, a functional effect on grazer growth rates is strong and persistent. Increased zoo-planktivory in shallower lakes eliminates the large-sized, effective grazers and allows the proliferation of less-defended phytoplankton species, resulting in higher resource quality for the remaining grazers. The pattern of a biomass cascade is not seen, but the process of cascading trophic interactions is revealed in the composition of the phytoplankton and the growth rates of the grazers. Explanations for why trophic biomass cascades are variable have focused on trophic heterogeneity and compensatory responses to top-down influences (Strong 1992, Leibold 1999). Some have argued that high diversity of plants and herbivores in terrestrial ecosystems limits wholesale cascades of trophic biomass compared to aquatic systems (Polis et al. 2000, Halaj and Wise 2001). Ecological diversity in predator defense and resource exploitation within a trophic level Fig. 5. Multidimensional scaling (MDS) of 11 lake samples based on composition of summer phytoplankton. Lengths of horizontal bars indicate Pearson correlations (vertical line = 0, scale between 1 and −1 on MDS axis) between the ordination axis and the abundance of each of the seven ecological groups of phytoplankton. Circles represent deep-refuge lakes, diamonds represent shallow lakes, and stars represent high-planktivory lakes. should dilute top-down influences but it is not apparent that such diversity will map directly on to taxonomic diversity or that aquatic systems harbor any less such diversity (Chase 2000). Further, compensation can occur at the level of individuals (Beckerman et al. 1997). For example, grazers in our deep lakes undergo diel vertical migration, which should restrict their foraging time on epilimnetic phytoplankton compared to grazers in shallow lakes. While we did not explicitly examine mechanisms of compensation, we did observe a systematic shift in the phytoplankton among the three lake types. Ecological diversity within phytoplankton is quite large; in particular, taxa greatly differ in vulnerability to grazers. There is strong evidence that traits that confer resistance to mortality from grazers (e.g., cell wall thickness) also decrease algal growth rates (Agrawal 1998). In the presence of large, effective grazers such as big Daphnia in deep-refuge lakes, selection for resistance to grazing seems a logical priority. But when planktivory is strong (i.e., shallow or small lakes) and the zooplankton are small in size and number, phytoplankton priorities may shift to competitive ability or rates of growth. Theoretical models that view phytoplankton assemblages as expressing a trade-off between grazer resistance and growth-competitive ability often predict that decreased mortality on the grazers (e.g., lower planktivory) should select for phytoplankton that are better defended against grazers (Grover 1995, Leibold 1996, Grover and Holt 1998). Changes in the species composition of phytoplankton along a gradient of grazer mortality could compensate for changes in grazing rate and result in little net change in phytoplankton biomass. However, from the perspective of a grazer, these models make the prediction that the food quality of the phytoplankton assemblage should increase with increased grazer mortality and that there might be little relationship between total phytoplankton abundance and grazer growth rate. Our bioassay growth approach provides a first test and confirmation of these theoretical predictions. Of course, it would be naïve to imagine that trophic cascade is the only mechanism contributing to compositional changes in phytoplankton across this large a lake size gradient. Obvious alternative mechanisms involve nutrient recycling. As basin size is decreased the opportunity for benthic-pelagic coupling is enhanced, resulting in faster recycling of nutrients. This may select for different forms of algae independent of top-down effects. Similarly, nutrient release by fish may also be higher in the high-planktivory lakes and so directly shape phytoplankton composition (Vanni and Findlay 1990). However, increased nutrient recycling alone cannot easily explain our results. In the absence of increased planktivory, grazer populations should increase in the shallow and high-planktivory lakes and ultimately select for better-defended algae. In fact, when we excluded fish from large enclosures in shallow and high-planktivory lakes, the grazers rapidly reduce phytoplankton abundance (A. J. Tessier and M. E. Matta, unpublished data). Still, we caution that experimental manipulation of planktivores and grazers across the lake size gradient is needed to quantify the relative significance of top-down planktivory vs. bottom-up productivity influences. In summary, we show that increased strength of fish planktivory in shallow and small lakes has a strong, indirect effect on phytoplankton as perceived by grazers. This cascade effect is hidden when measured in terms of biomass or size structure of phytoplankton, but is associated with shifts in composition of the phytoplankton. While trophic cascade is unlikely to be the only causal mechanism underlying shifts in phytoplankton composition along a gradient of lake size and depth, it is naturally confounded with other mechanisms, creating a general environmental gradient (Jeppesen et al. 1997, Moss et al. 1997). From a food web perspective, this suggests a major shift in the functional coupling of grazers and phytoplankton across this lake size/depth gradient. From an evolutionary perspective, grazers should perceive this as a correlated selection gradient of food quality and planktivory risk. We suspect that evidence of joint top-down; bottom-up selection will be found in the life histories of the grazers that exist along this gradient. Consequently, the zooplankton of these “deep-refuge” lakes is dominated by large-bodied Daphnia species that vertically migrate to feed on phytoplankton in the surface waters at night, but refuge in deep waters during the day to avoid fish. Centrarchids are the dominant fish in this and the next category of lake; bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus) and pumpkinseed (L. gibbosus) sunfish are the main planktivores, and largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) is the major piscivore (Werner et al. 1977). Lakes in our second category have large surface area relative to their depth and do not thermally stratify in summer. These “shallow” lakes have no refuge for zooplankton to avoid daytime planktivory, so zooplankton suffer a greater risk of predation than in the deep lakes (Tessier et al. 1992, Leibold and Tessier 1998). While not measured in our lakes, biomass of fish (per cubic meter) is generally known to be greater in shallow than in deep lakes (Jeppesen et al. 1997). Consequently, the zooplankton of shallow lakes is composed of a lower biomass of smaller-sized taxa than the big Daphnia of deep lakes (Fig. 1). Lakes in our last category are both shallow and small in water volume. Low oxygen under the ice in winter is a recurring stress in these lakes and results in partial winterkills (Greenbank 1945), to which largemouth bass is particularly sensitive (Moore 1942). Hence, lakes in this category lack strong piscivory, and the fish community is composed of high densities of efficient planktivores (Tonn and Magnuson 1982). Reflecting this “high planktivory,” the grazer assemblage is dominated by the smallest of cladocerans and copepods, and rotifers dominate the zooplankton in these lakes (Hall and Ellinger 1989, Mittelbach et al. 1995; Fig. 1). Hence, the three categories of lakes represent a gradient of intensity of fish planktivory; lowest in the deep-refuge lakes, intermediate in the shallow lakes, and highest in the partial winterkill lakes. We examined seven deep-refuge lakes, six shallow lakes, and six high-planktivory lakes over a period of 6 yr (Table 1). Most lakes were sampled in multiple years (>2 yr per lake) and on multiple dates throughout the summer (June–September). We also sampled each lake during the spring turnover and collected pelagic water for determination of total phosphorus. Daphnia diversity in water bodies of the Po River Basin Silvia MARKOVÁ,1 Catia MAURONE,2 Erica RACCHETTI,2 Marco BARTOLI,2 Valeria ROSSI2* 1Laboratory of Molecular Ecology, Institute of Animal Physiology and Genetics, Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic, Rumburská 89, 27721 Liběchov, Czech Republic; 2Department of Life Sciences, University of Parma, Viale Usberti 11/A, 43124 Parma, Italy *Corresponding author: valeria.rossi@unipr.it ABSTRACT Shallow water bodies dominate the areal extent of continental waters and host a proportion of biodiversity higher than the percentage of Earth’s surface they cover. Daphnia is a key component of small aquatic ecosystems food webs. Here we present the result of a survey in 24 ponds located in the core of Po river Basin, to assess the actual spreading of Daphnia species in one of the most productive areas of the Northern hemisphere. By using diagnostic genetic markers (12S rRNA and ND5 genes) we identified five Daphnia species: D. ambigua, D. curvirostris, D. longispina, D. obtusa and D. pulex in fourteen ponds. Additional analyses of two nuclear genes (LdhA and Rab4) revealed that D. pulex in the study area is native European strain. In opposite, D. ambigua shared haplotype with the North-Eastern American lineage that was introduced to Europe by long-distance dispersal. In the Po river Basin we identified a highly divergent lineage of D. longispina group that formed a clade with individuals from northern European Russia and might represent a new Daphnia species. Daphnia species in the Cremona province have European origin, except for D. ambigua which is a North American species spreading across Europe. Future attention will require monitoring of invasive species, particularly D. ambigua and the North American invasive clone of D. pulex that is already present in Northern Italy. Key words: Genetic diagnostic markers; invasive species; genetic differentiation; D. pulex complex; ponds. Received: June 2016. Accepted: November 2016. INTRODUCTION Although freshwater ecosystems cover less than 1% of the earth’s surface, they host almost 10% of the world’s species that are directly supported through a wide range of habitats including running water in rivers, standing waters of lakes, ponds, pools and swamps and areas of ephemeral wetlands (Loh and Wackernagel, 2004; Feld et al., 2016). In recent years much attention has been paid to large lakes and rivers while small lakes and ponds that dominate the areal extent of continental waters have been completely ignored (Downing, 2010). However, small aquatic ecosystems play a major role in global cycles and in the Earth’s most pressing environmental problems (Downing, 2010). In addition, permanent or temporary small, shallow water bodies offer a powerful potential for studies of ecology, evolutionary and conservation biology and provide high contribution to regional biodiversity (De Meester et al., 2005). The organisms that colonise ponds and pools have evolved specific adaptations to deal with often extreme, disturbed, short hydro-period habitats, such as very effective spatial and temporal dispersal mechanisms (Ripley and Simovich, 2009). Furthermore, shallow water bodies are highly sensitive to climate warming and human activities due to substantial changes in thermal and hydrological regimes that play important role in freshwater biodiversity decline (Scheffer et al., 2001; Dudgeon et al., 2006; Mitchell et al., 2005; Meerhoff et al., 2007; Feuchtmayr et al., 2009; Landkildehus et al., 2014). In Europe, up to 80% of the land is intensively used for settlements, infrastructure and production systems and aquatic biodiversity is probably impoverished accordingly (Feld et al., 2016). Many of the cladoceran taxa recognized by traditional taxonomists are actually an admixture of genetically divergent species (Hebert and Wilson, 1994; Schwenk et al., 2000). Now, the application of molecular tools is fundamental for the identification of new and cryptic species, for tracing distribution and dispersal of native and invasive species as well as for identification of hybrid taxa and their relatives (Pfenning and Schwenk, 2007). Furthering the study of freshwater zooplankton biodiversity by using techniques of molecular biology might help to reveal genetic diversity within and among species that could be otherwise hardly uncovered. Cladocera, small aquatic crustaceans, are a key component of aquatic food webs. They inhabit a range of freshwater habitats throughout the world. Some genera, such as Daphnia, have been intensively studied over the past 250 years in different fields. Recently, the growing impact of climate change on inhabitants of the most vulnerable freshwater habitats, such small lakes and ponds, is undoubtedly starting to be appreciated. Climate change is forcing Daphnia species to adjust their ways and may cause adverse effects on species diversity by means of elimination and/or replacement of sensitive species/strains by less sensitive ones, shifts in food-web interactions, acclimation of species/strains to stress, selection of tolerant genotypes, and outcome of predator–prey interactions (Belfiore and Anderson, 2001; Hunter and Pyle, 2004; Sakamoto et al., 2006; Riessen et al., 2012; Vadadi-Fülöp et al., 2012; Vadadi-Fülöp and Hufnagel, 2014). Additionally, environmental change creates ecological space for non-native species that can often replace native species. Recent invasion of the American Daphnia lineage to Africa was followed by rapid and complete continent-wide displacement of indigenous African D. pulex Leydig, 1860 throughout its native range (Mergeay et al., 2006) and was already recorded in Sardinia and Piedmont (Northern Italy) (Fadda et al., 2011; Marková et al., 2013). In a previous paper, we reported the occurrence of the D. pulex group in the permanent pond named bodrio del Pastore III, in the Po River Basin (Northern Italy) where it co-exists with D. longispina O. F. Müller, 1776 (Rossi et al., 2014). The presence of D. pulex in this area is important in the framework of conservation ecology. In fact, we have shown that it is the native European species instead of the invasive North American asexual clone (Rossi et al., 2015). Here we extend our research to 24 surrounding water bodies located in the Po river basin in the Cremona province that is one of the most productive areas of the Northern hemisphere (Bassanino et al., 2011). Because of intensive farming, this area is threatened by diffuse pollution that, together with climatic changes, is a major driver of changes in freshwater ecosystems of Cremona province. Our main objectives are: 1) to assess the actual spreading and genetic diversity of native D. pulex and other Daphnia species in the area; 2) to verify morphological identification of different Daphnia species by using diagnostic mitochondrial gene (12S rRNA); and 3) to assess species identity and origin of Daphnia belonging to the D. pulex complex based on mitochondrial (the ND5 gene) and nuclear phylogenies (Rab4 and LdhA genes). METHODS The study place is located in the Cremona province where temporary pools and ponds, locally named bodri, originated by dramatic flooding events of the Po River (the largest Italian river with an annual mean discharge of 1500 m³ s⁻¹) (Fig. 1). Erosive processes dig cone-shaped holes with depths up to 6-10 m and surface of some hundreds to some thousands m². At the end of flooding periods, these small ponds remain isolated from the main river course and start evolving as newly formed shallow aquatic environments. They display pronounced water level fluctuations, associated to the Po river hydrometric level, aquifer, pre- ![Geographic location of the 24 sampling sites included in this study.](page_104_1347_1732_670.png) Fig. 1. Geographic location of the 24 sampling sites included in this study. cipitations, runoff, groundwater vertical migration and summer evaporation. In 450 km² area, 61 water bodies were documented (AAVV, 1999). In this study, we focused on the occurrence of Daphnia species in 24 pools and ponds that were randomly selected in 200 km² area (Fig. 1). Many of the studied water bodies originated before 1723 [date of the first census of bodri (AAVV, 1999)]; however, some are more recent (for details see Tab. 1). Most of the time ponds and pools are separated from each other without possibility of seasonal stream connections, but some accidental link may occur during heavy flooding. Their size varied between 1529 to 7070 m²; twelve of the 24 ponds contained fish and/or Chaoborus larvae [for details see Tab. 1; (AAVV, 1999)]. Each pond was sampled twice: first time between May and June 2014 and second time between June and July 2015. Qualitative zooplankton samples were collected by 105 µm-mesh size plankton net. From 2 to 16 l of water were filtered for each sample according to the water volume and depth. All samples were preserved in 95% ethanol. All cladocerans present in the sample were sorted under a stereomicroscope and were identified to genus level. Then, all Daphnia species were morphologically identified according to Margaritora (1985). A contingency table analysis was performed to test whether the presence of Daphnia was negatively associated with the presence of fish or Chaoborus larvae (Tab. 1). The frequency of samples with and without Daphnia was compared in relationship with the presence or the absence of predators. To verify morphological identification of Daphnia species, one to 11 collected specimens per each locality were used in molecular analyses according to the number of species per site. In the locality where species replacement was recorded, Pastore III (Rossi et al., 2015), up to 5 individuals per species were analysed. To verify Daphnia species identity, 12S rRNA diagnostic marker was used. Because determining the species within the D. pulex complex based only on morphological characters is notoriously difficult (Colbourne et al., 1998) and 12S rRNA gene is not a diagnostic marker for lineages within this complex, D. pulex complex, species from Po river Basin were analysed for an ~711 base-pair (bp) long fragment Tab. 1. To assess the hybrid origin of specimens from D. pulex complex, we used two nuclear protein-coding loci: Rab4 (subunit gene of the GTPase family) and LdhA (lactate dehydrogenase A). Total genomic DNA was extracted from Daphnia stored in 95% ethanol using the QIAGEN DNeasy Tissue Kit (Valencia, CA). Parts of two mitochondrial genes, 12S rRNA and ND5, were amplified and sequenced with published primers in accordance with the PCR conditions described by Taylor et al. (1996) and Dufresne et al. (2011), respectively. The entire LdhA gene and a part of the gene coding the small GTPase Rab4 were amplified and sequenced according to Marková et al. (2013) and Omilian et al. (2008), respectively. All nucleotide sequence data from the present study have been deposited in the GenBank database under accession numbers KY196420 - KY196435 (12S rRNA), KY196436 - KY196439 (Rab4) and KY196440 (LdhA). Altogether, we analysed 54 individuals from fourteen localities in the Po river Basin for mitochondrial 12S rRNA phylogeny and an additional 63 sequences from GenBank (Supplementary Tab. 1) were used to provide wider phylogenetic framework for our study. After we identified the specimens as D. pulex mtDNA type on the basis of 12S rRNA phylogeny, we directly amplified and sequenced mitochondrial ND5 gene of 14 individuals from 3 populations. Additionally, we analysed the sequences of two nuclear genes (the Rab4; the LdhA) of eight individuals from three populations possessing D. pulex mtDNA. The 12S rRNA sequences were used to estimate the nucleotide diversity Pi (Nei, 1987; Nei and Miller, 1990) within Daphnia groups (Tab. 2) by using DnaSP software (Librado and Rozas, 2009). Phylogenetic analyses using maximum-likelihood (ML) criterion were performed in MEGA software version 6 (Tamura et al., 2013). Firstly, we reconstructed mitochondrial phylogenies of 12S rRNA and ND5 by employing T92+G+I (Tamura 92) and HKY+I (Hasegawa et al., 1985) substitution models selected according to the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), respectively. Then we applied ML criterion to reconstruct nuclear phylogeny of Rab4 and LdhA by using T92 and T92 with gamma distribution substitution models, respectively. Bootstrap support estimated from 1000 replicates using NNI (nearest neighbour interchange) branch swapping algorithm was applied in all phylogenetic analyses. RESULTS Altogether, we identified five Daphnia species in fourteen of 24 analysed pools and ponds (Tab. 3). In 10 sites, no water fleas belonging to the genus Daphnia were found. Among 54 analysed individuals, D. ambigua Scourfield, 1947, D. curvirostris Eylmann, 1887, D. longispina, D. obtusa Kurz, 1874 and D. pulex were determined (Tab. 3). The most frequent species, D. curvirostris and D. longispina, were found in six and five ponds, respectively. In contrast, D. ambigua was identified only in one pond (Pastore IV) while D. obtusa and D. pulex were detected in three ponds (Tab. 3). Three Daphnia species (D. longispina, D. curvirostris and D. obtusa) were identified in the pond Sabbie. Additionally, coexistence of D. pulex with D. longispina was found in three ponds (Pastore I, Pastore III and Bosco Valloni) and coexistence of D. curvirostris with D. obtusa in the pond Bosco Valloni (Tab. 3). The D. longispina group was the most genetically variable group in the sampling area where we identified five unique 12S rRNA haplotypes (DLONG A, B, C, D and E; Fig. 2 and Tab. 3). Nucleotide diversity of D. longispina from Cremona area was 0.02077 (Tab. 2). However, once we excluded the most divergent haplotype within this group (DLONG E), nucleotide diversity decreased to 0.00205. To reveal the phylogenetic origin of this haplotype, we included into the phylogenetic analyses also sequences of several divergent lineages of the D. longispina complex (Ishida et al., 2011; Petrusek et al., 2012; for details see Supplementary Tab. 1). Interestingly, the haplotype DLONG E clustered together with two individuals from the Pechora delta (northern European Russia) and formed the clade V of D. longispina complex (named by Petrusek et al., 2012). Altogether, four 12S rRNA haplotypes of D. curvirostris group were identified in the study area (DCUR A, B, C and D; Fig. 2 and Tab. 3). Interestingly, in the temporary pond located close to the pond Pastore III, different 12S rRNA haplotypes were found in 2014 and 2015. In 2015, the dominant haplotype DCUR C was replaced there by a new haplotype DCUR D. This is the sole case of shift in genetic variability between years within D. curvirostris group. In ponds Bosco Valloni and Sabbie, where D. curvirostris co-exists with D. obtusa and with D. longispina and D. obtusa, respectively, only the most common haplotype DCUR C was identified. Even though the nucleotide diversity of D. curvirostris from the study area was low (0.00180), overall nucleotide diversity of D. curvirostris group was just a little bit higher (0.00228; Tab. 3). D. obtusa inhabited four ponds in the study area and within the D. obtusa group three 12S rRNA haplotypes were identified (DOBT A, B, and C; Fig. 2 and Tab. 3). The nucleotide diversity of D. obtusa from the study area was the lowest one (0.00104) within all analysed Daphnia groups, while total nucleotide diversity of the D. obtusa group was relatively high (0.04651; Tab. 2). The pond Pastore IV was the only locality in the study area where we found D. ambigua in two years sampling period (2014 and 2015). The D. ambigua we identified shared 12S rRNA haplotype (DAMB A) with individuals from France and USA (Fig. 2). D. pulex was found in three ponds (Pastore III, Pastore I and Forche) during our sampling in 2014 and 2015 (Tab. 3). Altogether 12 individuals were analysed and genetically determined as European D. pulex (Fig. 2, Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2). All individuals carried unique haplotype (DPX A) at both mitochondrial genes (12S rRNA and ND5) and clustered into the European D. pulex clade. Additional analyses of two nuclear genes (LdhA and Rab4) revealed that D. pulex from the study area carried only European D. pulex haplotypes at both analysed nuclear markers (Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2). DISCUSSION In this study, we have sampled 24 pools and ponds that covered 200 km\(^2\) area of the Po river Basin in Cremona province. By using diagnostic genetic markers, we assessed ![Maximum likelihood mitochondrial phylogeny based on ND5 haplotypes. Numbers along branches indicate the percent bootstrap frequencies for bipartitions with greater than 70% support.](page_420_1042_1042_1042.png) Fig. 2. Maximum likelihood mitochondrial phylogeny based on ND5 haplotypes. Numbers along branches indicate the percent bootstrap frequencies for bipartitions with greater than 70% support. the presence of five Daphnia species (D. ambigua, D. curvirostris, D. longispina, D. obtusa and D. pulex) in a relatively small area of the Po river Basin intensively devoted to agricultural activities and vulnerable to diffuse pollution. We discuss these results in wider phylogenetic context. In the 70’s, D. pulex was identified in the Po river Basin (Caorso and Ozzano dell’Emilia, about 50 km west and 100 km east from our study area, respectively) by Margaritora (personal communication), however no information about its origins was reported. Firstly, we recorded D. pulex in the pond Pastore III in 2011 (Rossi et al., 2014) and later we extended our sampling and focused on phylogenetic origin of those Daphnia species that could pose a threat for local populations. A well-known invasive asexual clone of D. pulex has spread from North America and replaced the native one throughout Africa, Spain (Mergeay et al., 2006) and recently has been also recorded in Sardinian reservoir (Sardinia Island; Fadda et al., 2011) and in Avigliana Lake (Piedmont Region, Northern Italy; Vergilino et al., 2011; Crease et al., 2012; Marková et al., 2013) that is only about 200 km west from our study area. Because of that, the chance that this highly invasive clone could be present also in the Po river Basin was high. Phylogenetic analyses of several individuals from the Po river Basin, morphologically determined as D. pulex, revealed that D. pulex from the study area is true European D. pulex (Fig. 3; Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2). While mitochondrial haplotypes of 12S rRNA and ND5 genes were carried only by individuals from the Po river Basin, nuclear LdhA and Rab4 haplotypes were shared also by D. pulex from the Czech Republic, Sweden, Germany, Lithuania and United Kingdom with exception of two unique Rab4 haplotypes for the Po river Basin (DPX B and C; Supplementary Fig. 2). Even though the low genetic variability was identified at most of the analysed loci, the presence of adult males, ephippial females and free ephippia indicate that the population of D. pulex from the Po river Basin reproduce by cyclical parthenogenesis, and so clearly differ also by reproductive strategy from invasive asexual clone inhabited Sardinian reservoirs and Lake Avigliana (Rossi et al., 2014). Additional analyses of tens of D. pulex from the study area could reveal some genetic diversity also at the mitochondrial genes. D. ambigua was the only invasive Daphnia species in the Po river Basin, and belongs to the North-Eastern American strain that was introduced by long-distance dispersal and is spreading across Europe (Hebert et al., 2003). We determined D. ambigua only in one of 24 studied ponds (Pastore IV) which is located in the core of our sampling area. However, this Daphnia species is very successful in spreading because of small body size, which makes it pre-adapted to eutrophied ponds that are over-stocked with fish (De Meester et al., 2002). In Belgium (Lake Donk, Eastern Flanders), D. ambigua was recorded for the first time in the 60’s by Dumont (1974). By 2002 it was already widespread in Flanders (De Meester et al., 2002). Even though D. ambigua was recorded in England (Johnson, 1952), France (Amoros, 1980), Germany (Krause-Dellin, 1992; Maier and Buchholz, 1996) and Czech Republic (Hamrová and Černý, 2007), the only available European 12S rRNA sequences in GenBank database are from France (Schwenk et al., 2000; Hebert et al., 2003). We showed that D. ambigua haplotype from the Po river Basin (DAMB A) is identical with haplotypes from France (AF277283, AF523738) and New York (USA; AF523735; Fig. 3). The rapid colonization of Europe by D. ambigua and the occupancy of large blocks of territory by a single haplotype support little genetic diversity in the early phases after colonization of a new continent (De Meester et al., 2002). Our record of invasive D. ambigua supports well known high dispersal capacity of freshwater cladocerans inhabiting island-like aquatic habitats (Slusarczyk and Pietrzak, 2008). In fact, D. ambigua has been already recorded in Northern Italy (Margaritora, 1985; Manca et al., 2005) and in Sicily (Marrone et al., 2005) but no information about its origin was reported. Manca et al. (2005) recorded D. ambigua only in the Lago di Mantova superiore that is less than 50 km east from our study area. D. ambigua from Lago di Endine (Northern Italy) was not cyclomorphic and showed some morphological characters that differentiated it from other European populations (Margaritora, 1985). D. ambigua from the pond Pastore IV seems cyclomorphic, showing a small pointed helmet, and does not have the ocello (Rossi; personal observation). Dispersal potential of D. ambigua is enormous and will require monitoring, because this small invasive species could pose a threat to native Daphnia populations in the Po river Basin where eutrophication and fish presence made local water bodies suitable for it. In the Po river Basin, we found a high genetic diversity within the D. longispina complex (five haplotypes with Pi 0.02077). Between 2011 and 2014, D. pulex dominated in the pond Pastore III while in 2015 it was partly replaced by D. longispina (Rossi et al., 2015; Rossi et al., in preparation). Due to high population fluctuation and spatial/temporal dispersal by resting eggs, D. longispina could have colonized the pond Pastore III from surrounding ponds. An alternative scenario is that D. longispina have been present in the pond Pastore III already before, but in low hardly detectable density and/or in ephippial eggs bank, or could colonized this pond recently by long distance dispersal from other sources (e.g. some introductions by huntsmen, by fishers, by vehicles, by migrant birds). Interestingly the haplotype DLONG E, carried by Daphnia from the pond Bosco Piazza, clustered into the highly divergent clade V of D. longispina complex (named by Petrusek et al., 2012) together with two individuals from Pechora Delta (northern European Russia). However, 12S rRNA haplo- types (JX069356, JX069357) carried by individuals from Pechora Delta are distinct from the Po river Basin one (nucleotide diversity 0.02874) that negotiates a scenario of recent invasion. Instead of that, our phylogenetic data suggested that the clade V of D. longispina complex is not restricted only to northern European Russia but has a much wider area of distribution. Daphnia from the pond Bosco Piazza (DLONG E, Fig. 3) likely represents a distinct biological species. Because this putative new species co-exists in the pond Bosco Piazza with D. longispina, sequencing of additional marker(s) with focus on hybridization will be required. An additional two Daphnia species (D. curvirostris and D. obtusa) with low nucleotide diversity (0.00180 and ![Maximum likelihood mitochondrial phylogeny based on 12S rRNA haplotypes.](page_1012_1042_1012_1012.png) Fig. 3. Maximum likelihood mitochondrial phylogeny based on 12S rRNA haplotypes. Numbers along branches indicate the percent bootstrap frequencies for bipartitions with greater than 70% support. 0.00104) inhabited six and four ponds in the study area, respectively. Generally, low genetic variability within whole D. curvirostris group (nucleotide diversity 0.00228) containing D. curvirostris from Europe (JN903648, JN903649) and from Canada (FJ427415, AF277280; Fig. 3) was detected. The D. obtusa clade involved two groups, one formed by D. obtusa from Europe including study area and the other by D. obtusa from North America. Phylogenetic analyses showed that both Daphnia species from the Po river Basin have European origin. The finding of five Daphnia species in a relatively small area (20,000 ha) of the Po river Basin is in accordance with previous studies at the regional scale and from different parts of Europe. The analysis of Cladocera community including 29 lakes in the Po River watershed during the period 1998-1999 revealed the presence of five Daphnia species (D. longispina, D. ambigua, D. hyalina, D. galeata and D. cucullata) and four relative hybrids (Manca et al., 2005). Between November 1987 and May 1989, during a study focused on distribution and genetic variability of D. obtusa, in 97 ponds and pools sampled in the Po river catchment (Parma province), Bachiorri found four Daphnia species (D. obtusa, D. longispina, D. ambigua and D. hyalina) in 18 sampling sites (Bachiorri et al., 1991 and unpublished data). In 25 temporary ponds located in a wetland zone spread over an area of 180,000 ha in Doñana (South-west Spain) 3 species of Daphnia (D. longispina, D. magna and D. pulex) were found (Frish et al., 2006). In 33 interconnected shallow ponds in a small area (200 ha) in Belgium, 3 species, D. pulex, D. ambigua and D. galeata were recorded (Cottenie et al., 2001). CONCLUSIONS Here we identified phylogenetic origin of five Daphnia species from Cremona province and showed that four of them are native European species. Until now, only the D. ambigua invasive species in the Po River Basin was found. In addition, we identified, within the D. longispina complex, a highly divergent haplotype that clustered together with individuals from northern European Russia and might represent a distinct biological species. This finding has important implication for biodiversity conservation in agricultural areas. Future attention will require monitoring of the dispersal of North American D. pulex which presents a high risk for natural populations in the Po River Basin. In this study, we focused on the occurrence of Daphnia species in 24 pools and ponds that were randomly selected in 200 km² area (Fig. 1). Many of the studied water bodies originated before 1723 [date of the first census of bodri (AAVV, 1999)]; however, some are more recent (for details see Tab. 1). Most of the time ponds and pools are separated from each other without possibility of seasonal stream connections, but some accidental link may occur during heavy flooding. Their size varied between 1529 to 7070 m²; twelve of the 24 ponds contained fish and/or Chaoborus larvae [for details see Tab. 1; (AAVV, 1999)]. Each pond was sampled twice: first time between May and June 2014 and second time between June and July 2015. Qualitative zooplankton samples were collected by 105 µm-mesh size plankton net. From 2 to 16 l of water were filtered for each sample according to the water volume and depth. All samples were preserved in 95% ethanol. All cladocerans present in the sample were sorted under a stereomicroscope and were identified to genus level. Then, all Daphnia species were morphologically identified according to Margaritora (1985). A contingency table analysis was performed to test whether the presence of Daphnia was negatively associated with the presence of fish or Chaoborus larvae (Tab. 1). The frequency of samples with and without Daphnia was compared in relationship with the presence or the absence of predators. To verify morphological identification of Daphnia species, one to 11 collected specimens per each locality were used in molecular analyses according to the number of species per site. In the locality where species replacement was recorded, Pastore III (Rossi et al., 2015), up to 5 individuals per species were analysed. To verify Daphnia species identity, 12S rRNA diagnostic marker was used. Because determining the species within the D. pulex complex based only on morphological characters is notoriously difficult (Colbourne et al., 1998) and 12S rRNA gene is not a diagnostic marker for lineages within this complex, D. pulex complex, species from Po river Basin were analysed for an ~711 base-pair (bp) long fragment Tab. 1. Dry habitats sustain high CO\(_2\) emissions from temporary ponds across seasons Biel Obrador\(^1\), Daniel von Schiller\(^2,3\), Rafael Marcé\(^2\), Lluís Gómez-Gener\(^1,4\), Matthias Koschorreck\(^5\), Carles Borrego\(^2,6\) & Núria Catalán\(^1,2,7\) Despite the increasing understanding of the magnitude and drivers of carbon gas emissions from inland waters, the relevance of water fluctuation and associated drying on their dynamics is rarely addressed. Here, we quantified CO\(_2\) and CH\(_4\) fluxes from a set of temporary ponds across seasons. The ponds were in all occasion net CO\(_2\) emitters irrespective of the presence or absence of water. While the CO\(_2\) fluxes were in the upper range of emissions for freshwater lentic systems, CH\(_4\) fluxes were mostly undetectable. Dry habitats substantially contributed to these emissions and were always a source of CO\(_2\), whereas inundated habitats acted either as a source or a sink of atmospheric CO\(_2\) along the year. Higher concentrations of coloured and humic organic matter in water and sediment were linked to higher CO\(_2\) emissions. Composition of the sediment microbial community was related both to dissolved organic matter concentration and composition, but we did not find a direct link with CO\(_2\) fluxes. The presence of methanogenic archaea in most ponds suggested the potential for episodic CH\(_4\) production and emission. Our results highlight the need for spatially and temporally inclusive approaches that consider the dry phases and habitats to characterize carbon cycling in temporary systems. Inland waters are an important component of the global carbon (C) cycle\(^1\). They intensely bury C in their sediments and emit high amounts of gaseous C species to the atmosphere, mostly as a result of the input and subsequent biological processing of terrestrial organic matter\(^2\). A myriad of local and regional studies in the last two decades have aimed at quantifying carbon dioxide (CO\(_2\)) and methane (CH\(_4\)) emissions from streams, rivers, lakes and reservoirs, allowing for increasingly accurate global estimates\(^3-10\). We have gained a better understanding of the processes determining C emissions across wide environmental and geographical gradients\(^5-9\) but uncertainties regarding the variability and controls of such fluxes in some ecosystems still remain. In particular, C processing in temporary systems that recurrently run dry, a natural hydrological feature of many watersheds in the world, has received little attention\(^11\). As an example, current global estimates do not consider C emissions from temporary rivers when they are dry\(^11\). Small temporary lentic systems are one example of an understudied ecosystem in terms of C biogeochemistry. Small systems in general (i.e. ponds, small lakes and impoundments) are deemed as potential hotspots of C cycling\(^12,13\) and host high emission rates at different latitudes\(^10,14-18\). The intense rates of C processing in small systems along with their global abundance\(^19,20\) (77% of lentic systems have a surface area between 0.002 and 0.01 km\(^2\)) suggest the potentially major role of small lakes and ponds at the global scale\(^10,13\) and an increasing relevance of their C emissions due to their high sensitivity to warming\(^21\). Temporary ponds are small inland water bodies that experience a recurrent dry phase of varying duration, which can imply complete or partial drying\(^22\). The few existing studies on C processing in temporary ponds show their relevance as C emitters17,25,26. However, their emissions have seldom been measured directly17, for CO2 concentration has been used to indirectly estimate gas fluxes in most cases. Moreover, the approaches used to date have been restricted to the aquatic phase, so dry habitats within ponds or temporal phases without any water at all have not been considered10,25,26,31. In contrast, a recent study on Mediterranean temporary ponds has shown the relevance of CO2 emissions from their dry habitats during the flooding phase17. These results agree with recent works reporting high CO2 emissions from the dry areas of temporary rivers and reservoirs27–30. The paucity of data on C emissions from temporary ponds is paired with a poor understanding of the environmental drivers that shape them. Catalán et al.17, showed that spatially integrated CO2 emissions during the flooding phase of Mediterranean temporary ponds were not related to the properties of the catchment, but rather to the intrinsic properties of the pond such as the amount of organic matter present in water and sediments. In contrast, Holgerson31 found that variables related to the processing of terrestrial organic matter largely explained dissolved CO2 and CH4 dynamics in the water of temporary ponds in temperate forested areas, pinpointing the need for a better understanding of CO2 and CH4 regulation in ponds. Here, we quantified CO2 and CH4 fluxes in Mediterranean temporary ponds along the different phases of their hydrological cycle. We selected ten temporary ponds located on the island of Menorca (Western Mediterranean) covering a wide range of physicochemical, geomorphologic and hydrological properties (Table 1). To characterize contrasting situations along their hydrological cycle, we sampled the ponds in autumn (the flooding phase); in spring when the ponds are mostly full (the wet phase); and in summer, when the ponds were entirely dry (the dry phase). Moreover, to capture all variability across and within ponds, we sampled the three habitats present in the ponds: dry habitats, comprising 1) emerged-vegetated sediments (non-inundated areas with presence of vascular plants), and 2) emerged-bare sediments (non-inundated areas with bare sediments); and 3) inundated habitats (areas with a water layer; see Table S1 for habitat areas). We performed direct measurements of gas fluxes in all these habitats separately and integrated them to estimate total fluxes for each pond. We hypothesized that fluxes would be comparable or higher to those in other lentic ecosystems and highest during the dry phase of the hydrological cycle due to large contributions from dry habitats. We also identified the main drivers of the variability in the fluxes by evaluating the roles of a wide set of geomorphological, physicochemical and biological variables such as water and sediment organic matter quantity and composition and microbial community composition in the ponds studied. Results Magnitude and variability of CO2 and CH4 fluxes. The ponds were net emitters of CO2 to the atmosphere irrespective of the hydrological phase, with a mean total flux (i.e. spatially integrated flux including all habitats, T-FCO2) of 107.8 ± 103.9 mmol m−2 d−1 (±standard deviation; n = 30; Table 2; Fig. 1). We observed small negative T-FCO2 only on one occasion (Table 2). There was high variability in T-FCO2 between ponds and between phases (range 15.7 to 492.5 mmol m−2 d−1). The maximum T-FCO2 was measured during the dry phase (Table 2; Fig. 1), although we did not observe any significant seasonal pattern in T-FCO2 along the hydrological cycle (ANOVA between phases, F = 0.34, p > 0.05; Fig. 1). In contrast, CH4 fluxes were of minor importance and only detectable on a few occasions in dystrophic systems (Tables 1 and 2; detection limit estimated to be 0.04 mmol m−2 d−1). The different habitats of the ponds (inundated, emerged-vegetated and emerged-bare) were all active in terms of CO2 fluxes (Fig. 2). Concentration and composition of organic matter was determined in the different habitats to identify the drivers of the CO2 fluxes. Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentration in the water column ranged from 3 to 36.6 mg L−1, with high variability between ponds (Fig. 3b). Dissolved organic matter (DOM) composition was assessed by optical spectroscopy. A Parallel Factor Analysis (PARAFAC) modelling of the excitation emission matrices of 99 samples revealed 4 independent components, (C1 – C4; see Supplementary Information S2). Components C1 (Ex: 250 (340), Em: 450) and C3 (Ex: <250 Em: 510) represent humic-like ubiquitous components related to terrestrial sources. Component C2 (Ex: 250 (300), Em: 400) is associated with humic materials having suffered some degree of microbial processing32. Finally, component C4 (Ex 280, Em: 340) presents protein-like characteristics similar to tryptophan33. A PLS regression model describing the response of T-FCO2 (i.e. spatially integrated flux; Fig. 4a; Table S3.1) extracted two significant components that explained 92% of variance (R2Y = 0.92) with high model predictability (Q2cum = 0.64). The T-FCO2 flux (Y-variable) was predicted by the amount and composition of organic matter across the different habitats (Fig. 4a). Specifically, the humic-like component C2 in the inundated sediment was the most important predictor, followed by organic matter concentrations in the inundated and emerged sediments, and, with slightly lower influence, DOC in water (Table S3.1). Other important predictors were total nitrogen and alkalinity (in the water column when present), temperature and humidity (in the emerged sediments), and the protein-like component C4 (in the inundated sediments), negatively correlated with FCO2. It was impossible to fit a PLS model to explain FCO2 in the dry habitats. The PLS model for FCO2 from inundated habitats (i.e. flux from water, W-FCO2; Fig. 4b; Table S3.2) extracted two significant components explaining 86% of variance (R2Y = 0.87) and presented high predictability power (Q2cum = 0.67). W-FCO2 was related to descriptors of DOC composition, such as the humification index (HIX), the PARAFAC components, and the spectral slope (SR). Autochthonous or microbial-like DOM descriptors such as the biological index (BIX), C4 or SR as well as oxygen concentration were well correlated with each other and negatively correlated with W-FCO2. Indicators of humic-like materials such as HIX or component C1 appeared to be associated with DOC concentrations and were positively related with W-FCO2. Accordingly, systems with higher DOC concentrations presented also higher contribution to DOM composition of humic-like components C1 and C3 and, in most cases, these humic-like compounds were lower in the flooding than the wet phase (Fig. 3b and c). In contrast, the relative contribution of components related to biological activity, C2 and C4, was higher in systems with lower DOC concentrations. In most cases this corresponded to negative W-FCO2 during the flooded phase.
