Inter-pond differences explained an additional 12% to 52% of the variation, highlighting the importance of differences in \( k_{600} \) among ponds. 3.4. Comparison Across Lake Sizes Across the 67 ponds and lakes where \( k_{600} \) was directly measured (Data Set S2), we found that \( k_{600} \) increased with surface area (\( R^2 = 0.29, p < 0.001 \)) but was highly variable among lake sizes. The measurement method (e.g., gas tracer or floating chamber) did not improve the models of \( k_{600} \), but there was a bias toward gas tracer studies in small ponds and chamber studies in large lakes (Data Set S2). When lakes were grouped into size classes, it appears that \( k_{600} \) is fairly constant in lakes smaller than 0.1 km\(^2\) and is larger and more variable in larger lakes (Figure 3). The relative standard deviation in \( k_{600} \) increased with lake size class (\( R^2 = 0.69, p = 0.02 \), and \( F_{1,5} = 11.17 \)) and ranged between 28 and 86% of the mean. It is also worth noting that the majority of the studies (66%) were conducted on lakes between 0.01 and 1 km\(^2\), meaning that small ponds and large lakes were underrepresented. 4. Discussion We found that the gas transfer velocity, \( k_{600} \), in four small, forested ponds was low, variable within and among ponds, and difficult to predict from environmental variables. When we compared gas exchange rates in our study ponds to larger lakes, we found that \( k_{600} \) increased and became more variable with increasing lake size. 4.1. Estimates of Gas Transfer Velocity The average \( k_{600} \) when smoothed across 12 h periods ranged between 0.22 and 0.72 m d\(^{-1}\) across the four small ponds (Table 2). These estimates are within the range of average \( k_{600} \) values estimated from direct measurements in 30 small (<0.1 km\(^2\)) water bodies (Figure 3 and Data Set S2). However, we observed high variability both within and among ponds (up to 1.23 m d\(^{-1}\) among ponds and 1.21 m d\(^{-1}\) within ponds for 12 h averages). This sort of variability is large, especially considering that it encompasses nearly the entire range of \( k_{600} \) values used across all lake sizes in regional and global carbon models. In these models, the Figure 3. Estimates of \( k_{600} \) for 67 ponds and lakes across a size gradient where \( k_{600} \) was directly measured via floating chambers or gas tracers. The box represents the interquartile range and median, whereas the whiskers extend 1.5 times the interquartile range. average \( k_{600} \) increases with lake size class. Two recent carbon budgets used \( k_{600} \) estimates that ranged from 0.36–0.54 in the smallest water bodies up to 1.16–1.90 m d\(^{-1}\) in the largest lakes [Raymond et al., 2013; Holgerson and Raymond, 2016]. Our study combined with our review of other water bodies (Figure 3) indicates that \( k_{600} \) may be much more variable than previously thought. We expected that our 12 h estimates of \( k_{600} \) would be greater at night than during the day due to greater convective cooling. As air cools more quickly than water overnight, this stimulates convective mixing that produces turbulence [MacIntyre et al., 2010; Poindexter and Variano, 2013; Holgerson et al., 2016]. Yet we only observed a larger nighttime \( k_{600} \) in one of the four ponds (Brookside, Table 2). This may be due to our small sample size (up to three days and three nights per pond) or because we only sampled during the day (08 h to 20 h) and therefore did not pick up on short-term fluctuations in gas exchange overnight. As \( k_{600} \) may increase significantly for short periods of time at night [Holgerson et al., 2016], future work should investigate overnight gas exchange with a higher temporal resolution. 4.2. Predictors of Gas Transfer Velocity The best predictive models of daytime \( k_{600} \) indicate that increased gas exchange occurred with higher wind speeds, lower air temperatures, and when the water was warmer than the air (Table 4 and Figure 2). These predictors were not surprising, given that air-water turbulence (which drives \( k \)) is largely influenced by wind speed, solar radiation, and heat flux [Read et al., 2012]. Wind generates turbulence through shear stress and is the primary driver of \( k \) in large lakes; however, when wind speeds are low, such as in sheltered and smaller water bodies, convection can be more important for generating turbulence [MacIntyre et al., 2010; Read et al., 2012; Holgerson et al., 2016]. To evaluate convective forces affecting turbulence, the heat budget must be considered, including turbulent fluxes (latent and sensible heat) and radiative fluxes (short- and long-wave radiations). Because we did not calculate the entire heat budget, we cannot determine the exact mechanisms in which temperature influences \( k \). However, we can make several inferences based on our observation that \( k \) was higher when air temperatures were lower and as the water became warmer than the air. Turbulent fluxes can influence gas exchange via both latent (i.e., evaporation) and sensible (e.g., convection) heat fluxes. While wind will increase both latent and sensible heat fluxes in small ponds, temperature influences the sensible heat flux [Woolway et al., 2015]. Indeed, the air-water temperature difference we measured is a good proxy for sensible heat flux [Jonsson et al., 2008; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2017] because when the water is warmer than the air, the boundary layer over the water becomes unstable, which generates turbulence and increases gas exchange [MacIntyre et al., 2002]. Small ponds may be more sensitive to the sensible heat flux because they can have higher and more extreme diel changes in water temperature relative to larger lakes [Woolway et al., 2016]. Additionally, long- and short-wave radiations influence heat flux, and outgoing long-wave radiation often contributes the most to surface cooling in small, sheltered ponds [MacIntyre and Melack, 2009]. Therefore, it is likely that warmer water and cooler air temperatures increased daytime \( k_{600} \) by altering the heat budget. Future work should measure the full suite of meteorological data necessary to calculate the heat budget and determine how temperature changes promote increases in \( k \). We also found no effect of rain on daytime \( k_{600} \), which was surprising as previous studies found that raindrops produce significant turbulence [Ho et al., 1997]. It is likely that we did not experience heavy enough rainfall to greatly alter \( k_{600} \). Rainfall <25 mm h\(^{-1}\) is considered light [Ho et al., 1997], and the maximum rainfall event in our study was 1.27 mm within 15 min, likely too low to drive gas exchange in our study ponds. Even though wind and temperature patterns were the best predictors of daytime \( k_{600} \), the fixed effects of the models only explained a small amount (10–27%) of overall variation (Table 4). Including pond as a random effect in the model explained an additional 12% to 52% of the variation, indicating differences among study sites (Table 4). But considering that most variance came from the random effect of each study site, or was unexplained, it appears that gas exchange cannot be well predicted from these environmental variables, at least not at our coarse resolution or short temporal scale. Our study was limited to three days and three nights per pond based on the rate of propane loss from the ponds. It would be useful to repeat this study multiple times throughout the open-water season and sample at a finer resolution, which might better match the scale at which environmental variables are acting. 4.3. Comparison Across Lake Sizes The variability we observed in \( k_{600} \) is similar to or smaller than variability seen in other ponds and lakes around the world (Data Set S2 and Figure 3). Across lake size classes, small ponds and lakes have fairly constant gas exchange rates, with \( k_{600} \) increasing and becoming more variable in lakes larger than 0.1 km\(^2\) (Figure 3). Perhaps there is a threshold around 0.1 km\(^2\), where larger lakes have enough fetch for wind to significantly increase \( k_{600} \). The variability we observed across all lake size classes may help explain why existing predictive models of gas exchange yield significantly different results depending on the model used [Dugan et al., 2016]. Because estimates of \( k \) are necessary to calculate ecosystem metabolism and gas emissions across local, regional, and global scales, improving our knowledge of \( k \) across space, time, and lake size is a top research priority. To improve predictive capacity of \( k_{600} \), we advise that future gas exchange studies sample during both the day and night and at a finer temporal and spatial scale. One particularly useful tool may be using eddy flux measurements, which directly measures turbulent scalar flows of gas over a given source area and therefore can capture an entire lake’s dynamics [Jonsson et al., 2008; Heiskanen et al., 2014]. Eddy covariance also provides insight into temporal and diel heterogeneities in \( k_{600} \) as it can automatically sample over long time scales [Podgrajsek et al., 2015]. Additionally, it would be interesting to consider how heat flux scales with lake size as small ponds experience greater changes in diurnal temperature and gas exchange appears to be more influenced by convection [Podgrajsek et al., 2015; Woolway et al., 2016]. Future studies also need to increase the representation of different lake sizes, particularly for small ponds and large lakes. Within the small pond size class, ponds can be extremely diverse across the landscape and factors such as depth, mixing, and presence of emergent vegetation may greatly influence \( k \) [Poindexter and Variano, 2013; Andersen et al., 2016], which needs further research. With increased efforts to improve spatial and temporal resolutions across lake sizes, our knowledge and predictive capacity of \( k_{600} \) will improve. 5. Conclusions This study adds small, low-wind ponds to the existing body of research on gas transfer velocities from inland waters. We found that small ponds had lower values of \( k_{600} \) relative to larger lakes, but we highlight that \( k_{600} \) is variable across space and time for all water bodies, especially large lakes. Because \( k_{600} \) was not easily predicted from environmental parameters, and because current predictive models of \( k_{600} \) yield significantly different results [Dugan et al., 2016], there is substantial uncertainty when upscaling \( k \) to regional or global analyses. Therefore, understanding the drivers and predictors of \( k \) is an important research priority, with implications for estimating ecosystem metabolism and global carbon emissions from inland waters. 2.4. Estimating Gas Transfer Velocity

Gas transfer between aquatic surfaces and the atmosphere is described by the equation:

\[
F = k (C_{\text{sur}} - C_{\text{eq}})
\] (1)

where \( F \) is the gas flux (mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)), \( k \) is the gas transfer velocity (m d\(^{-1}\)), \( C_{\text{sur}} \) is the gas concentration in the surface water, and \( C_{\text{eq}} \) is the gas concentration when in equilibrium with the atmosphere. For the propane additions, we directly measured \( F \), \( C_{\text{sur}} \), and \( C_{\text{eq}} \), allowing for the derivation of \( k \).

To derive \( k \), we first used a Grubbs outlier test to discount any erroneous propane concentrations that resulted from sampling error. We then converted the average propane concentrations (ppm\(_v\)) of the triplicates at each time point to units of mol L\(^{-1}\) by using Henry’s law constants [Mohebbi et al., 2012; Sander, 2015]. We calculated \( k \) across two different time scales: (1) for each 12 h sampling interval and (2) for each 2 or 3 h sampling period during the day. Longer time scales may more accurately reflect the overall ecosystem gas transfer velocity [Wanninkhof et al., 1987], while shorter time periods better allow for comparisons to be made to environmental conditions.

To calculate \( k \) (m d\(^{-1}\)), we used the following equation [Wanninkhof et al., 1987]:

\[
k = \frac{h}{\Delta t} \ln \frac{C_i - C_o}{C_f - C_o}
\] (2)

where \( h \) is the average depth of the pond, \( \Delta t \) is the time interval, \( C_i \) and \( C_f \) are the initial and final propane concentrations in the pond, respectively, and \( C_o \) is the background concentration of propane in the water. We computed average pond depth, \( h \), by taking the mean of the measured depths for each square meter measured in each pond. Since \( C_o \) of propane is negligible in this experiment, equation (2) becomes

\[
k = \frac{h}{\Delta t} \ln \frac{C_i}{C_f}
\] (3)

Because we measured propane concentrations multiple times during the day, to estimate \( k \) for 12 h daytime periods, we performed a linear regression to determine the slope of concentration change over time for each 12 h daytime interval of sampling, and this slope replaced \( \frac{1}{\Delta t} \ln \frac{C_i}{C_f} \) in equation (3). We did not take any gas samples between 20 h and 08 h during the experiment, so we calculated the \( k \) values for each night of sampling by using \( C_f \) from the previous day as the initial propane concentration and \( C_i \) from the following day as the final propane concentration. We normalized \( k \) values to a \( k_{600} \) for propane by using the following equation [Jähne et al., 1987]:

\[
\frac{k_{600}}{k_{\text{gas2}}} = \left( \frac{600}{\text{Sc}_{\text{gas2}}} \right)^n
\] (4)

where \( k_{600} \) is the \( k \) for propane at 20°C and corresponds to a Schmidt number of 600, which can be related to the \( k \) for any other gas [Raymond et al., 2012]. Sc denotes the Schmidt number for the particular gas of interest, and \( n \) is the Schmidt exponent, which varies from –0.5 to –0.67 depending on the boundary conditions. In low-wind environments (<3 m s\(^{-1}\)), \( n \) can be assumed to equal –0.67 [Jähne et al., 1987]. Occasionally, our measurements indicated that propane concentrations increased between sampling times, which likely resulted from spatial heterogeneity in the pond. We only report estimates of \( k \) for periods of time where propane concentrations decreased and indicate net propane evasion from the pond.

2.5. Comparison Across Lake Sizes

We conducted a meta-analysis to compare our results to other water bodies where \( k_{600} \) was directly measured. We identified 18 studies, including ours, representing 67 ponds and lakes ranging in size from 181 m\(^2\) to 520 km\(^2\) (Data Set S2 in the supporting information). With this data set, we examined the mean and variability of \( k_{600} \) across lake sizes and also explored the relationship between surface area and gas exchange rate.

2.6. Data Analysis

To evaluate if \( k_{600} \) was influenced by environmental variables, we used linear mixed-effects models with pond as a random effect. Models were created in R (R version 3.2.4, R Core Team) by using the “lme4” package [Bates et al., 2014]. Models were constructed by using daytime 2 or 3 h estimates of \( k_{600} \), only including

Identification of total phosphate, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size thresholds for success of biomanipulation in peri-urban eutrophic ponds Sylvia De Backer · Samuel Teissier · Ludwig Triest Received: 23 November 2012 / Accepted: 27 October 2013 / Published online: 8 November 2013 © Springer Science+Business Media Dordrecht 2013 Abstract In small shallow lakes and ponds, the clear-water state can generally be maintained at higher nutrient concentrations compared to larger shallow lakes. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for total phosphorus (TP), submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size that determine biomanipulation success in peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationship between transparency and TP is discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Using classification trees, a threshold TP concentration of 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\) was determined below which a clear-water state was generally maintained after biomanipulation. When the average TP concentration was >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), the stability of the clear-water state largely depended on the presence of sufficiently large zooplankton (>0.87 mm) or a submerged vegetation cover of >82% at some point during the year. This threshold TP concentration is considerably higher than the threshold of 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) which is generally suggested for longer-term success of biomanipulation in shallow lakes. Such threshold nutrient concentration is important when restoring ecological quality in eutrophic small lakes and ponds. Extended follow-up of biomanipulation success in eutrophic ponds could provide more insight into the feasibility of these thresholds on the longer term. Keywords Ponds · Shallow lakes · Eutrophic · Clear-water state · Restoration · Turbid Introduction During the past decades, ecological quality of shallow lakes and ponds has often been degraded as a result of eutrophication due to human activities, causing a transition to a turbid, phytoplankton-dominated state, often associated with severe blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria (Willame et al., 2005; Peretyatko et al., 2007b). Nutrient reduction alone as a method to restore such lakes and ponds is often expensive and inefficient, as recovery is often delayed by internal phosphorus loading or biological resistances (Søndergaard et al., 2005a; Jeppesen et al., 2007). Internal loading was found to be a significant part of total P loading during the productive summer period in eutrophic Danish lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2013). Next to nutrient reduction measures, biomanipulation, through complete or partial fish removal, is often performed to improve ecological quality of shallow lakes (Meijer et al., 1994; Lammens, 1999; Jyväsjärvi et al., 2013). In shallow lakes, a short-term response to biomanipulation is generally dependent on the ability of large zooplankton, once released from its predation pressure, to control phytoplankton sufficiently to create a clear-water state, irrespective of the nutrient levels (van Donk et al., 1990; Meijer et al., 1999). In eutrophic ponds, zooplankton grazing was shown to be a first important mechanism for obtaining a clear-water state (Peretyatko et al., 2009). Once a clear-water state is obtained, the increased water transparency could promote the growth of macrophytes (Bakker et al., 2013) which, in turn, could stabilize the clear-water state on the longer term by a series of mechanisms (Van den Berg et al., 1997; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002; Peretyatko et al., 2007a). On the longer term, however, the success of biomanipulation is more speculative and has often been related to elevated nutrient concentrations (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2008; Hobbs et al., 2012). The negative relationship between nutrient loading and water transparency in shallow lakes is generally well recognized. Scheffer et al. (1993) already suggested a stepwise rather than a gradual shift from a macrophyte-dominated to a phytoplankton-dominated state when nutrients are gradually increased. Although the theory of only two alternative states has been nuanced lately, the general idea remains that once a certain threshold nutrient concentration is surpassed, a more dramatic increase in turbidity can occur and a return to a clear-water state will be very difficult (Scheffer & van Nes, 2007; Hobbs et al., 2012). Another important factor influencing biomanipulation success in shallow lakes and ponds is the level of nutrients. It is often suggested that the clear-water state in ponds and small lakes is generally less dependent on nutrients compared to larger shallow lakes (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2005b). In small shallow lakes and ponds, a lower Chlorophyll \( a \) (Chl \( a \)) yield per unit of nitrogen or phosphorus is generally observed (Søndergaard et al., 2005b). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that ponds (<3 ha) deviated considerably from the overall relationship between water transparency and total phosphorus (TP) in Danish shallow lakes, because both a high transparency and submerged vegetation were still found at higher TP concentrations than for larger lakes. This phenomenon has several possible explanations. Jeppesen et al. (1990) already mentioned that conditions are more favourable for macrophytes in small lakes. Additionally, in smaller lakes and ponds, macrophytes suffer less from wind stress and wind-induced resuspension of the sediment. Also, a reduced depth provides a better light availability for macrophytes at a given water transparency and as such, macrophytes can colonize larger parts of the lake area (Scheffer and van Nes, 2007; Van Geest et al., 2007). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that for a given shallow lake, transparency was higher when an average submerged vegetation cover of >30% was present, compared to cases with a cover <30%, confirming the positive effect of submerged vegetation on transparency (Scheffer, 1998; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002). Favourable conditions for macrophytes in ponds thus could contribute to an increased transparency, despite high nutrient concentrations. Also, in ponds, some piscivorous fish, such as northern pike (Esox lucius L.), benefit from an abundant vegetation and a higher shore to total area ratio (Grimm, 1989). Winter fish kill due to oxygen depletion could also play a major role, increasing zooplankton grazing during summer, resulting in a more efficient control of phytoplankton (Søndergaard et al., 2005b), which can favour the growth of submerged macrophytes. When biomanipulation is performed on shallow lakes or ponds, it can be useful to determine above which nutrient level a clear-water state can no longer be achieved. When nutrient concentrations (mainly phosphorus) are above a certain threshold, a shift back to the turbid state after biomanipulation might be inevitable and in such cases a nutrient reduction is recommended before biomanipulation is performed. According to Jeppesen et al. (1990), a long-term effect of biomanipulation can only be achieved when the average TP concentration is below 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) in shallow lakes larger than 3 ha. Hosper & Jagtman (1990) came to similar conclusions and suggested 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) as a threshold for a stable clear-water state after biomanipulation of shallow lakes. In shallow lakes with a TP concentration higher than 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\), only short-term effects can be expected. Higher nutrient threshold levels could be an advantage for deciding and attempting a restoration of eutrophic ponds through biomanipulation. Nevertheless, even for ponds, beyond a certain threshold, nutrient levels might be too high to obtain a stable clear-water state after fish removal on the longer term. For management purposes, it is crucial to determine the threshold nutrient concentrations above which biomanipulation will no longer be successful in highly eutrophicated ponds. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for key factors (TP concentration, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size) that are known to strongly determine the outcome of biomanipulation in a series of peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationships between transparency and TP, and the obtained thresholds for eutrophic ponds are discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Materials and methods Study area For this study, 13 ponds, located in the Brussels Capital Region (Belgium), were biomanipulated and monitored during 2004–2010. All ponds are located within the same catchment (Woluwe river catchment) in a close proximity of each other (<10 km) and their connectivity is rather high. All the ponds were man-made and created more than a century ago by the damming of small low-order streams (Marlier, 1971). They are shallow (maximum depth 3 m), flat-bottomed and range in surface area from 0.2 to 6 ha and are mainly fed by small rivulets and ground water seepage. Fish communities in the Brussels Capital Region generally consist of species that are typical for Western European fresh waters, such as common carp (Cyprinus carpio carpio L.), northern pike (Esox lucius L.), perch (Perca fluviatilis L.), roach (Rutilus rutilus L.) and tench (Tinca tinca L.) (De Backer et al., 2010). More detailed characteristics of the studied ponds, including an overview of the applied restoration measures for each pond, are given in Table 1. Restoration measures Biomanipulation was performed in 13 ponds during 2005–2009 by water drawdown and complete fish removal (Table 1). This was generally done in winter or early spring to avoid the presence of numerous juvenile fish which could easily escape or survive in the mud for some time. In most ponds, the water level could be lowered manually, due to their artificial nature. During water drawdown, fishermen removed all or as much fish as possible using fishing nets. More than 500 kg of fish per ha was removed in each pond, confirming that all ponds were overstocked with fish before biomanipulation. A few weeks to several months after fish removal, the ponds were slowly refilled through overflow of neighbouring ponds, groundwater seepage or inflow of small rivulets. In a second phase, northern pike (Esox lucius L.) were added in an attempt to stabilize the clear-water state. Addition of piscivores is often performed in an attempt to control planktivorous fish after biomanipulation, allowing large zooplankton to increase grazing pressure on phytoplankton and, as such, further stabilizes the clear-water state (Lammens, 1999; Ha et al., 2013). The individuals that were added in the studied ponds were larger than the 0+ pike that are generally used for this purpose, as the result of 0+ pike additions is often not just temporary (Søndergaard et al., 1997) or the added pike lack piscivory (Skov et al., 2003). In February 2008, only 1+ pikes were added to 10 biomanipulated ponds (Table 1). In February 2010, various densities of 1+, 2+ and 3+ pike (with a size of 20, 30 and 45 cm, respectively) were added into 7 biomanipulated ponds. Sampling and sample processing Samples were taken 1 year before and 1–5 years after biomanipulation during the warm season (May–September) on 3–5 occasions per year. A detailed overview of all sampling occasions is given in Table 2. Except for very small ponds, all samples were taken from a boat. Secchi depth was measured using a 30-cm-diameter disc. In case the Secchi disc was still visible when reaching the pond bottom, Secchi depth was estimated as the actual pond depth plus 1 m in case the disc was still clearly visible or plus 0.1 m in case it was only partially visible. This approach is similar to the method of Cottenie et al. (2001) and was used to obtain a more realistic Secchi depth when the disc was still visible at the pond bottom. Quantitative phytoplankton, Chl \( a \), main nutrient (TP, soluble reactive phosphorus—SRP, and dissolved inorganic nitrogen i.e. \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) and \( \mathrm{NO}_x \) (NO\(_2^-\) and NO\(_3^-\))) and zooplankton samples were collected on each occasion. Mixed water samples based on 10 random subsamples were taken from each pond (including vegetated parts) with a plastic tube sampler of 4.5 cm diameter and 70 cm length that closes in the lower part. An extension was fixed to the sampler to reach the deeper parts of the ponds when appropriate. In case of deeper ponds (depth >1 m), subsamples were taken alternately from shallower and deeper parts of the pond in order to obtain a sample representative of the whole water column. After stirring the collected water, 500 ml was taken for phytoplankton identification and quantification, 1 l for chemical analyses and 1 l for Chl \( a \) determination. Samples for Chl \( a \) analysis were filtered onto Whatman GF/C filters and stored at −18 °C for a maximum of 7 days before analysis. Pigments were extracted in 90% acetone in the dark for 8 h. Pigment concentrations were measured spectrophotometrically. Nutrient concentrations were measured according to standard methods (APHA-AWWA-WEF, 1995). Phytoplankton samples were fixed in the field with alkaline lugol, sodium thiosulphate and buffered formalin (Sherr & Sherr, 1993) and stored in the dark before identification and enumeration to genus level using inverted microscopy. Biovolumes were calculated using the approximations of cell shapes to simple geometrical forms (Wetzel & Likens, 2000). Total phytoplankton biovolume was mainly used as a proxy for turbidity of the water column. Eight phytoplankton groups were differentiated: Cyanobacteria, Bacillariophyta, Euglenophyta, Chlorophyta, Cryptophyta, Dinophyta, Chrysophyta and Xanthophyta. In order to assess the zooplankton community structure, 10 subsamples of 1 l were collected with the same sampler used for phytoplankton and nutrients. Statistical data analyses To identify the factors that determine the outcome of biomanipulation (i.e. ‘failure’ or ‘success’), it is essential to define exactly what ‘failure’ is or what can be considered as ‘success’. In terms of phytoplankton biovolume and composition, ‘failure’ of biomanipulation is essentially a return to a situation that is comparable to the phytoplankton composition and biomass before biomanipulation. Therefore, a hierarchical cluster analysis was performed on averaged per year phytoplankton data (division level). All data were log-transformed to obtain normality if needed. By arranging the data into different clusters, we could study how the situation before biomanipulation was related to the situation after biomanipulation for each pond, in each year. The cluster analysis was performed using PC-ORD (McCune & Mefford, 2006). Sørensen distance was used as a dissimilarity measure and the farthest neighbour linkage as group linkage method. One-way clustering was carried out on both samples and phytoplankton groups. For the latter, data were relativised (i.e. each value divided by the maximum value observed per phytoplankton group). This is generally done to avoid separation of more common species into separate groups from rare species (McCune & Mefford, 2006). Based on previous field observations and the nature of the data, we expect a clustering into two main groups, corresponding to clear with low phytoplankton biomass and to turbid with high phytoplankton biomass conditions. Based on the position of each data point within the cluster, successfully biomanipulated ponds (situation 1), situated inside a low phytoplankton biomass group, could be further subdivided into two categories: before (1b) and after (1a) biomanipulation. Ponds where biomanipulation failed (situation 2) were defined as ponds where data of at least 1 year after biomanipulation were situated inside a high phytoplankton biomass group within the cluster. Situation 2 could be further subdivided into three categories: before biomanipulation (2b), after biomanipulation but before failure (2a, situated in the low phytoplankton subcluster) and after biomanipulation when it failed (2f, data with high phytoplankton biovolume). Essentially, the cluster analysis based on phytoplankton data was performed to assign each data point to one of the 5 predefined categories (1b, 1a, 2b, 2a or 2f). Differences between these 5 categories were analyzed further using One-way ANOVA. A Tukey HSD test, modified for unequal sample size, was used as a post hoc comparison test to compare mean values between individual groups. The one-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to investigate the data for normality and the Brown–Forsythe test was used to check for homogeneity of variance. When one of both assumptions was not met (as was the case for SRP and submerged vegetation cover), a non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis test was used to investigate differences between the groups. For all analyses, averaged per year per pond data were used. Three repeated-measures ANOVA were carried out on the considered variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, length of large Cladocera and %SVmax) with time (year) as factor because biomanipulations were not carried out in the same year for every pond. ANOVA was done for the years ‘before biomanipulation’, for the first year following biomanipulation and for all follow-up years after biomanipulation. An additional repeated measure ANOVA was done for the same variables for all ponds in 2010 but using pike addition as a factor in three classes, namely no addition, pikes added in 2008 and pikes added in 2010. Previous research indicated that the impact of total phosphorus concentration (TP), large Cladocera length (LCL) and submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}) on phytoplankton biovolume in these ponds did not show a linear but a threshold relationship (De Backer, 2011). Therefore, classification trees (Breiman et al., 1984) were used to estimate the thresholds of different environmental factors that determine the outcome of biomanipulation (i.e. phytoplankton biovolume). This type of analysis could allow us to identify threshold values for each predictor (TP, LCL and SV_{max}), below or above which biomanipulation will most likely fail or be successful. All classification tree analyses were performed with Statistica version 8 (Statsoft Inc., Tulsa, OK, USA). The goodness of fit of each split was estimated by the Chi square statistic. Only the best fitting option was shown in the resulting graph. The ‘prune on deviance’ option was used as a stopping rule with a minimum of 10% of the total number of cases needed to allow a subsequent split. For all classification tree analyses, averaged per year per pond values of post-biomanipulation data were used. A series of classification trees was performed to explore the relationships between phytoplankton biovolume and the three predictors (all together or each predictor individually). Since submerged vegetation can affect phytoplankton, phytoplankton can also affect submerged vegetation cover, using average submerged vegetation cover (SV_{av}) as a predictor of phytoplankton biovolume seems irrelevant, as the percentage of cover might be negatively influenced by phytoplankton itself. Use of SV_{max} as a predictor variable of phytoplankton biovolume, rather than SV_{av}, allows us to identify the threshold cover of submerged vegetation above which an increased phytoplankton growth is prevented. Finally, the relationship between phytoplankton biovolume and submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}), LCL and TP concentration was studied using Pearson product-moment correlations. Results Classification of biomanipulated ponds Hierarchical cluster analysis of averaged per year phytoplankton biovolume (per division) of biomanipulated ponds constructed two main groups (Fig. 1). In Group A, as indicated by relative abundances and percentiles of each phytoplankton group, phytoplankton biovolume was generally lower when compared to Group B. For all phytoplankton groups (with the exception of Chrysophyta and Xanthophyta that clustered separately from all other groups), the highest phytoplankton biovolume values were found in pond samples of Group B. All pre-biomanipulation samples aggregated into Group B, except for two cases (VKn1 and WtMl). For 8 ponds (Beml, Dens, PRB1, Sbsk, Fig. 1 Hierarchical cluster analysis based on averaged per year phytoplankton data (2004–2010) for all biomanipulated ponds using Sørensen distance as a dissimilarity measure and the farthest neighbour linkage as group linkage method. Years are indicated by the number before the pond name, for example: 8Beml = Beml in 2008. Asterisks indicate situations before biomanipulation. A colour gradient ranging from white to black was used to colour the matrix based on percentiles (left group of squares) and on relative abundance (right group of squares) per phytoplankton group (vertically). Symbols indicate biomanipulation status: 1b, 1a—successfully biomanipulated ponds before and after biomanipulation; 2b, 2a, 2f—unsuccessfully biomanipulated ponds before biomanipulation, after biomanipulation but before failure, and after biomanipulation failure VKn1, VKn2, WPk1 and WtMI), all post-biomanipulation samples were situated in Group A. These 8 clear-water ponds, therefore, were considered as successfully biomanipulated (named ‘situation 1’). For the remaining five ponds, several (for Leyb-a, Leyb-b and MIKI) or all (for NrPd1 and PRB2) post-biomanipulation samples remained situated in Group B, indicating that phytoplankton composition in these ponds during some years after biomanipulation was more similar to the situation before biomanipulation when compared to other succeeded post-biomanipulation situations. These five ponds were considered as ponds where biomanipulation failed (named ‘situation 2’). Based on this cluster analysis, we split up ‘situation 1’ for the successfully biomanipulated ponds (i.e. ponds of which all post-biomanipulation samples were a part of Group A) into their before (1b) and after (1a) biomanipulation conditions. For ponds where biomanipulation failed (i.e. ponds of which some or all post-biomanipulation samples were classified under Group B), this ‘situation 2’ was split up into three conditions, namely pond samples before biomanipulation (2b), samples of those ponds that temporarily turned into clear water during at least 1 year (2a) and finally samples of these ponds after failure i.e. in turbid conditions (2f). There was only a marginal effect of time on the variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, LCL and SV_{max}) when considering the year before biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 2.32, P = 0.058 \)) due to a higher TP and phytoplankton biovolume in 1 out of 13 ponds (PRB1 in 2008). There was no effect of time when considering all ponds just 1 year following biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 1.22, P = 0.319 \)) or all years after biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 0.59, P = 0.910 \)). There was no effect of pike addition on the variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, LCL and SV_{max}) in the years after biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 1.23, P = 0.348 \)). Features of ponds before and after biomanipulation All the ponds studied were rich in nutrients with a mean TP >0.1 mg, before and after biomanipulation. Nutrient levels were generally higher in situations where biomanipulation failed, as TP concentrations were significantly lower in clear-water situations after biomanipulation (1a) when compared to turbid ponds following a failure (2f) (Fig. 2; Table 3). All other TP concentrations were intermediate between those of 1a and 2f. SRP concentrations did not differ significantly between before and after biomanipulation but this is only in cases where biomanipulation was successful (1b and 1a). On the other hand, dissolved nutrients (SRP, NH_4^+ and NO_x) often attained more elevated concentrations after biomanipulation (Fig. 2) and this was significantly higher for SRP in ponds where biomanipulation failed (2f). The five status groups (1b, 1a, 2b, 2a and 2f) showed significant differences in total phytoplankton biovolume, relative cyanobacterial biovolume, Secchi depth, large Cladocera length, %SV_{max} cover and SRP, whereas large Cladocera density was only marginally significant (Table 3, Fig. 2). For NH_4^+ and NO_x concentrations, no significant differences were obtained (Table 3; Fig. 2). The three proxies for phytoplankton biomass (averaged total phytoplankton biovolume, Chl a concentrations and Secchi depth) showed a very similar pattern for the distinguishable situations (Fig. 2; Table 3). Phytoplankton biomass was high in all starting conditions prior to biomanipulation and was comparably high for failed situations of subsequent years (1b, 2b and 2f). Significantly low phytoplankton biomass was measured in situations where biomanipulation was immediately (1a) or temporarily successful (2a). In those situations where biomanipulation temporarily kept a clear-water condition before returning to a turbid state (2a), phytoplankton biovolume also did decrease significantly; however, returned in the following year(s) again to failure (2f) up to a level that was comparable to their origin situation before biomanipulation. Although average relative cyanobacterial biovolume did not differ significantly between most of the situations, it varied considerably in those ponds where biomanipulation failed, namely reaching up to 40% prior to biomanipulation (2b) or when the water shifted to a turbid state again (2f). In temporarily successful conditions (2a), the average relative cyanobacterial biovolume (Fig. 2) could reach up to 20% before turning into failure with higher abundances. In ponds where biomanipulation was successful in maintaining clear-water conditions (1a), the relative cyanobacterial biovolume also was <10% in the period prior to biomanipulation (1b). Determining thresholds of TP, LCL and SVmax needed for successful biomanipulation A first classification tree was performed to differentiate between ponds where biomanipulation failed and ponds where biomanipulation succeeded, based on TP, LCL and SVmax. For this purpose, only data after biomanipulation were used. The classes that were determined for different post-biomanipulation situations were used as a categorical, dependent variable: 1a (after biomanipulation when it was successful, \( N = 31 \)), 2a (after biomanipulation but before failure, \( N = 6 \)) and 2f (when biomanipulation failed, \( N = 11 \)). As such, differences between failure and success situations in the level of TP, LCL or SVmax (added as predictors of the categorical variable) could be identified (Fig. 3). The first split of the resulting tree was based on a TP concentration of 0.300 mg L−1 and separated most of the cases in which biomanipulation was successful (1a) from most of the cases in which biomanipulation failed, both before (2a) and after (2f) failure. 27 out of 30 cases (90%) with an average TP concentration below 0.300 mg L−1 were successfully biomanipulated (1a; Fig. 3; ID = 2). Out of the 18 cases with an average TP concentration of >0.300 mg L−1, 14 cases (78%) are from ponds where biomanipulation failed, before (2a) or after failure (2f; Fig. 3; ID = 3). Thus, a threshold of 0.300 mg L−1 of TP was determined below which biomanipulation is generally successful. When TP >0.300 mg L−1, cases in which biomanipulation has not yet failed (2a) are separated from the cases in which biomanipulation failed (2f) by a larger length (>0.99 mm) of large cladocerans (Fig. 3; ID = 15). Thus, when TP is >0.300 mg L−1, failure of biomanipulation can be prevented as long as cladocerans are sufficiently large (except for one case of ‘2f’ in which LCL is also >0.99 mm). Once LCL decreases to ≤0.99 mm, failure is most likely (Fig. 3; ID = 18). Regarding the % cover of submerged macrophytes that restored after biomanipulation, a threshold of failure in highly eutrophic conditions (TP >0.300 mg L−1) could be considered as 87% of submerged vegetation covering the pond surface (Fig. 3; ID = 16). Next, in order to quantify the difference between failure and success situations in terms of phytoplankton biovolume, a threshold of phytoplankton biovolume was estimated that determines success (1a) or failure (2f). For this purpose, a classification tree was used with the ‘post-biomanipulation status’ (‘1a’, ‘2a’ or ‘2f’) as a response variable and averaged phytoplankton biovolume as a predictor. An almost ‘pure’ split was obtained at 10.8 mm3 L−1 of phytoplankton biovolume, separating all clear-water situations (\( N = 38 \) i.e. ‘1a’: after successful biomanipulation and ‘2a’: before failure) with an average phytoplankton biovolume ≤10.8 mm3 L−1 from all failure situations (2f with \( N = 11 \)) with an average phytoplankton biovolume of >10.8 mm3 L−1 (except Fig. 3 Classification tree for three categories of after biomanipulation situations: 1a—successfully biomanipulated ponds after biomanipulation; 2a, 2f—unsuccessfully biomanipulated ponds after biomanipulation: before and after failure, for one case of 2f with a low phytoplankton biovolume). The obtained threshold of 10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\) of phytoplankton biovolume was then used in further analyses to differentiate between clear-water and turbid situations. Based on this threshold, 2 categories were created: categories ‘0’ and ‘1’ for cases in which phytoplankton biovolume was \( \leq \) or \( > \) than the threshold biovolume of 10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\), respectively. For all remaining analyses, the phytoplankton data were transformed to ‘0’ or ‘1’ values and used as such instead of the original phytoplankton data. These two categories of phytoplankton biovolume were then used in further analyses. Using all three predictors in the same analysis might blur the effect of some predictors individually on phytoplankton biovolume. Therefore, the classification tree analysis based on these two phytoplankton categories was executed with TP, LCL or SV\(_{\text{max}}\) individually as categorical predictors to study the behaviour of phytoplankton depending on each respectively. Averaged per year TP, averaged large Cladocera length (LCL) and maximum submerged vegetation cover (SV) were used as continuous predictors of biomanipulation category. ID node number, N number of cases in node predictor separately (Fig. 4). For TP, the threshold of 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\) was confirmed below which all 30 cases (100%) had an average phytoplankton biovolume of less than 10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\) (Fig. 4a; ID = 2). Above 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), both categories of phytoplankton biovolume could occur (Fig. 4a; ID = 3). Additionally, it appears that at an average TP concentration above 0.74 mg L\(^{-1}\), all cases are turbid (Fig. 4a; ID = 5). Large Cladocera size showed a threshold of 0.87 mm (LCL) and such larger sizes were found at low phytoplankton biovolume (<10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\)) in 29 out of 30 cases (97%; Fig. 4b; ID = 5). In vegetated ponds a very large cover % at maximum development (SV\(_{\text{max}}\)) at a threshold of 82% was obtained, for which 14 out of 15 cases (93%) were associated with a phytoplankton biovolume less than 10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\) (Fig. 4c; ID = 3). No significant correlation was observed between phytoplankton biovolume and TP, LCL or SV\(_{\text{max}}\) for values below 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP (Table 4; Fig. 5). Discussion On the short term, a clear-water state can be established in ponds after biomanipulation, independent of the level of nutrients. The likelihood of obtaining such a clear-water state depends mostly on the development of sufficiently large cladocerans after biomanipulation, irrespective of the nutrient levels present (Peretyatko et al., 2009). On the longer term, nutrients will play a more important role in determining biomanipulation success. Biomanipulated ponds with a TP concentration below 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\) resided in a clear-water state with low phytoplankton biomass, relatively independent of large cladoceran size or the extent of submerged vegetation cover (except for one case without submerged vegetation Fig. 5 Relationship between phytoplankton biovolume and TP, large Cladocera length (LCL) and maximum submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}) when TP \leq 0.300\ \mathrm{mg\ P\ L}^{-1} (left) or >0.300\ \mathrm{mg\ P\ L}^{-1} (right) in ponds after biomanipulation. Significant Pearson correlations (\( P < 0.05 \)) are indicated by a line; for the lower two graphs, a dotted line corresponds to all cases with LCL \leq 0.87; a full line corresponds to all cases with LCL >0.87. More details concerning the Pearson correlations are given in Table 4 and where large cladoceran length is <0.83 mm). Above 0.300 mg P L^{-1}, the maintenance of the clear-water state mainly depended on large Cladocera size. As long as sufficiently large cladocerans were present (average length >0.87 mm), phytoplankton biomass remained low, even at high TP concentrations. If, however, in such case, large Cladocera size decreased due to predation by recolonizing fish (De Backer et al., 2012), a shift to the turbid state was unavoidable, except for a few cases in which submerged vegetation cover reached >82% and where a clear-water state was maintained despite the lack of sufficiently large cladocerans. Despite the often high cover of submerged vegetation that was often observed in spring, several ponds still developed a high phytoplankton biomass in summer and, nevertheless, returned to a turbid state. Long-term follow-up of these ponds could clarify if this is only a transitional stage to a permanent turbid state where macrophyte cover will eventually be absent, even in spring. Failure of biomanipulation thus appears to be related mainly to a combination of both elevated nutrient concentrations and the lack of large Cladocera grazing, independently of the extent of the submerged vegetation cover. After biomanipulation, all ponds remained in a clear-water state below 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP, independent of the extent of the submerged vegetation cover. It should, however, be noted that in biomanipulated ponds, in most of the ponds with an average TP concentration <0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\), LCL was >0.87 mm, which could have been the main reason for low phytoplankton biomass below 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP. Although the positive effect of large zooplankton grazing and the presence of submerged vegetation is generally well recognized (Van den Berg et al., 1997; Scheffer, 1998; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002), few studies have shown the direct impact of these factors on Chl \(a\)--TP relationships in shallow lakes or ponds. Chl \(a\)--TP relationships were studied in the same 13 biomanipulated ponds, showing that after biomanipulation, for a given TP concentration, the yield of Chl \(a\) was lower in ponds with an extensive submerged vegetation cover and high grazing pressure, compared to the same ponds before biomanipulation (Teissier et al., 2012). This directly shows that other factors than nutrients, such as submerged vegetation cover and large zooplankton grazing, can considerably influence the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship in eutrophic ponds. An additional difference between the situation before biomanipulation and during the first years after biomanipulation is the presence of large benthivorous fish in the former. Benthivorous fish that resuspend the sediment, thereby increasing suspended solids, nutrients and phytoplankton abundance in the water column, can cause a reduction of transparency and prevent macrophyte recolonization (Roozen et al., 2007). Next to the effect of planktivorous fish removal on zooplankton grazing, removal of benthivorous fish also contributes to an increased sedimentation and an improved transparency after biomanipulation (Meijer et al., 1990). This aspect could also have contributed to the lower Chl \(a\)--TP yield in biomanipulated ponds. As in several ponds, fish recolonized after biomanipulation, large benthivorous fish might eventually be present again in these ponds. We did not observe any significant improvement on large zooplankton density or length in 2010 in any of the ponds in which pike were added. Therefore, it is unlikely that the numbers of pike that survived were sufficient to reduce predation pressure on zooplankton in any pond in 2010. In a similar study on non-biomanipulated ponds (De Backer, 2011), no clear-water state is found when TP is >0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\). Therefore, it also is unlikely that biomanipulated ponds with an average TP concentration above this threshold will remain clear in the future (if biomanipulation did not already fail). Consequently, nutrient reduction is recommended before biomanipulation when average TP concentrations exceed the threshold concentration of \( \sim 0.300 \) mg L\(^{-1}\). It is often suggested that in smaller lakes and ponds, phytoplankton is less influenced by nutrients (Jeppesen et al., 1990) and that factors other than nutrients are more important for phytoplankton control (Søndergaard et al., 2005b; Peretyatko et al., 2007b). Our results confirm this, although the threshold levels obtained should be interpreted carefully due to limited number of data and additionally need to be validated with an additional training set using non-biomanipulated ponds. The threshold TP concentration of \( \sim 0.300 \) mg P L\(^{-1}\) below which a clear-water state can be maintained is considerably higher than the threshold of 0.1–0.125 mg P L\(^{-1}\) that is often suggested for shallow lakes (Hosper & Jagtman, 1990; Jeppesen et al., 1990). As already mentioned, high submerged vegetation cover and large zooplankton grazing can considerably influence the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship in eutrophic ponds. Possibly, the strong effect of both factors can be the reason for the lesser dependence of phytoplankton biomass on nutrients in ponds, compared to shallow lakes. Similar studies on shallow lakes could demonstrate whether the effect of zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation on the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship would be as strong as it is in the case of the pond systems studied here. Conclusions For biomanipulation of eutrophic ponds, our results suggest that, although a clear-water state can be obtained even when TP concentrations are >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), the stability of this clear-water state is insufficient and largely depends on the presence of sufficiently large-sized zooplankton or of a nearly full cover of submerged vegetation. Once they disappear, generally through predation or disturbance by recolonizing fish, a shift to the turbid state is very likely. As fish recolonization is almost inevitable at some point in these peri-urban ponds (or at least difficult to avoid in the near proximity of recreational fishing areas), we suggest that nutrient reduction measures should be undertaken before biomanipulation, in case the average TP concentration is >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\). After 2–4 years following biomanipulation, all biomanipulated ponds with a TP concentration below this threshold showed promising results, as they remained in a clear-water state during the whole study period. Longer term studies on biomanipulated ponds are necessary to see how the situation in these ponds will evolve. The threshold concentration of 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP above which biomanipulation is likely to fail is considerably higher than similar thresholds known for shallow lakes. Such lesser dependence of phytoplankton biomass in the studied biomanipulated ponds could be caused by the strong effect of large zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation cover on phytoplankton biomass in eutrophic ponds. Higher nutrient threshold levels could be an advantage for deciding and attempting a restoration of eutrophic ponds through biomanipulation. Nevertheless, even for ponds, beyond a certain threshold, nutrient levels might be too high to obtain a stable clear-water state after fish removal on the longer term. For management purposes, it is crucial to determine the threshold nutrient concentrations above which biomanipulation will no longer be successful in highly eutrophicated ponds. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for key factors (TP concentration, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size) that are known to strongly determine the outcome of biomanipulation in a series of peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationships between transparency and TP, and the obtained thresholds for eutrophic ponds are discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Materials and methods Study area For this study, 13 ponds, located in the Brussels Capital Region (Belgium), were biomanipulated and monitored during 2004–2010. All ponds are located within the same catchment (Woluwe river catchment) in a close proximity of each other (<10 km) and their connectivity is rather high. All the ponds were man-made and created more than a century ago by the damming of small low-order streams (Marlier, 1971). They are shallow (maximum depth 3 m), flat-bottomed and range in surface area from 0.2 to 6 ha and are mainly fed by small rivulets and ground water seepage. Lake metabolism scales with lake morphometry and catchment conditions Peter A. Staehr · Lars Baastrup-Spohr · Kaj Sand-Jensen · Colin Stedmon Received: 21 January 2011 / Accepted: 2 May 2011 / Published online: 17 May 2011 © Springer Basel AG 2011 Abstract We used a comparative data set for 25 lakes in Denmark sampled during summer to explore the influence of lake morphometry, catchment conditions, light availability and nutrient input on lake metabolism. We found that (1) gross primary production (GPP) and community respiration (R) decline with lake area, water depth and drainage ratio, and increase with algal biomass (Chl), dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and total phosphorus (TP); (2) all lakes, especially small with less incident light, and forest lakes with high DOC, have negative net ecosystem production (NEP < 0); (3) daily variability of GPP decreases with lake area and water depth as a consequence of lower input of nutrients and organic matter per unit water volume; (4) the influence of benthic processes on free water metabolic measures declines with increasing lake size; and (5) with increasing lake size, lake metabolism decreases significantly per unit water volume, while depth integrated areal rates remain more constant due to a combination of increased light and nutrient limitation. Overall, these meta-parameters have as many significant but usually weaker relationships to whole-lake and benthic metabolism as have TP, Chl and DOC that are directly linked to photosynthesis and respiration. Combining water depth and Chl to predict GPP, and water depth and DOC to predict R, lead to stronger multiple regression models accounting for 57–63% of the variability of metabolism among the 25 lakes. It is therefore important to consider differences in lake morphometry and catchment conditions when comparing metabolic responses of lakes to human impacts. Keywords Lake metabolism · Lake morphometry · Catchment conditions · Intrinsic drivers · Temporal variability Introduction Research on lake metabolism has shown that gross primary production (GPP), respiration (R) and net ecosystem production (NEP = GPP – R) vary considerably among lakes and over time within lakes (Cole et al. 2000; Hanson et al. 2006; Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007; Staehr et al. 2010a). Many lakes have a negative NEP and most release CO₂ to the atmosphere. This is due to the considerable supply and substantial degradation of allochthonous organic material from the surrounding landscape (Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). While day-to-day differences in metabolism within a lake are primarily driven by changes in light, temperature and vertical mixing (Hanson et al. 2006; Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007), long-term differences in metabolism between lakes are strongly related to changes in concentrations of total phosphorus (TP), phytoplankton chlorophyll (Chl) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) (Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). Thus, autotrophic lakes (NEP > 0) typically have high TP, high Chl and low DOC concentrations, whereas the most heterotrophic lakes have low TP, low Chl and high DOC (Hanson et al. 2003; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). Lake morphometry (surface area and depth), catchment properties (geology, size and land use) and hydrology have a strong influence on lake temperature, physical mixing, nutrient concentrations, DOC, Chl and transparency (Fee et al. 1996; Hanson et al. 2007; Nõges 2009), suggesting that these conditions operate as meta-parameters with an indirect but potentially strong effect on lake metabolism. Implicit scaling of lake productivity to lake size has been considered for decades (Thienemann 1927; Brylinsky and Mann 1973; Fee et al. 1992), and location in forests or open landscapes is also known to affect metabolism (Tranvik 1992; del Giorgio and Peters 1994; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). Thus, lake area is statistically positively related to wind exposure, water depth and mixing depth and inversely related to external input of nutrients and DOC per water volume and surface area (e.g., Brylinsky and Mann 1973; Duarte and Kalff 1989; Fee et al. 1996). Drainage ratio (catchment area:lake area) is positively related to external input of nutrients, CO\(_2\) and DOC (Gergel et al. 1999). Forest cover is negatively correlated with nutrient input and incoming irradiance for small lakes and positively correlated with DOC input and light attenuation by coloured DOC (Xenopoulos et al. 2003; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). In contrast to the substantial literature on the importance of meta-parameters for lake chemistry and physics, there are few comparative measurements of whole-lake metabolism, for a sufficiently large number of lakes, to evaluate the importance of lake size and catchment conditions on whole-lake metabolism and atmospheric CO\(_2\) exchange. This study investigates the effect of these meta-parameters on GPP, R and NEP, and compares their role with that of traditional direct drivers of metabolism (i.e., Chl, DOC, light and temperature). Our general expectation is that meta-parameters are significant though probably not as strong predictors of GPP, R and NEP as the intrinsic variables directly involved in metabolic processes. If so, more general predictive models can be derived and new understanding of control mechanisms can be obtained. Our first specific prediction is that both volumetric GPP and R should decline with increasing lake area, water depth and drainage ratio, as the concentrations and input of nutrients and DOC decrease (Nõges 2009). Although light availability decreases with increasing depth of the photic zone, light availability, is, however, expected to be similar across lake sizes as lower inputs of light absorbing material and greater mixing depth in larger lakes should cause mean light availability to remain similar among lakes of different sizes. Areal rates of GPP integrated over the entire water column is therefore expected to vary little with lake size, and the influence of lake size for GPP expected to be higher for volume specific rates. Our second specific prediction is that small lakes should have higher DOC input and concentrations and be more net heterotrophic (NEP < 0) than large lakes and that forest lakes should be more net heterotrophic than lakes in open landscapes. Small lakes have a greater contact and possibility of exchange of organic material with the terrestrial landscape along its periphery relative to lake surface area than large lakes. Forest lakes have a direct transfer of litter from the surrounding tree vegetation, receive less light for photosynthesis on the lake surface and have higher DOC concentrations in the water column competing with photosynthetic pigments for available photons causing mean light availability to remain low despite of a shallow mixed depth (Staehr et al. 2010a). Conversely, reduced input of DOC in larger lakes should favour positive NEP as mean light availability for primary production is the same but less allochthonous material is supplied for bacterial oxygen consumption. A final mechanism may restrict benthic photosynthesis relative to respiration in small forest lakes, namely the typical organic-rich sediments of flocculated humic material of low mass density that is physically instable for microalgae and unfavourable for growth of rooted plants (Barko and Smart 1986; Sand-Jensen et al. 2005). Our third specific prediction is that the contribution of benthic processes to whole-lake metabolism declines with increasing water depth. Because light penetration to sediments decreases with water depth, the benthic primary production should be more constrained by water depth than respiration and this should be particularly so in forest lakes with high DOC concentrations and poor light conditions. To the extent that lake depth and lake area are correlated, the role of benthic processes should also decline with increasing lake area, while surrounding forest vegetation may stimulate benthic R but impede GPP and NEP. Our fourth specific prediction is that the day-to-day variability of lake metabolism should decline with increasing lake area and depth. Measurements of whole-lake metabolism were performed over 1 week in each lake for subsequent comparison among all 25 lakes. This duration permits reliable calculations of mean daily metabolism and mean values for other physical, chemical and biological properties (Hanson et al. 2003; Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007). Moreover, 1 week measurements permit calculation of daily variability of metabolic parameters and their relationship to meta-parameters and within-lake parameters. With increasing lake area and water depth, temporal variations in the magnitude of physical mixing affecting different pelagic populations are likely to decline. Reduced external input of nutrients and DOC per unit water volume with increasing lake size should also reduce the carrying capacity for phytoplankton, zooplankton, bacteria and fish per unit volume and, thereby, dampen population changes and blooms. Materials and methods Study sites We studied lake metabolism in relation to physical, chemical and biological characteristics for about 1 week (6–8 days) in 25 medium to high alkaline lakes during May and June 2007. Systems ranged from ponds (0.1 ha) to midsized (1,729 ha) lakes, and were all located in calcareous moraines in Denmark (Table 1). Lakes were sampled in a random order to avoid bias from changing meteorological conditions during the study. Throughout the study, meteorological conditions were measured from a buoy placed on Lake Slotssø. Daily average wind speed (0.3–5.4 m s\(^{-1}\), min–max) and solar irradiance (5–55 mol photons m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) showed large daily variability, but did not change significantly during the course of the study. Lakes were chosen to cover large ranges in lake size, forest cover, TP, Chl and DOC concentrations. Lake area, catchment area, %forest cover in the catchment and drainage ratio (catchment area:lake area) were obtained for each lake using the digital Areal Information System (Nielsen et al. 2000). To evaluate effects of forest cover on local wind and light conditions, we also determined the proportion of forest in the 200 m wide riparian zone around the lakes from aerial photographs. Limnological variables Triplicate water samples were collected once from each lake as a depth integrated sample from the upper mixed layer at the center between 10 and 12 o’clock. Samples were analyzed for chlorophyll a, DOC, nutrients, alkalinity and pH. Samples for Chl and phaeopigments were filtered through Advantec\textregistered{} GC-50 filters, extracted in 96% ethanol for 24 h and measured according to Jespersen and Christoffersen (1987) using a Shimadzu UV-160A spectrophotometer. Absorbance of colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM) was measured in a GF/F filtrate (0.7 µm) at 300, 340, 360 and 400 nm in a 5 cm cuvette. DOC concentrations (mg C L\(^{-1}\)) were estimated from the linear relationship to CDOM absorption at 360 nm (m\(^{-1}\)): \( \text{DOC} = 0.454 \text{CDOM}_{360} + 1.9 \) (\( r^2 = 0.80 \)) found in a study of 399 water samples from Danish lakes and streams (C. Stedmon, unpubl. data). Total phosphorus (TP) was determined for unfiltered samples by persulfate digestion according to Eaton et al. (1995) and assayed according to Kragh and Sondergaard (2004). Water for determination of pH, alkalinity and CO\(_2\) was transferred to closed, dark glass bottles to avoid CO\(_2\) exchange with the air and prevent photosynthesis before measurement in the laboratory within 2 h. The pH was measured with Radiometer equipment (accuracy 0.01 pH unit). Acidimetric titration of alkalinity (acid neutralizing capacity, ANC), ionic strength, pH and temperature were used to calculate concentrations of free CO\(_2\) according to Rebsdorf (1972). The calculated CO\(_2\) concentrations have previously been shown to be in close agreement with direct CO\(_2\) measurements on an IRGA using a headspace equilibration technique (Sand-Jensen and Frost-Christensen 1998). Fluorescence of DOC was measured on a Varian Eclipse fluorescence spectrophotometer. An emission spectrum was measured every 2 nm between 300 and 600 nm, whilst exciting at 370 nm. The fluorescence index (FI; McKnight et al. 2001) was derived by taking the ratio of the fluorescence at 450 to that at 500 nm. This index can be used to characterize the chemical composition of DOC and indicate the relative contribution of terrestrial and aquatic organic matter. Index values typically range between 1 and 2, with terrestrial plant material resulting in low values. Depth profiles of oxygen and temperature were recorded in situ by an YSI 600XL multisonde. The vertical light attenuation coefficient (K\(_D\), 400–700 nm) was determined from the depth profile of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) using a LiCor 4π sensor. K\(_D\) was calculated as the slope of a linear regression model of irradiance (E\(_z\)) versus depth (z): \( \ln(E_z) = b + K_D \ z \). Physics and metabolism from sonde measurements We deployed a buoy at the centre of each lake to measure surface PAR, wind speed, water temperature and dissolved oxygen concentration (DO) for about 1 week. Three sets of this equipment were moved between lakes in a random order. Surface PAR was measured 1 m above the surface using a HOBO 2π quantum sensor. Wind speed was measured 1.2 m above the lake using a HOBO anemometer. Surface PAR and wind speed at the centre of each lake were normalized to measurements made throughout the summer in medium-sized Lake Slotssø (22 ha, 15% forest cover; Table 1). Normalization was simply the ratio of the wind speed at a lake to that of Lake Slotssø. This permitted comparison among the 25 lakes despite changes in mean weekly wind velocity and surface PAR during the summer. Water temperature was measured every 10 min during buoy deployment at several water depths, using a string of Stow Away Tidbit loggers. These data permitted calculation of mixing depth (Z\(_\text{mix}\)) at high frequency according to an empirical curve-fitting procedure (Staehr et al. 2010a). Dissolved oxygen was measured at 0.5 m either with an Oxyguard DO sensor or a YSI 600XL multisonde. Oxygen sensors were cleaned and calibrated prior and after each application. Electrode drift was small and was corrected for assuming it is linear over time. Oxygen concentrations recorded every 10 min were used to calculate NEP for 30 min intervals, according to the guidelines presented in Staehr et al. Atmospheric exchange was calculated as \( D = k(O_2 - O_{2sat}) \), where \( O_2 \) is actual oxygen concentration, \( O_{2sat} \) is oxygen concentration in water in equilibrium with the atmosphere at ambient temperature, and \( k \) is oxygen exchange calculated for each time step from the estimate of \( k_{600} \) and the ratio of Schmidt numbers as \( k = k_{600} ((Sc/600)^{-0.5}) \) according to Jähne et al. (1987). \( k_{600} \) [k for a Schmidt number (Sc) of 600] was estimated as a function of wind speed at 10 m above the lake surface as: \( k_{600} \) (cm h⁻¹) = 2.07 + 0.215 U¹.⁷ according to Cole and Caraco (1998). Assuming a neutrally stable boundary layer, wind speed (U) at 10 m was calculated from our measurements at 1.2 m using the relationship in Smith (1985). Because there is no photosynthesis at night, we assume nighttime R equals nighttime NEP measured from 1 h past sunset until 1 h before sunrise. Assuming that the daytime rate of R is equal to the nighttime rate (Hanson et al. 2003; Lauster et al. 2006) we calculated daily respiration rates as hourly R during nighttime × 24 h. GPP was determined as the sum of daytime NEP and R, and daily NEP was finally calculated as GPP – R (where R is in positive numbers). For ease of comparison, we present GPP values as positive and R values as negative. Volumetric metabolic rates (mmol O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹) were turned into areal rates (mol O₂ m⁻² day⁻¹) by multiplying with daily estimates of \( Z_{mix} \) for stratified lakes and mean water depth for fully mixed lakes. Pelagic metabolism from bottle measurements While calculation of whole-lake metabolism from sonde measurements are relatively common, measurements of benthic metabolism are rare because they require special sediment chambers and Scuba diving to set up and many replicates are needed because of great spatial heterogeneity. Because we wanted to make a comparative analysis among many lakes, direct sediment measurements were not an option. Instead, we evaluated the influence of benthic processes on free water measures of metabolism as the difference between measured whole-lake metabolism by oxygen sondes in open waters and simultaneous measurements of pelagic metabolism in bottle incubations. Replicate water samples from 0.5 m depth were used to determine net photosynthesis and respiration as the rate of oxygen change in closed 10 ml bottles during incubation for 13.5–23.4 h at ambient temperature. Bottles were placed on a rotating wheel (12 rpm) in a temperature-constant incubator and illuminated by cool-white fluorescence tubes from one side. Oxygen concentrations in the samples before and after incubation were measured using an oxygen electrode (OX500, Unisense with a picoammeter, PA2000, connected to a laptop computer). The electrode was calibrated at the incubation temperature in water at 100 and 0% air saturation. The irradiance was measured inside the incubation bottles with a minute 4π LiCor underwater light sensor. Samples were exposed to seven different irradiances ranging from 36 to 714 μmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ by using a set of neutral filters in front of the bottles. Samples for dark respiration measurements were wrapped in aluminum foil. From the obtained rates of net oxygen production (NP) at different irradiances (I), NP-I curves were constructed using the nonlinear model of Webb et al. (1974) in SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute Inc., 1994): \[ NP = GP_{max} \times \left[ 1 - \exp \left( \frac{(-\alpha \times E_{mean})}{GP_{max}} \right) \right] + Int \] where \( NP \) is net and \( GP_{max} \) is maximum gross photosynthesis (mg O₂ L⁻¹ h⁻¹), \( \alpha \) is the initial slope of photosynthesis versus irradiance, \( Int \) is the intersection with the y-axis corresponding to dark respiration and \( E_{mean} \) is the mean available irradiance in the mixed zone. Daily light availability (\( E_{mean} \); mol photons m⁻² day⁻¹) was calculated as an average for the mixed surface zone. Using data for surface irradiance (\( E_0 \); μmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹), mixing depth (m), and light attenuation (\( K_D \); m⁻¹), with a constant of 0.1 for back-scattering and surface reflection, \( \beta \) (Kirk 1994), \( E_{mean} \) was calculated from the equation: \( E_{mean} = E_0 (1 - \beta) (1 - e^{-K_D Z_{mix}})/(K_D Z_{mix}) \), modified from Riley (1957). Each NP-I curve was examined visually and obvious outliers were excluded to obtain reasonable models. NP-I models that did not saturate at high irradiance were also excluded. The calculated models yielded maximal net photosynthesis (\( NP_{max} \)), dark respiration (R), light utilization efficiency (\( \alpha \)), light compensation point (E_C) (the irradiance of which NP = 0) and light saturation point (\( E_K = NP_{max}/\alpha \)) (the irradiance at which photosynthesis starts to saturate). Using the derived NP models and measurements of ambient irradiance, we calculated net primary production in daylight (NPP_bottle; mg O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹) by integrating hourly NP rates from sunrise to sunset as: NPP = mean NP × h of daylight. Daily respiration (R_bottle; O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹) were calculated by multiplying hourly rates by 24. Daily rates of gross primary production (GPP_bottle; mg O₂ m⁻³ day⁻¹) were calculated as the sum of NPP and R_bottle. Daily values of GPP_bottle and R_bottle were calculated for the duration of the buoy deployment and average values were finally calculated for each lake to compare with averages of sonde-based metabolic rates. Statistical analysis Simple relationships between metabolic rates and physical and chemical variables were evaluated using a two-tailed Pearsons correlation analysis. All variables were log transformed to normalize distributions, ensure variance homogeneity and linearize relationships. To avoid negative NEP values in the analyses we added +1,000 to turn all NEP values positive. In our analysis, we applied p < 0.05 as a criteria for significant correlations. Empirical models of the variation in GPP, R and NEP as a function of lake size, forest cover were analysed by stepwise regression analysis. Only parameters which contributed significantly (p < 0.05) were included in the final regression models performed in SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute Inc., 1994). Results Lake characteristics The 25 lakes varied substantially in surface area (0.1–1,729 ha), mean depth (0.5–13.5 m), mixing depth (0.7–10.3 m; 12 out of 25 lakes were stratified) and forest cover in the catchment (1–91%; Table 1). Lake trophy ranged from mesotrophy to hypereutrophy and dystrophy according to the levels of TP (17–249 mg m^{-3}), Chl (4–402 mg m^{-3}), K_D (0.5–5.7 m^{-1}) and DOC (2.6–45.6 mg L^{-1}; Table 1). Lakes were medium to high alkaline (ANC; 2.3 ± 0.1 mq L^{-1} mean ± SE) and usually supersaturated (22 lakes) with CO_2 (Table 1). With increasing lake surface area, lakes became deeper, had deeper mixing depth (Table 2), were more wind exposed and received more incident light (Fig. 1; Table 2). Forest cover was not related to lake surface area and mean water depth (Table 2), but wind exposure and surface irradiance declined significantly with forest cover (Fig. 1b, d; Table 2). With increasing surface area, deeper water and lower drainage ratio, lakes contained less phosphorus, were more transparent and had significantly less phytoplankton (Chl), while none of these variables were significantly correlated to forest cover (Fig. 2; Table 2). According to the sonde-bottle estimates of GPP and R, the influence of benthic processes declined significantly with increasing lake area, water depth and drainage ratio (only R, but almost GPP), but showed no significant relationship to forest cover (Fig. 6a, b; Table 2). This result suggests that benthic processes become less important for the net metabolic balance as lake area and water depth increased (Fig. 6; Table 2).
