Crowding does alter respiration in invertebrates (Lampert 1984). Growth (\( G \)) of instars I–III of C. punctipennis was calculated as the exponential rate of increase in mass required to attain the observed mean mass of each instar at stations 1–3 (Fig. 3) over its development time (\( D_i \)). \( D_i \) was calculated from the temporal centers of mass, i.e., the abundance-weighted mean dates of occurrence (\( t_i \)), of each instar at stations 1–3. Lewis’s (1979: 51–53) methods were used to calculate \( t_i \) and, hence, \( D_i \). To calculate \( G \) for fourth-instar C. punctipennis, we assumed growth was 0 before 8 August 1983 because mean mass never increased prior to that date (Fig. 3). Thereafter, we assumed they grew at the average exponential rate required to support the increase in mean mass between sampling dates (Fig. 3). Growth of fourth-instar C. americanus was estimated in a similar way, but only when enough animals were captured that their abundance was reliably estimated, i.e., after 23 August 1983. Reported assimilation efficiencies (AE) for Chaoborus range from 0.52 to 0.91 (Cressa and Lewis 1986) and vary with larval development, prey type, and meal volume (Giguère 1981, Cressa and Lewis 1986). Values have not been determined for C. punctipennis or C. americanus. Because interpretation of our consumption data was not influenced by the choice of AE values spanning the range reported in the literature, we used Swift’s (1976) value of 0.67, for compatibility with Elser et al. (1987). First-order error analysis (Carpenter 1984) was used to calculate 95% confidence intervals in consumption from errors in estimates of larval Chaoborus growth and respiration. Variance in production of prey should be calculated from errors in estimates of prey biomass and birth rates. Because we pooled zooplankton samples from the three stations prior to enumeration, we estimated errors in production from errors in estimated birth rates alone (calculated following DeMott 1980). Therefore, the estimated errors for consumption of prey by Chaoborus and production of the prey should be considered minima, the former because they were calculated by error propagation, the latter because the contribution of spatial variation in prey biomass was not considered. RESULTS Plankton community structure The phytoplankton community of Swan Lake was very simple. Green algae, principally Oocystis parva West and West, were the dominant taxa in the early summer of 1983. Dinoflagellates, especially Peridinium inconspicuum and a large (30 \( \mu \)m diameter), spherical, unidentified Gymnodinium, formed virtually all of the biomass for much of the rest of the year. There was a large bloom of the chrysophyte Dinobryon bavaricum in November (Fig. 4). The zooplankton community was simple and unusual. The biomass of planktonic Rotifera was, on average, an order of magnitude higher than that of Crustacea (Fig. 4). Polyarthra spp. and Keratella tau-rocephala were the dominant rotifers, although the abundance of the latter species was much reduced from 1977 when the lake was more acidic (MacIsaac et al. 1986). Trichocerca similis was also very abundant (averaging 107 animals/L), but because of its small size (Table 1) it contributed little to total rotifer biomass. The small, acid-tolerant, herbivorous cladoceran Bosmina longirostris was the dominant crustacean zooplankter. Its biomass was quite variable. Maximum values were observed in the early spring (Fig. 4), an unusual time in a temperate lake. Daphnia spp. and Holopedium gibberum were absent from the lake. This is typical of acid and metal-contaminated lakes near Sudbury (Yan and Strus 1980), and is probably a direct consequence of the acid sensitivity of Daphnia (Keller et al. 1990) and the metal sensitivity of H. gibberum (Lawrence and Holoka 1987). The ubiquitous calanoid copepod Diaptomus minutus was present, although its contribution to total biomass was negligible. Orthocyclops modestus was the only cyclopoid copepod observed in the lake (Fig. 4). Phytoplankton, rotifer, and crustacean assemblages observed in 1983 were similar to those observed in 1982 and 1984 (W. Keller, H. J. MacIsaac, and N. D. Yan, personal observations). There were an average of 0.19 Chaoborus punctipennis/L and 0.009 C. americanus/L during the ice-free season of 1983. Monthly samples collected in 1982 produced somewhat higher average densities of 0.49 and 0.04 larvae/L, respectively. The seasonal patterns of abundance of C. punctipennis were similar at the Fig. 4. Seasonal changes in cumulative contribution of taxa to total plankton biomass (\( \mu g/L \) wet mass for the algae and dry mass for the animals) of phytoplankton, Rotifera, Crustacea, and Chaoborus in Swan Lake in 1983. The uppermost line indicates the total biomass of the group. Major contributing taxa are indicated. three pelagic and the two littoral stations (Fig. 5). Adults emerged over the entire summer with peak emergence during July and August. The substantial decline in the measured planktonic abundance of \( C. punctipennis \) in the fall is most likely attributable to the failure of the larvae to migrate into the water column at that time of year (Wood 1956). Abundances of the early instars of \( C. americanus \) were clearly underestimated (Fig. 4). We assumed they must have inhabited either extremely shallow waters or the relatively large areas of the lake we did not sample (Fig. 1). Rotifers contributed a remarkable 62% of the average zooplankton biomass (including Chaoborus) during the ice-free season in Swan Lake in 1983. Chaoborus larvae contributed 32%, and crustacean zooplankton the remaining small fraction (6%) of the total biomass (Fig. 4). The Crustacea : Chaoborus ratios are not unusual for acid lakes in Canada supporting populations of \( C. americanus \) (N. D. Yan, personal observation). Chaoborus diet The relative numbers of organisms identified in the crops of \( C. punctipennis \) changed both within and among developmental stages. Excluding algae, the crops of first-instar animals contained only rotifers, and those of second-instar animals contained little but rotifers (Fig. 6). The relative abundance of \( K. taurocephala \) in the crops increased with larval stage. In contrast, the importance of the smaller Trichocerca sp. in the diet declined in older larvae. \( B. longirostris \) was virtually the only crustacean zooplankter consumed. It formed roughly 30% of animals encountered in the crops of third-instar and young fourth-instar larvae, but the older fourth-instar larvae, those captured in the spring and late fall, fed almost exclusively on \( B. longirostris \) (Fig. 6). With the exception of one nauplius, copepods were 1–2 orders of magnitude less abundant than \( B. longirostris \) in the plankton of the lake. Fig. 5. Seasonal changes in the total abundance of Chaoborus punctipennis at the three open water and two littoral stations in Swan Lake in 1983, and the proportional contribution of developmental stages to the total. The range in total abundance among stations is indicated. The prey identified in C. americanus crops closely resembled that of C. punctipennis. The crops of first- and second-instar animals contained only rotifers. The relative importance of K. taurocephala peaked in third-instar larvae. Crustacea, principally B. longirostris, first appeared in the diets of third-instar larvae (Table 2). Diaphanosoma sp. were not observed in the crops of either Chaoborus species, although it was occasionally an important contributor to zooplankton biomass (Fig. 4). Remains of either species of Chaoborus were not observed in the crops of C. americanus or C. punctipennis. A dinoflagellate resembling the large Gymnodinium that dominated the phytoplankton community for much of the summer (Fig. 4), was observed in crops of both species of Chaoborus, its frequency of occurrence declining with larval development. It was observed in an average of 15, 9, 3, and 0.2% of instars I through IV of C. punctipennis, respectively. Unfortunately, isolated cell wall fragments were often observed; hence, we could not estimate the number of dinoflagellates that were consumed. This suggests that predation by Chaoborus does not generally limit the abundance of this species in the lake. In contrast, the production of B. longirostris was less than its rate of apparent consumption by C. punctipennis from July to early September, and its consumption by both species of Chaoborus after mid-October (Fig. 9). We could not distinguish the magnitudes of the rates of production of B. longirostris and its consumption by Chaoborus in May and June, because the variance in estimated consumption was large at that time (Fig. 9), a consequence of the large variation in abundance of Chaoborus among stations (Fig. 5). Estimated finite rates of loss of all planktonic Crustacea to Chaoborus were much higher than estimates of loss rates of all planktonic Rotifera (Fig. 10). This is a consequence of the relatively small contribution of rotifers to the diet of latter instar Chaoborus species in the lake (Fig. 6, Table 2), and the relatively large contribution of latter instars to total estimated consumption. Estimates of loss of Crustacea were particularly high, >1 d^{-1}, when the biomass of Chaoborus was high (Fig. 4) and was composed mainly of instar III and IV larvae, the principal consumers of Crustacea. DISCUSSION Chaoborus diet While identification of the prey of Chaoborus was not the major objective of this study, such information is rare enough for the widely distributed C. punctipennis that some discussion of its crop contents is warranted. In midsummer collections from Post Pond, New Hampshire, Moore (1988) recorded a diet of C. punctipennis remarkably similar to that observed in Swan Lake animals. She observed large algae and rotifers in the crops of all instars. The contribution of rotifers to total crop biomass declined monotonically with increases in larval development, as in Swan Lake. Crustacea, including B. longirostris, were only observed in III- and IV-instar larvae, as in Swan Lake. In summary, it is clear that C. punctipennis from Swan Lake can maintain a diet resembling that of a nonacidic lake despite the impoverishment of the plankton assemblages of the lake. Dinoflagellates were observed in the crops of many young C. punctipennis in Swan Lake. While it has generally been assumed that Chaoborus is zooplanktivorous, it is now clear that large algae, dinoflagellates in particular, may often be important in the diet of small Chaoborus species such as C. punctipennis (Elser et al. 1987, Hare and Carter 1987, Moore 1988). Early Chaoborus instar mortality is usually very high in oligotrophic lakes (Neill and Peacock 1980). Dinoflagellates, particularly *Peridinium limbatum* and *Peridinium inconspicuum* commonly dominate the phytoplankton of acidified, north-temperate lakes (Fig. 4; Stokes 1986). *Impact of Chaoborus predation on zooplankton* There is no doubt that *Chaoborus* can dramatically alter zooplankton community structure and standing stocks in nutrient-rich lakes in the absence of fish. A large proportion of early-instar larvae survive because food is plentiful (Neill and Peacock 1980), and older larvae prosper in the absence of predation from fish. The resulting large *Chaoborus* populations can decimate a zooplankton community (Lynch 1979, Neill and Peacock 1980, Yan et al. 1982). Predation by *Chaoborus* may also be important in oligotrophic lakes in the absence of fish (Dodson 1972, Vanni 1988); however, Neill (1981) indicated that the zooplankton community structure of a fish-free, oligotrophic lake in western Canada was rarely influenced by resident *Chaoborus* populations. Therefore, the absence of fish from oligotrophic lakes does not guarantee that zooplankton community structure will be regulated by *Chaoborus*. The evidence supporting the hypothesis that *Chaoborus* regulate zooplankton community structure in acidified lakes is actually quite weak. While Nyman et al. (1985) purported to test the hypothesis, their experiment was not performed in an acidic lake, and it was of unrealistically short duration (3 d). Yan et al. (1982) showed that *Chaoborus* regulated zooplankton community structure and biomass in an acidic lake after it was fertilized, but fertilization produced such unusually large populations of *Chaoborus* that the data set is of limited use. Stenson and Oscarson (1985) argued that the biotic changes that followed the additions of rotenone to a nonacidic lake (Stenson et al. 1978) provided support for the hypothesis. However, there is no reason why community changes induced by the addition of rotenone to nonacidified lakes must match those changes accompanying the acidification of lakes. Nyberg (1984) attempted the only previous quantification of the impacts of predation by *Chaoborus* on the zooplankton of lakes acidified by atmospheric deposition of strong acid. Prior to the addition of neutralizing agents and fish to Lakes Iglafallssjön and Blanksjön in Sweden, Nyberg estimated consumption rates of third- and fourth-instar *Chaoborus* larvae using Kajak and Rybak's (1979) methods. Our Swan Lake analyses indicate that consumption from these instars should approximate total consumption (Fig. 8). Nyberg concluded that, from May to October, *Chaoborus* predation exceeded prey production in the former but not the latter lake, prior to treatment. Because he recorded an average of only 0.033 *Chaoborus*/L in Iglafallssjön over the time period, while there were an average of 0.154 larvae/L of the same developmental stages in Swan Lake (calculated from Fig. 5), we should not be surprised if *Chaoborus* influence zooplankton community structure in Swan Lake. The Swan Lake analyses suggest that *Chaoborus* regulated the abundance of *B. longirostris* in Swan Lake for much of the ice-free season of 1983 (Fig. 9). Further, a comparison of loss rates of Crustacea to *Chaoborus* (\( L \) in Fig. 10) with published production/biomass (\( P/B \)) ratios of the planktonic Crustacea of lakes of nutrient status comparable with Swan Lake suggests *Chaoborus* probably maintain the unusually small crustacean zooplankton biomass in the lake. For example, Makarewicz and Likens (1979) reported daily \( P/B \) values for crustacean zooplankton of 0.04, 0.04, 0.05, and 0.06 for Mirror Lake, Lakes 239, Clear, and Naroch, respectively. Values of \( L \) in Swan Lake exceeded these values on all but the first visit to the lake (Fig. 10). While all *Chaoborus* instars consumed rotifers, the abundance of *K. taurocephala*, the favored rotifer prey, was apparently not regulated by *Chaoborus* (Fig. 9). Further, it is unlikely that *Chaoborus* predation controlled total rotifer biomass. Estimated daily rates of loss of rotifer biomass to *Chaoborus* never exceeded 0.1 and were frequently <0.01 (Fig. 10). In contrast, Makarewicz and Likens (1979) recorded much higher average daily \( P/B \) ratios of planktonic rotifers in oligotrophic lakes, e.g., 0.11 in Mirror Lake and 0.35–0.37 in Clear Lake and Lake 239. The validity of these conclusions hinges largely on the accuracy and precision of the estimated consumption rates, which in turn depend on the estimates of growth, respiration, and assimilation, and on the identification of *Chaoborus* prey. Our choice of assimilation efficiency is not worrisome, because the differences be- tween consumption and production rates were generally so large (Fig. 9), that a selection of values covering the published range for nonsatiated larvae (0.6–0.9) did not alter our conclusions. We cannot verify the accuracy of our respiration estimates because the influence of temperature and stage of development on the respiration of C. punctipennis has not been determined. Nonetheless, because the value of \( b \) in Eq. 3 (0.67, \( b - 1 = -0.33 \)) lies satisfyingly near the midpoint of the range of values reported for aquatic invertebrates (0.52–0.88, Lampert 1984), we do not think our respiration estimates bias our conclusions. In contrast, the consumption estimates of Rotifera and Crustacea are biased to high values by our failure to include consumption of algae in the calculations. Because Elser et al. (1987) and Moore (1988) observed that algae contributed an average of only \( \approx 10\% \) of the biomass of the crop contents of third- and fourth-instar C. punctipennis, we think the magnitude of this bias is probably small. Our estimates of Chaoborus growth are the most worrisome component of the calculations. The problem is not that the estimated rates of growth (Table 3) are impossibly high. From Pawson and McEachern’s (1987) length-mass relationships of Chaoborus flavicans and Hanazato and Yasuno’s (1989) reported body lengths and development times of this species cultured at saturating food conditions, we estimate that the mass of instar II and III C. flavicans can increase at 50–60%/d at 20°C, growth rates comparable with subtropical larval chironomids (Stites and Benke 1989). Clearly, Chaoborus can grow at rates exceeding those we calculated in Swan Lake (Table 3). Indeed, our estimates of growth of C. punctipennis in Swan Lake may be too low, because our weakest assumption was that C. punctipennis was univoltine (Fig. 5). While the species is usually univoltine at north-temperate latitudes (Hilsehnoff and Narf 1968, Carter and Kwik 1977, von Ende 1982, Sardella and Carter 1983), a bivoltine population has been described (Miller 1941). Our assumption of univoltinity produces conservative estimates of larval growth. Therefore, potential consumption rates of Crustacea may actually be higher than indicated in Fig. 9. It would clearly be useful to have laboratory measurements of both growth and respiration of C. punctipennis. Yan and Geiling (1985) suggested that the unusually high biomass of rotifers observed in Swan Lake in 1977, might be attributable to an abundant food supply linked to unusually low densities of crustacean competitors. Hurlbert and Mulla (1981), Neill (1984), and MacIsaac and Gilbert (1989) provide strong experimental support for such an hypothesis. However, Yan and Geiling could not explain the unusually low crustacean zooplankton biomass in the lake. The results presented herein indicate that predation by Chaoborus can account for the currently low crustacean zooplankton biomass of Swan Lake. In this report, we wished to investigate not the frequency with which Chaoborus regulate zooplankton community structure in acidified lakes, but the possibility of such regulation. Therefore, we selected a study lake we thought likely to show the effect, a mesotrophic, acidic lake with abundant Chaoborus. Apparently Chaoborus do not have much impact on zooplankton community structure in north-temperate lakes at abundances <30–50 individuals/m³ (Allan 1973, Nyberg 1984). Chaoborus abundance was lower than this threshold in four of five fish-less, acidified lakes (the exception being Swan Lake) surveyed by Yan et al. (1985). Therefore, while we support Nyberg’s (1984) demonstration that Chaoborus can regulate community structure in acidified lakes, an assessment of the frequency of occurrence of such control must await the assessment of Chaoborus population size in many more acidified lakes. Investigators planning such surveys should consider both presence of fish and lake nutrient status during lake selection, because both influence the abundance of Chaoborus (Neill and Peacock 1980, Yan et al. 1985). Further, such surveys should not be focused solely on the nonmigratory species of Chaoborus that are more sensitive to fish predation. In Swan Lake and in Nyberg’s Lake Iglafallssjön, the species of Chaoborus that were the major zooplanktivores were C. punctipennis and C. flavicans, respectively. Both are migratory species (Borkent 1981). Many of the biological changes that accompany the acidification of lakes are directly attributable to the toxicity of acid lake waters (Holtze and Hutchinson 1989, Keller et al. 1990). However, there is increasing evidence that other changes may be indirectly related to habitat acidification (reviewed by Stenson and Eriksson 1989). Examples of indirect agents of community change include alterations in lake thermal regimes (Yan 1983), reductions in nutrient supply (Jansson et al. 1986), increased prevalence of parasites (France and Graham 1985), and alterations in magnitude and type of competitive (Eriksson 1979) and predatory (Stenson and Eriksson 1989) pressures. In this report we have provided quantitative support for a biological change accompanying acidification that has an indirect cause, unusual zooplankton community structure maintained by invertebrate predation. Your use of the JSTOR archive indicates your acceptance of the Terms & Conditions of Use, available at https://about.jstor.org/terms Relationships between species number, lake size and resource diversity in assemblages of breeding waterfowl Johan Elmberg*, Petri Nummi, Hannu Pöysä and Kjell Sjöberg Finnish Game and Fisheries Research Institute, Game Division, PL 202, FIN-00151 Helsinki, Finland, Department of Applied Zoology, University of Helsinki, P.O. Box 27 (Viikki, C), FIN-00014 University of Helsinki, Finland, Finnish Game and Fisheries Research Institute, Evo Game Research Station, Kaitalammintie 75, FIN-16970 Evo, Finland and Department of Animal Ecology, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, S-901 83 Umeå, Sweden Abstract. Breeding waterfowl, habitat diversity and food diversity were studied in 31 boreal lakes in Finland and Sweden. Lakes were 2–48 hectares in size, and had zero to eleven waterfowl species each. In all, sixteen species of Gaviiformes, Podicipediformes, Anseriformes and Fulica were recorded. The observed species distribution deviated from the ‘null’ expectation derived from a model of random placement, indicating a low importance of lake area per se. However, lake area was found to be a better predictor of species number than was length of shoreline, and lake area–species number regressions gave values between 0.255 and 0.345. We further evaluated ‘the area per se (sampling)’ hypothesis and ‘habitat diversity’ hypothesis separately by multiple stepwise regressions, in which lake area explained most of the variation in species number in species dependent on the lake for brood-rearing. Richness of more mobile species and of all species was best explained by the number of prey taxa encountered in the lake. Key words. Sampling hypothesis, habitat diversity hypothesis, island biogeography, waterfowl, lake area. INTRODUCTION Among other early workers, Palmgren (1930) made the observation that big survey areas generally support more bird species than small (see Coleman, et al., 1982, and Ås, Bengtsson & Ebenhard, 1992, for further examples). Palmgren also discussed the processes behind the pattern, explicitly in the context of adaptation to edaphic factors and interspecific competition, and implicitly in relation to habitat heterogeneity. The topic was later treated within a more rigid and unified theoretical framework by MacArthur & Wilson (1967), who used archipelagos as a model system, and who theorized that colonization-extinction dynamics is the process behind the pattern. One of the disputed questions of island biogeography is whether there is an ‘island size effect’ as such, or whether big islands support more species than small islands simply because they have a greater diversity of habitats (Abbott, 1978 v. Tonn & Magnuson, 1982; Williamson, 1981; Price, 1984; Blake & Karr, 1987; reviews in Begon, Harper & Townsend, 1990, and Ås et al., 1992). With special reference to birds, which are good dispersers, Lack (1976) argued that habitat heterogeneity is crucial as to whether a species will become established on an island or not. Williamson (1981), Coleman et al., (1982) and Haila (1983), among others, have discussed shortcomings of the theory of island biogeography. Nevertheless, it has proven to be of immense heuristic value, and it is now being widely applied in conservation biology and in management of biodiversity (e.g. Harris, 1984; Hansson, 1992; but see Ashton, 1992, for a review of competing paradigms in plant ecology). As Haila (1983) and Wiens (1989) have pointed out, there are still relatively few studies of species number–island area relationships in birds which include direct measurements of several aspects of habitat diversity. In this paper we examine patterns of species richness in breeding assemblages of migratory waterfowl in North Europe in relation to characteristics of lake size, habitat diversity and food diversity. After testing the observed pattern of species richness against a null model of random placement (cf. Coleman et al., 1982; Möller, 1987) we evaluate alternative predictions supposed to operate in ecological time, namely that species number increases with the following. Sampling When not given here, the dates and details of the methods are the same as in Elmberg et al. (1993). In brief, we did the following. All field data were gathered with identical methods in 1990 (Västerbotten, Häme and Karjala) and 1991 (Lappi). For the justification of using data from 2 years, see Elmberg et al. (1993). Many of the species in this study place their nest on land. In some of them, adults as well as broods forage mainly in shallow water along the shore. Therefore it can be argued whether the appropriate measure of 'island area' is the lake's area or the length of its shoreline. Hence, we estimated both from topographical maps (scale 1:10,000 in Sweden, and 1:20,000 in Finland). We used the point count method of Koskimies & Väisänen (1991) to census waterfowl, i.e. all Gaviiformes, Podicipediformes, Anseriformes, and coot (Fulica atra L.). This was done four times in the early part of the breeding season, when pairs had arrived on the lakes and breeding had started. The total number of species recorded in a lake is here referred to as 'all waterfowl'. However, it is a heterogeneous group, comprising species with different food preferences. Our method of sampling invertebrates (see below and Elmberg et al., 1992) well reflects the availability of food preferred by dabbling ducks (genus Anas), some diving ducks (genera Aythya and Bucephala), and coot. If food diversity is important to species number, we would expect a stronger correlation with species number in this group than, say, with the number of species of loons (Gavia), grebes (Podiceps), (1) Increasing lake size. (2) Increasing vegetation heterogeneity of the habitat. (3) Increasing food resource diversity. In his review of the literature about species–area relationships in birds, Wiens (1989) concluded that functionally different groups may differ from one another in their response to area. Here we use different subsets of the waterfowl species pool to evaluate such patterns, also in relation to utilization of surrounding areas (see Möller, 1987). METHODS Study area The theory of island biogeography is based on the assumption that the archipelago studied has been colonized by species belonging to the same species pool (MacArthur & Wilson, 1967). Out of a larger data set from sixty lakes in Sweden and Finland (Elmberg et al., 1993) we therefore selected thirty-one lakes in four regions well within the boreal forest zone (Fig. 1). Apart from sharing the same general species pool and not being just parts of larger lakes, the study lakes (Appendix 1) are thus characterized by being: (a) ice-covered in winter, (b) permanent, with slight between-year variations in water level, and (c) inhabited by completely migratory waterfowl populations. The species studied are closely tied to lake habitats for nesting, brood-rearing as well as for post-breeding molt. Since they are migratory every lake is colonized anew each year. Hence, the study lakes are functional islands to breeding waterfowl from a resource point of view, but they are not very typical islands from an immigration and emigration point of view (cf. Brown & Dinsmore, 1988; Haila, 1990).

In his study of woodlot 'islands' in an agricultural landscape, Möller (1987) distinguished between patch foragers and species which forage also outside the patch ('island'). A similar distinction can be made here. Among the species studied, dabbling ducks and Whooper swan (Cygnus cygnus L.) easily and frequently move their brood to another lake to forage (the subset here called 'lake changing species') (Beard, 1964; Talent, Krapu & Jarvis, 1982; Duncan, 1987; own observations). Diving ducks (Aythya, Bucephala and Mergus), on the other hand, do not undertake such movements so often (here called 'intermediate species') (Eriksson, 1978; Pöysä & Virtanen, in press). Artic loon (Gavia arctica L.), grebes and coot, finally, do not move their young over land at all ('one-lake species'). Further, chicks of dabbling ducks have a shorter fledging period than chicks of the 'intermediate' and 'one-lake species' (mean for species in this study 41, 58, and 63 days, respectively; data from Cramp & Simmons, 1977, 1980). DISCUSSION As the observed species-richness patterns did not fit the random placement null model, we proceed to evaluating the role of different aspects of food and habitat diversity. Our method of sampling aquatic prey best reflects the availability of that consumed by the 'non-piscivore' species group (e.g. Cramp & Simmons, 1977, 1980). If food diversity is important to the number of species, we predict the number of species in this group to be: (a) correlated with the number of prey taxa, (b) correlated with prey size diversity, and (c) less or not correlated with lake area. Predictions (a) and (c) were met, and the notion that the number of prey taxa is important to species number was further sustained by the results of the stepwise regression analysis. In agreement with Möller (1987) our data indicate that patch area is the more significant determinant of species number the more functionally dependent the species are on the patch (see also Blake & Karr, 1987). Pairwise correlations as well as stepwise multiple regression analysis showed that area is an important determinant of species number in the two subsets of species which are most dependent on the lake for brood-rearing. On the other hand, richness of 'lake-changing species' (= 'non-patch' species) was not correlated with lake area. Instead, food diversity and habitat structural diversity were crucial. Further, our study warrants the following generalizations: (a) aspects of food diversity, i.e. the number of prey taxa, may generally be as important as lake area to species richness. Nilsson & Nilson (1978) argued similarly with respect to the general productivity of lakes. (b) The relatively low \( R^2 \) values obtained in the final models imply that other factors than the two measures of size and the four diversity variables may be important to species number. What might such other factors be? Abundance of prey is a likely complement (Nilsson & Nilsson, 1978; Haila, 1983). In a previous analysis of local assemblages of dabbling ducks in a larger number of lakes, we presented a model which explains more of the variation in species number than does the model in the present paper (Elmberg et al., 1993). The former model includes two measures of prey abundance a well as a composite (PCA) measure of habitat structural diversity. In the waterfowl community studied area as well as habitat diversity (cf. Ås et al., 1992, p. 220) thus appear important to species richness, sometimes each by itself and sometimes both at the same time, but area per se only in smaller groups of species strongly functionally dependent on the lake (island). Some Observations on Internal Recycling, Regeneration and Oscillation of Dissolved Nitrogen and Phosphorus in Shallow Self-contained Lakes By Jan Barica, Winnipeg With 15 figures and 3 tables in the text Abstract From the fluctuations in mass of nutrients in the water column of four productive shallow lakes in the Erickson area, southwest Manitoba, it is possible to assume that the decomposing plankton is an important source of ammonia and phosphate. The cycle of these nutrients appears to be essentially internal and periodically repeated. The nutrients were released from decomposing algae during totally or partially anoxic conditions in mid-winter under the ice and during short periods in the summer following the collapses of algal blooms. The ammonia and phosphate was subsequently assimilated by algae, transformed into particulate or dissolved organic form and released again. Oscillatory pattern of rates of chemical changes in the bloom-collapse period was demonstrated. Dissolved organic nitrogen and dissolved organic phosphorus were produced by both living and decomposing algae. The midwestern pothole winterkill lakes are small water bodies located in isolated depressions. They lack any permanent inflow or outflow, and depend on temporary surface runoff and groundwater seepage for their water supply (Fig. 1). The lakes are usually shallow (2—3 m) with no pronounced thermal stratification. Some of the surrounding land is intensively farmed and the lakes have reached high degrees of eutrophy. Many of the lakes experience noxious algal blooms in the summer. In addition most of them also develop anoxic conditions during the 5—6 month long ice cover period. Hence the name "winterkill" lakes. In spite of this drawback, these lakes represent a great potential for summer fish farming (Johnson et al. 1970). In this paper some observations on internal recycling of dissolved nitrogen and phosphorus are presented. They deal with four representative shallow self-contained lakes, with the objective of determining the mechanism and kinetics of chemical changes taking place during characteristic periods of the annual cycles of the lakes. This work presents a part of broader chemical-limnological studies, currently in progress as a part of the aquaculture program of the Freshwater Institute. Fig. 1. Aerial photograph of a group of pothole winterkill lakes. Lake 885 and surrounding lakes. Study Area and Methods The four lakes discussed in this paper are some of about 50 being used for experiments with rainbow trout farming in midwestern winterkill lakes. They are located near Erickson in southwestern Manitoba, south of the Riding Mountain National Park, at about 50° 30' N, 100° 10' W. The area is characterized by morainal deposits resulting from a series of glaciations during the Pleistocene. Many "potholes", formed by remaining blocks of ice after the general ice-sheet retreat, subsequently became small discrete lakes with neither inflow nor outflow. They depend on temporary surface runoff and groundwater seepage for the maintenance of their water levels, which fluctuate significantly. Most of the area is cultivated with natural forest remaining on hillsides and lake shores (Sunde et al. 1970). The lakes vary significantly as far as their water quality is concerned: some lakes are clear with no apparent algal blooms in the summer, others experience water blooms without any radical changes in their quality. The most problematic group of lakes are those containing nearly pure cultures of Aphanizomenon flos aquae, reaching in mid-summer noxious levels of 0.5 to 2 ml/liter. The sudden dieoff and decomposition of the algal cells in the "summerkill" lakes can cause a complete depletion of dissolved oxygen (Barica 1973) and death of fish. The rationale for selection of representative lakes for this paper was as follows: 1. Lake 885: a representative example of the most extreme cases of summerkill lakes, with several consecutive blooms and collapses of Aphan. flos-aquae during the year. No fish stocks are able to survive the summer months. 2. Lake 154: a lake with less severe conditions of fish kills, having only one algal bloom collapse in late summer with a partial fish kill. 3. Lake 302: with blooms involving algae other than Aphan. flos-aquae. The collapse of the bloom does not cause a total oxygen depletion and subsequent fish mortalities. 4. Lake 255: A "good" lake in a fish farming and water quality sense, with algal populations evenly distributed throughout the summer and never reaching noxious blooms or bloom collapse conditions. All the above lakes are winterkill lakes, reaching anoxic conditions between December and February. They are re-stocked with fish every spring for summer fish farming (Johnson et al. 1970; Sunde et al. 1970). Morphometry, chemistry and phytoplankton data characterizing selected lakes are presented in Tables 1—2. The lakes are small (2.4 to 17.3 hectares), shallow (2—5 m) and fairly saline (specific conductance 780 to 1750 \( \mu \)mhos/cm). Magnesium and sulphate are the predominant ions. The four lakes were under observation from the middle of summer 1971 until April 1973 with the frequency of sampling adjusted according to the advance of the algal blooms, more frequently in summer (1—7 days) than in winter (1—2 months). The lakes were sampled in the center in a vertical profile (usually 0, 1, 2, 3 m in the upper part and 25—50 cm near the bottom), using a Kemmerer or Friedinger sampling bottle. Dissolved oxygen (DO) was measured at 50 cm vertical intervals in before-noon hours using a Model 4 Y.S.I. oxygen meter which was regularly calibrated by the Winkler method (APHA Standard Methods 1971). Ammonia and phosphate, i.e., soluble reactive phosphate as defined by Strickland & Parsons (1968) expressed as PO\(_4\)-P, were determined spectrophotometrically in the field laboratory at Erickson on a Spectronic 88 colorimeter (Bausch and Lomb). The phenol-hypochlorite (Solórzano 1969) and acid-molybdate-ascorbic acid (Murphy & Riley 1962) methods, respectively, were used. Nitrate was determined by reduction to nitrite with a Cd-Cu couple (Wood et al. 1967). Water samples were filtered using GF/C filters in the field laboratory and analyzed in Winnipeg for particulate C, N and P (Carlo-Erba elemental analyzer for particulate C and N, ignition and acid digestion for particulate P). Part of the filtrate was irradiated by ultraviolet light and analyzed for total dissolved nitrogen (TDN) and total dissolved phosphorus (TDP) (Henriksen 1970). Concentrations of dissolved organic nitrogen (DON) and dissolved organic phosphorus (DOP) were obtained by subtracting the inorganic forms from total dissolved N and P. Other major and minor constituents were determined by standard procedures of Freshwater Institute Analytical Laboratory (MS). The values shown here were calculated on the basis of determinations for various depths as integrated values for each vertical profile \[ M = A \int_{z_0}^{z_{\text{max}}} C(z) \, dz \] where M = total mass of the substance in the water column, A = area of the water column (1 m^2) and C(z) = concentration of the substance at depth z. Computations were done for DON, NH_3-N, NO_3-N, DOP, PO_4-P and compared with dissolved oxygen and particulate CNP, i.e., the sum of particulate C + particulate N + particulate P, representing the total biomass. CNP, and DO concentrations in Lake 154 from 1971 to 1973.](page_246_180_1347_1042.png) Fig. 3 lakes, as indicated by DO and particulate CNP lines, and are much more pronounced in lakes which produced blooms than in Lake 255, which is a non-blooming lake. Fluctuations in total N and P contents occur chiefly in 3 characteristic periods: 1. during the ice cover, mainly in its last phase (February—March); 2. prior to and during the algal blooms; 3. during the die-off or sudden collapse of the algal blooms. In all four lakes presented here there is an obvious periodicity as far as increase or decrease (release or uptake) of the nutrients is concerned; in mid-winter there is an appreciable accumulation of dissolved N and P in the lakes as a result of anoxic bacterial decomposition of organic matter and subsequent regeneration of N and P in inorganic forms. This process is intensified by the substantially limited uptake by algae at this time of the year due to their minimum production (winter 1972). In this period nitrate, ammonia and phosphate reach their peak concentrations and represent a potential nutrient supply for the productive period ahead. Since there is no L 302 DON — NH₃-N — NO₃-N DOP — PO₄-P — Partic. CNP — DO — Fig. 4 significant input of nutrients from the basin during the winter, we can presume that all inorganic N and P present was regenerated from dead plankton produced the previous season. This is in accordance with the results of laboratory experiments performed by Krause (1961, 1964). However, dead phytoplankton play the major role in these lakes due to their relative abundance over zooplankton. The degree of mineralization of organic matter in the winter period is highest in the most productive lake (L. 885), where the reserve of DON and DOP sank to zero levels and was quantitatively transformed into inorganic forms. This process was clearly pronounced in the "normal" winter conditions of '71/'72, while the unusually mild winter in '72/'73 and the continuing primary production under the ice until Fig. 5 Seasonal variations in total content of ammonia, nitrate, and dissolved organic nitrogen; reactive phosphate and dissolved oxygen and plankton biomass (expressed as particulate C + N + P) in the lake water column below 1 m^2 of the lake surface at the site of maximum depth (integrated values). December and a new start from February left an appreciably higher amount of unmineralized DON and DOP in the lakes. The basic source of ammonia and phosphate is obviously DON and DOP, which is either directly excreted by living algae in the previous productive season (Fogg 1966; LEAN & NALEWAJKO 1973) or liberated from the dead cells by bacteria during their lysis. Mainly DON shows a proportional decrease in its content during the winter period with the increasing ammonia concentration, which indicates that ammonia is produced by deamination of DON. Deamination of various dissolved organic N-compounds reaches its maximum in anaerobic late winter conditions. This applies also to the increase in NO_3-N content at the same time, although there is no evidence that the increase in NO_3-N is not only due to the minimum uptake by algae and the continuous input from groundwater. However, nitrate concentration was usually only a small fraction of the total inorganic nitrogen, as compared with NH_3-N. From among all N- forms present in the systems, DON is the most abundant form (3—6 times higher than NH_3-N). This is quite characteristic for lakes with blue-green algae (Prescott 1959). Following the ice break-up and the first occurrence of algal blooms the spring reserves of ammonia, nitrate, and phosphate are reduced to undetectable limits. This is accompanied by their transformation into the particulate form (see the appropriate lines for particulate CNP) together with photosynthetic production of DO. This state remains unchanged as long as the bloom stays alive. Then, if either a sudden collapse of the bloom or its gradual die-off takes place, ammonia and phosphate are rapidly released again via bacterial decay of dead algae. This decomposition, accompanied by a release of ammonia and phosphate, takes place in both settled algae on the bottom as well as sinking algae passing through the water column. The peaks of ammonia and phosphate release in the bloom-collapse periods correspond always to a sudden decrease in seston concentrations (as particulate CNP) and to a nearly total depletion of DO, reaching anoxic conditions in the whole water column for several days. There is usually a certain time lag between the decrease of DO and responding changes in N, P and seston, varying from 1 to 4 days, however, in some instances the response is faster. This depends presumably on the multiplication rates of bacterial populations decomposing the dead plankton and depleting DO, and the time lag required to reach their exponential phase. This at the same time makes any statistical correlation between DO, seston and various organic and inorganic N and P forms impossible. The released ammonia and phosphate are subsequently taken up by the upcoming new algal blooms, which can occur for several times a year (L. 885). Lake 255, which had no blooms, shows steady conditions in the summer without any significant fluctuations in the discussed chemical parameters and shows an appreciable release of nutrients only under sub-ice anaerobic conditions in the mid-winter. It is noteworthy that the release of ammonia or phosphate occurs even during the relative decrease of DO concentrations and not necessarily its complete depletion to anoxic conditions. With the progressing primary production, DON and DOP gradually increase their content and reach their maxima during the algal bloom collapses. This indicates on the one hand that they are produced by phytoplankton itself and do not enter the lakes from allochtonous sources, and on the other hand that they are released additionally from the dying plankton prior to their deamination (peaks of DON in the summer bloom period precede those of NH_3-N by several days in the blooming lakes). If the chemical parameters are compared with the occurrence and duration of algal bloom periods and algal bloom collapses, with resulting anoxic conditions as shown on the baselines of graphs 2—5, it can be seen that the fluctuations in the nutrient content correspond to blooms and decomposition periods, whether they be in the winter or in the summer. Decrease in DO content indicates subsequent releases of N and P from dissolved or particulate organic matter back into the water column. This supports the classical theories on phosphate and ammonia release during the reductive conditions (see Discussion). As far as cycling in release or uptake of nutrients is concerned, there are two distinct patterns: 1. the major year-to-year cycle, characterized by an initial stage in January—March which represents the substantial part of the nutrient supply (additional supplementary input by spring run-off is negligible and limited to a very short period of time — currently under study). The source of this nutrient supply is primarily the decomposed plankton and the mineralized dissolved extracellular products. This amount, since the further surface input from the trainage basin practically does not exist, must meet the demand of algae for the whole ice-free season. Since this amount is extremely high, it is sufficient to support an excessive growth of algae in all lakes except L. 255, where the initial supply is much lower. The initial supply is exhausted sometimes in mid-May, when the first algal blooms reach their maxima (L. 885, 154 and 302). 2. At this point, a series of short-time "minor" cycles starts. The first non-Aphanizomenon blooms (Table 2) die off (gradually without a depletion of DO) and a part of the nutrients is released back into solution by bacterial decomposition of dead cells. The new succession usually favours occurrence of Aphanizomenon flos aquae (L. 885, 154), which takes over completely, soon reaching densities as high as 1—2 ml/liter in near-shore parts of the lakes. Collapse of this bloom is accompanied by a greater oxygen depletion than the previous time. In the case of aquaculture lakes, fish stocks are killed partially or totally, depending on the severity and duration of the DO depletion. In this stage a new release of ammonia and phosphate takes place, with about 30—60\% of the initial winter supply being released again. These "little" cycles can occur several times during the ice-free season, with the new fraction of nutrients being released again and subsequently taken up by new blooms. In the most productive lakes, the algal blooms can occur under the ice (L. 885, 154). Eventually, the cycles end with the death of the last bloom and its bacterial decomposition, and the release of a new initial supply in the winter which is available for the new algal blooms in the forthcoming ice-free season. Both patterns are schematically illustrated in Fig. 6. Vertical distribution of N and P concentrations From the absolute increases or decreases of nutrients in water column shown earlier it is possible to assume that the decomposing plankton is the Fig. 6. Schematic diagramm showing a year-to-year cycling of regenerated N and P in shallow self-contained winterkill lakes. 1 — basic "major" cycle in a lake without any algal blooms (L. 255); 2 — supplementary summer "minor" cycles in lakes experiencing algal die-offs and fish kills (L. 885). major source of ammonia and phosphate in the shallow self-contained lakes discussed above and that their cycle is essentially internal, with released N and P being assimilated by algae, transformed into dissolved organic or particulate form, sedimented and released again to serve as nutrients for new algal populations. Since there is little surface inflow and outflow and groundwater movement is probably negligible, this explanation seems to be credible. However, the integrated values for the whole depth of each lake, presented in Figs. 2—5 and affected by the maximum depth of each lake, do not present an adequate picture of an actual movement of nutrients in the whole profile as well as the actual concentrations in conventional units (\( \mu g/l \)). To eliminate this drawback as well as to enable mutual comparison of the lakes discussed here, some representative vertical profiles, covering typical phases of the "large" or "small" cycles, are shown in Figs. 7—10. They present a vertical distribution of the mentioned chemical parameters starting with an initial stage in winter 1972 and ending with a new starting point for the new season, including summer uptake maxima during the bloom periods and the maxima releases of P and N during the algal collapses. Regardless of the time cycling, which was discussed earlier, this form of data presentation shows that the starting base for the release of nutrients during the reducing condition (DO depletion) is the lake bottom, i.e., the decomposing sediments. Thus, the positive \( dM \) values for ammonia and phosphate would represent nutrient release rates (\( g/day \) in water column of a \( 1 \ m^2 \) surface area), and the negative ones the uptake rates caused by algae. For DON and DOP the \( +dM \) values would represent rate of release by living or decomposing phytoplankton and the \( -dM \) values a bacterial uptake or mineralization rates respectively. For DO, \( +dM \) means a photosynthetic production, \( -dM \) on the other hand the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) rates (total oxygen uptake). In the case of seston (particulate CNP) it will be the net production or sedimentation respectively. From all presented derivation curves it follows that most of the chemical changes take place in the summer during the algal collapses, whereas the winter changes are much slower. The zero-axis shows a steady-state situation when chemical changes are evenly distributed over time. The shape of these L885 NH₃-N DON PO₄-P DOP DO Partic. Phosphate cancels itself only in L. 255 (no blooms) and in September—September cycle in L. 302. This indicates a periodicity of the nutrient release and uptake in a year-to-year cycle, i.e., a return to the initial stage, and is ultimately another formulation of the law of conservation of matter in an ecosystem of self-contained lakes. Positive D values in the balance sheet indicate an absolute increase of the particular substance in the water column, negative ones a decrease or a transfer into a refractive material in the sediments and a temporary exclusion from the cycle. DON and DOP values show an increase ranging from 22 to 32 % for DON and 7 to 28 % for DOP, as a result of continuous organic production and accumulation of organic substances in the lake in time. The highest D values of DON and DOP are in the non-blooming lake, 255, whereas in the other blooming lakes bacterial mineralization of DON and DOP reduces appreciably the net production of dissolved organic matter. An increase as high as this could presumably occur only on a short-time scale; a complete mineralization under anoxic winter conditions to balance the accumulated organic matter (as it happened in winter '71—'72) is highly probable (currently under study). However, in the other three lakes cancellation of positive and negative values shows that all N and P in an available form is completely regenerated, i.e., transformed from an organic form into an inorganic one. This cycle is completed within one year or less regardless when it initiates. Discussion Since the pothole lakes have no surface inflow during most of the year, and the groundwater movement in isolated basins is not expected to be significant, the question of the source of the plant nutrients, particularly phosphorus and nitrogen, arises, and it is natural to look for it in the lakes themselves. According to widely accepted theories by EINSELE (1938), OHLE (1938), MORTIMER (1941, 1942), and HUTCHINSON (1957), phosphorus is found in the form of an insoluble ferric salt in the lake bottom if the redox conditions are favorable, and is released into water column when iron is reduced to the ferro state in anoxic conditions of a lake hypolimnion. This concept has been further elaborated in recent years and shifted from a simple ferric-ferro model to more complex physical-adsorption approaches taking into account various mineral fractions of the lake sediments and their P-binding capacity (STUMM & LECKIE 1970; GOLTERMAN et al. 1969). LEE (1969) pointed out that knowledge is particularly lacking on the role of the lake sediments in maintaining phosphate levels in water. It is not known whether the sediments act as a sink in which the majority of nutrients is refractory, not available for exchange (HAYES 1964; LATTERELL et al. 1971; SCHINDLER et al. 1971), or whether the sediments act as a buffer in which phosphate concentrations in the overlying water are controlled by sediment-water exchange reactions (OHLE 1964, 1968; SERRUYA & BERNAN 1970; BURNS 1972; TESSENOW 1972; GOLTERMAN 1973). Our data indicate that an important source of nutrients in self-contained shallow lakes are the decomposed algal cells, i.e., the sediments and that the whole nutrient cycle is closed and periodically repeated. This can be characterized by a cycle: ![Diagram showing the nutrient cycle: N & P release from algal cells → N & P uptake, incorporation into particulate form → Die-off, sedimentation → Bacterial decomposition → Refractory N & P in the sediments](page_1012_1342_627_388.png) This cycle does not at this stage depend on external sources of nutrients from the drainage basin (these were however important in earlier stages of lake eutrophication history and over a long period of time — in a geological sense — which brought about the existing high nutrient supply). The absolute amount of the available nutrients in the lakes on a year-to-year basis apparently does not change substantially. These conclusions, although quite in agreement with the classical theories, differ in the geochemical aspect of the problem. Concentrations of Fe- or PO_4-absorbing clay minerals at the enormous production of phytoplankton and limited influx of mineral matter from the drainage basin cause that the sediments are formed mostly by dead algae in the summer and the total PO_4-P far exceeds stoichiometrically the available Fe (Fe/PO_4 meq. ratios are 9.32, 1.97, 2.67 and 1.75 respectively for the maxima (Table 1)). The chemical reactions in sediments may be therefore a result of biological processes as well as geochemical ones. I would rather see an analogy of our lakes as compared to large-scale algal cultures in flasks which are allowed to decompose. Indeed, our conclusions are very similar to those obtained from regeneration experiments performed with algal cultures in laboratory scale (Golterman 1960; Grill & Richards 1964; Foree et al. 1970). Particularly Golterman's (1973) model of P-recycling in shallow lakes, with an emphasis on the internal part of his recycling diagram, and his findings on the high efficiency of mineralization, agrees with the present results. The oscillatory patterns of daily release and uptake rates, presented in this paper, allow, both visual and mathematical assessment of the "normal" conditions of a lake. A lake system is in an equilibrium when dM values approach zero. A sudden collapse of an algal bloom, a rapid oxygen depletion and a take-over by decomposition processes act as a force causing disturbance of this equilibrium. The first amplitude of the released N or P is followed by its uptake. After a series of complete cycles, which takes usually several weeks, relaxation oscillations gradually fade out and the equilibrium is reached again. Since any oscillating matter vibrates above and below a mean equilibrium value (in our case it is zero), the sum of displacements in either direction should cancel out. This actually happens in most instances except for DON and DOP values. It proves a periodicity of the process, its return to the initial stage, and, in fact, the law of conservation of matter in self-contained lakes. In this context there is a basic difference between anoxic conditions in the winter, which occur gradually, and the rapid oxygen depletion following the bloom collapses in the summer. The latter affect the chemical equilibrium in lakes more significantly. Summary Variations in total mass of ammonia-, nitrate and dissolved organic nitrogen, phosphate and dissolved organic phosphorus, as compared with total mass of dissolved oxygen and plankton biomass (expressed as particulate CNP) in four productive shallow lakes in the Erickson area, southwest Manitoba, are described. The lakes are groundwater-fed with no permanent surface inflow or outflow. They belong to a pothole winterkill type, producing heavy algal blooms. The data collected between summer 1971 — spring 1973 are presented as total mass under a unit surface area as well as daily release or uptake rates. There are two distinct patterns in the nutrient regime of these lakes: 1) the major year-to-year cycle, characterized by an initial stage in January—March which represents the substantial part of the nutrient supply. The source of this is the decomposed plankton and the mineralized dissolved extracellular products. This amount is sufficient to support an excessive growth of algae. 2) The initial supply is exhausted sometimes in May, when the first algal blooms reach their maxima. At this point, a series of short-time "minor" cycles starts. The algal blooms die off and a part of the nutrients is released back into solution by bacterial decomposition of algal cells. In the case of aquaculture lakes, fish stocks are killed partially or totally, depending on severity and duration of the oxygen depletion. Oscillatory pattern of distribution of daily release or uptake rates of nutrients and other chemical constituents demonstrates a significant disturbance of the chemical equilibrium of the lakes caused by severe oxygen depletion following a collapse of algal blooms. It also shows that a release of ammonia and phosphate from organic matter occurs also during a relative decrease in dissolved oxygen concentrations and not only during its complete depletion to anoxic conditions. This work is a part of broader studies carried out within the aquaculture program of the Freshwater Institute. Zusammenfassung Die Schwankungen der Gesamtmengen von Ammonium, Nitrat und gelöstem organischem Stickstoff sowie von Phosphat und gelöstem organischen Phosphat werden in vier produktiven Flachseen im Ericksongebiet, Südwest-Manitoba, beschrieben und verglichen mit der Gesamtmenge an gelöstem Sauerstoff und der Planktonbiomasse, ausgedrückt als partikulärer C+N+P. Es handelt sich um Grundwasser-Seen ohne permanenten Oberflächen-Ein- oder Ausfluß. Sie gehören zu einem „pothole“ Typ mit starken Algenblüten und winterlichen Fischsterben. Die Ergebnisse von Sommer 1971 bis Frühjahr 1973 werden sowohl als Gesamtmenge unter einer Oberflächeneinheit als auch als tägliche Freisetzung- und Aufnahme-Raten dargeboten. Zwei verschiedene Zyklen des Nährstoffhaushaltes dieser Seen lassen sich unterscheiden: 1. Der umfangreichere Jahreszyklus, charakterisiert durch ein Anfangsstadium in den Monaten Januar bis März, welches den wesentlichen Teil der Nährstoffauffüllung darstellt. Die Nährstoffquellen sind das zersetzte Plankton und die mineralisierten gelösten extrazellulären Produkte. Diese Nährstoffquellen reichen aus für ein exzessives Algenwachstum. 2. Diese Nährstoffmenge aus der Anfangsphase ist in manchen Fällen im Mai erschöpft, wenn die ersten Algenblüten ihr Maximum erreichen. In diesem Zeitpunkt beginnt eine Serie von kleineren Kurzzeit-Zyklen. Die Algenblüten sterben ab, und ein Teil der Nährstoffe wird durch bakterielle Zersetzung der Algen wieder in Lösung zurückgeführt. In den fischereilich genutzten Seen sterben die Fischbestände teilweise oder total ab, abhängig von der Intensität und Dauer der Sauerstoffzehrung. Periodische Schwankungen des Verhältnisses von täglicher Freisetzung und Wiederaufnahme von Nährstoffen und von anderen chemischen Komponenten zeigen eine signifikante Störung des chemischen Gleichgewichtes der Seen, verursacht durch starke Sauerstoffzehrung, bzw. -entleerung als Folge eines Zusammenbruches der Algenblüten. Es zeigt sich ferner, daß eine Freisetzung von Ammono- nium und Phosphat aus organischer Substanz schon während eines relativen Abfalles der Konzentrationen des gelösten Sauerstoffes eintritt und nicht nur während des völligen Sauerstoffentzugs unter anaeroben Bedingungen. Strength of phytoplankton–nutrient relationship: evidence from 13 biomanipulated ponds Samuel Teissier · Anatoly Peretyatko · Sylvia De Backer · Ludwig Triest Received: 28 January 2011 / Accepted: 1 May 2011 / Published online: 18 May 2011 © Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2011 Abstract Phytoplankton biomass–nutrient relationship is widely used by lake managers to assess the eutrophication impact and to set the nutrient targets. Submerged vegetation and large zooplankton grazing have long been identified as factors weakening the relationship by decoupling phytoplankton from nutrients. Proving this decoupling unambiguously is difficult because, in natural systems, many factors act together, blurring each other’s effect. In this article, we present the results of continuous monitoring of 13 ponds where the effects of submerged vegetation and zooplankton grazing were enhanced by biomanipulation (fish removal). The monitoring allowed these effects to be assessed and compared with the pre-biomanipulation situations when phytoplankton biomass was mainly nutrient driven. The comparison showed a strong weakening effect of submerged vegetation and large zooplankton grazing on the chlorophyll \( a \)–total phosphorus relationship suggesting that a considerable degree of ecological quality of ponds affected by eutrophication can be restored even when nutrient-loading reduction is not feasible. Keywords Phytoplankton · Nutrient · Macrophyte · Zooplankton grazing · Pond Introduction Factors regulating biomass of phytoplankton, often represented by chlorophyll \( a \) (Chl \( a \)) concentrations, received considerable attention from aquatic ecologists. Nutrients are usually considered as the main determinants of the level of phytoplankton biomass in lakes and ponds. Higher nutrient levels generally imply higher phytoplankton biomass (Dillon & Rigler, 1974; Phillips et al., 2008). Because phosphorus is often the limiting nutrient for primary producers in fresh waters, it is used for the classification of lakes and ponds based on their nutrient richness, i.e. trophic status (UNEP, 2003; Bronmark & Hansson, 2005). Prediction of Chl \( a \) by total phosphorus (TP) is widely used for lake management. Some studies show, however, that the Chl \( a \)–TP relationship is weaker in shallow lakes and ponds than in deep lakes because in the former both turbid and clear-water states can exist over a wide range of nutrient levels (Moss et al., 1996; Scheffer et al., 2001). It becomes increasingly evident that the main factors weakening the relationship are large zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation, which are known to inhibit phytoplankton growth through a number of associated mechanisms, such as grazing, nutrient cycling, stabilisation of the water column, shading, and allelopathy (Hansson & Carpenter, 1993; Sondergaard & Moss, 1998; Cottingham & Schindler, 2000; van Donk & van de Bund, 2002). Although the effects of zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation on the Chl \( a \)–TP relationship are well known (Sarnelle, 1992; Steiner, 2002; Dokulil & Teubner, 2003), they have rarely been investigated and confirmed unequivocally because of their complex interaction with other factors blurring them in natural systems. This sometimes led to ambiguous results, e.g. difficulties to separate phytoplankton responses to planktivory-related changes in zooplankton from responses to changes in nutrient cycling caused by fish, macrophytes or bottom-up physical factors (Carpenter & Kitchell, 1992; DeMelo et al., 1992; Gragnani et al., 1999). Ponds are less than a few hectares in size (Sondergaard et al., 2005b) and, therefore, are easier to study and manipulate than lakes. Except for size, depth and residence time, however, almost all other variables having bearing on phytoplankton biomass in the ponds studied could be greater than in lakes (nutrient levels, zooplankton size, vegetation coverage, fish density, etc.). Therefore, ponds “magnify” the processes that occur in lakes, which helps us have better understanding about them. Planktivorous fish removal or piscivorous fish addition, generally referred to as biomanipulation, further enhances the effects of zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation on phytoplankton biomass (Shapiro, 1990; Perrow et al., 1997). Forty-eight eutrophic to hypereutrophic ponds from the Brussels Capital Region (Belgium) were studied from 2004 to 2009. The results obtained confirmed the importance of submerged vegetation and large zooplankton grazing for phytoplankton biomass control (Peretyatko et al., 2007b, 2009). Thirteen ponds have been biomanipulated during the study period to prevent the occurrence of noxious algal blooms and improve their ecological quality. Biomanipulation generally enhances the effects of zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation on phytoplankton biomass, thus underlining the importance of trophic interactions and competition for nutrients and light for phytoplankton biomass control. Continuous monitoring of these ponds have allowed the effects of these factors on nutrient–phytoplankton relationship to be assessed. The objective of this study was to compare the strength of the Chl \( a \)–TP relationship corresponding to situations where phytoplankton biomass was mostly nutrient driven with situations where it was mostly determined by submerged vegetation and/or large zooplankton grazing. Methods Forty-eight urban and peri-urban ponds from the Brussels Capital Region (Belgium) have been studied between 2004 and 2009. All the ponds studied are artificial, created by damming of low order streams in the twentieth century or earlier. They are all shallow (maximum depth <3 m) and flat-bottomed and range in surface area from 0.1 to 6 ha. A number of ponds are used for different recreational activities of which fishing and boating are the most common. The ponds are populated by fish communities typical of northern Europe. Many of them have large stocks (often more than 500 kg ha\(^{-1}\)) of plankti-benthivorous fish (mainly common carp: *Cyprinus carpio*, and bream: *Abramis brama*). In varying degrees, however, all of the ponds studied are affected by eutrophication caused by the historical and current urban pollution. Many of them are, therefore, prone to mass developments of phytoplankton generally dominated by bloom-forming cyanobacteria. This often leads to a formation of extensive surface scums and occasional fish and waterfowl kills (Peretyatko et al., 2010). The 11 ponds most affected by eutrophication (persistent phytoplankton blooms often dominated by bloom forming cyanobacteria, recurrent anoxic/hypoxic conditions, fish and waterfowl kills) were biomanipulated (emptied with fish removal) between 2005 and 2008 to improve their ecological quality, to reduce phytoplankton biomass and to prevent the formation of noxious cyanobacterial blooms. Two other ponds, less affected by eutrophication, were temporarily emptied for infrastructure works. Continuous monitoring of these ponds allowed for the assessments on the effects of fish removal. They were sampled monthly or at least on three occasions per warm season and at least 1 year before and 1 year after biomanipulation. The other Brussels ponds used in the analyses were sampled according to the same methodology (see Peretyatko et al., 2010 for details). Integrated water column samples based on 10 random sub-samples were taken from each pond with a plastic tube sampler. After stirring the collected water, dissolved oxygen, pH, conductivity and temperature were measured with a portable meter (WTW 340i), from which 500 ml was taken for the identification and enumeration of phytoplankton and 1 l for the analysis of Chl \( a \). For the determinations of soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP), ammonium and dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN), a 100-ml water sample was filtered through a GF/C glass microfiber filter and stored in a cooler. In the laboratory, the samples were frozen until analysis on a Quatro-segmented flow analysis system (Seal Analytical limited) according to the manufacturer’s procedures. For TP determination, a 100-ml water sample was stored in a cooler. TP was determined using the persulphate digestion method (APHA-AWWA-WEF, 1995). The samples for Chl \( a \) determination were kept in a cooler until delivery to the laboratory where they were immediately filtered onto GF/C glass microfibre filters. Filters were stored at \( -18^\circ \mathrm{C} \) for several days before analysis. Pigments were extracted in 90% acetone in the dark, at 4°C, overnight. Chl \( a \) concentrations were measured spectrophotometrically with due correction for pheophytin a (APHA-AWWA-WEF, 1995). For zooplankton, a combined 10-l sample consisting of 10 random sub-samples of 1 l was taken from each pond at the same location and with the same sampler as used for nutrients and phytoplankton. Zooplankton samples were filtered in the field through a 64-\( \mu \)m mesh net and preserved in 4% formaldehyde (final concentration) before being identified and counted with an inverted microscope. Different levels of identification were used: cladocerans were identified with respect to genus level; copepods were divided into cyclopoids, calanoids and nauplii; rotifers were not discriminated. For the analyses, cladocerans were divided into two groups: ‘large’ (Daphnia spp., Eurycercus spp., Sida spp. and Simocephalus spp.) and ‘small’ (Acroperus spp., Bosmina spp., Ceriodaphnia spp., Chydorus spp., Moina spp. and Pleuroxus spp.) (Moss et al., 2003). Predatory cladocerans, Leptodora spp. and Polyphe-mus spp., that feed mainly on other zooplankters (Reynolds, 2006), were not included in the group of large cladocerans. Because of their rarity, few individuals were only occasionally observed in a small number of ponds, their impact on large cladocerans was considered as negligible. Copepods and rotifers had no significant negative relationship with phytoplankton biomass. For these reasons, only large cladocerans were treated here. The length of large Cladocera species was measured and taken as an indicator of grazing intensity and size-selective predation (Pourriot, 1995; Carpenter et al., 2001). At least 20 or, if less, all present individuals of large cladocerans were measured in each sample. Zooplankton’s size and composition was considered as a proxy of fish community structure (Pourriot, 1995). The total surface cover of aquatic vegetation was mapped visually from a boat during each field visit. The presence/absence of the vegetation was verified with a rake when water was not sufficiently transparent. Because submerged macrophytes were often associated with filamentous green algae, which are also known to inhibit phytoplankton growth (Irfanullah & Moss, 2005; Peretyatko et al., 2007a), their combined surface cover was used in statistical analyses. Some ponds were recolonised by fish after biomanipulation (mainly juvenile planktivorous fish). Owing to the size of the fish being generally very small, it was difficult to make reliable quantitative estimates of fish density. The presence of fish in the biomanipulated ponds was assessed visually and by fishing with a landing net (4-mm mesh size) during each field visit. Ponds where fish reappeared in large numbers were considered as recolonised by fish. Hydraulic retention time was estimated on the basis of the outlet discharge (measured on each field visit during the period after biomanipulation) and the corresponding pond volume. Because retention time affected phytoplankton composition more than biomass, even in ponds with low retention time, it was not considered in the analysis of the Chl \( a \)-TP relationship. For statistical analyses, the data from biomanipulated ponds were averaged per pond per year and divided into subsets corresponding to three situations: (1) before biomanipulation; (2) after biomanipulation with submerged vegetation cover \( \geq 30\% \) and/or mean large Cladocera length \( \geq 1 \) mm; and (3) after biomanipulation with submerged vegetation cover \( <30\% \) and mean large Cladocera length \( <1 \) mm. The thresholds for submerged vegetation cover and large Cladocera length, seemingly the main controlling factors of phytoplankton biomass, beside nutrients, were derived from the analysis of the data collected from the 48 ponds studied and confirmed by other reports (see “Results” section for the threshold corroboration). Because large Cladocera length was not measured in 2004, there are less number of cases used in the analysis where large Cladocera length was involved. The statistical comparisons of the two different outcomes of the biomanipulation (ab1, ab2) with the before biomanipulation situation (bb1, bb2) were done using Wilcoxon matched pairs test; only 1 year before biomanipulation and 1 year after biomanipulation were used in the comparison (see Table 1 for details). The strength of the Chl \( a \)-TP relationships for the three situations was estimated by linear regression analysis of the log-transformed data. The slopes were compared using Tukey HSD test in the homogeneity of slopes model (StatSoft, Inc. STATISTICA version 8.0). Results All the ponds studied were characterised by high nutrient levels (Peretyatko et al., 2010). The biomanipulated ponds were particularly affected by eutrophication with TP concentrations well above 100 \( \mu \)g l\(^{-1}\) before fish removal. Dissolved inorganic nitrogen concentrations varied substantially from pond to pond, but often exceeded the level of 50–100 \( \mu \)g l\(^{-1}\) (Table 2) at which phytoplankton growth is likely to be slowed down due to nitrogen limitation (Reynolds, 1998). The data from the 48 ponds studied showed threshold relationships between Chl \( a \) yield per unit of TP and submerged vegetation cover and large Cladocera length, 30% and 1 mm, respectively. The thresholds are outlined by the minimum yields. The minimum values and mean Chl \( a \) yields are markedly lower above the thresholds (Figs. 1, 2). These thresholds are consistent with the submerged macrophyte threshold reported by Meijer et al. (1999) where low Chl \( a \) yield coincides with macrophyte cover exceeding 25% and *Daphnia* length threshold reported by Mazumder (1994) and Mazumder and Havens (1998) where Chl \( a \) yield is significantly lower in the presence of *Daphnia* exceeding 1 mm in size. Therefore, for the analyses, the data from the biomanipulated ponds were split into the groups corresponding to these thresholds. Before biomanipulation, the 13 biomanipulated ponds lacked submerged vegetation (mostly no or \( <30\% \) cover) and large-bodied cladocerans (mean large Cladocera length \( <1 \) mm; bb1, bb2; Fig. 3). Data from 48 Brussels ponds averaged per pond per year; a dashed line indicates the threshold used in statistical analyses Fish removal resulted in marked decrease of phytoplankton biomass in 12 out of 13 biomanipulated ponds and general increase in density and size of large cladocerans as well as restoration of submerged vegetation (submerged macrophytes and/or filamentous green algae) in nine ponds (Peretyatko et al., 2009). Submerged macrophytes were mostly represented by Potamogeton spp., Chara spp. and Ceratophyllum sp., filamentous green algae by Spirogyra spp. The magnitude of phytoplankton biomass decrease was highly dependent on the size of large cladocerans and abundance of submerged vegetation. Submerged vegetation cover above 30% and/or large Cladocera length exceeding 1 mm were associated with a significant decrease in Chl a concentrations (bb1–ab1; Fig. 3). Phytoplankton biomass was low in the presence of both extensive submerged vegetation and large-bodied cladocerans as well as either of them alone. The size of large cladocerans appeared to be much more important than their density for phytoplankton control (Fig. 2). Large cladocerans were generally smaller (<1 mm) in the 10 ponds that were recolonised by planktivorous fish at different times after biomanipulation (Peretyatko et al., 2011). When large cladocerans were small, whether numerous or not, and submerged vegetation was lacking, Chl a level was not significantly different from the pre-biomanipulation situation (bb2–ab2; Fig. 3). Biomanipulation led to a significant decrease in TP concentrations in the ponds where phytoplankton biomass was reduced (bb1–ab1; Fig. 3). It should be noted, however, that TP level remained high (mostly above 100 μg l−1) owing to high concentrations of SRP. When phytoplankton biomass was not reduced the TP level was not significantly different from that of the pre-biomanipulation situation (bb2–ab2; Fig. 3). Soluble reactive phosphorus showed an opposite trend to that of TP as a result of biomanipulation (Fig. 4).
