Regression analysis showed that Chl \( a \) had significant relationship with TP in all the three situations investigated: pre-biomanipulation, after biomanipulation without and with large-bodied cladocerans and extensive submerged vegetation (Table 3; Fig. 5). The strength of the relationship, both in terms of slope and \( R^2 \), appeared to be dependent on the presence of extensive submerged vegetation and/or large-bodied cladocerans. The test of homogeneity of slopes rendered significant differences (Tukey HSD test; \( P < 0.05 \)) between the situations characterised by the lack of submerged vegetation and large-bodied cladocerans (situations 1 and 3) and that characterised by the presence of extensive submerged vegetation and/or large-bodied cladocerans (situation 2; Table 3; Fig. 5). There was no significant difference between the pre-biomanipulation situation and after biomanipulation situation lacking submerged vegetation and large-bodied cladocerans (situations 1 and 3). TP explained 51% of the variation in Chl \( a \) before biomanipulation, 77% after biomanipulation when submerged vegetation and large-bodied cladocerans were lacking and 28% in the presence of extensive submerged vegetation and/or large-bodied cladocerans. Discussion Human-induced increase in the productivity of ponds and lakes caused a considerable degradation of their water quality often resulting in noxious phytoplankton blooms (Paerl, 1988; Hudnell, 2008). Adequate management decisions require the effects of elevated nutrient levels to be quantified. The Chl \( a \)–TP relationship is often used by managers to assess eutrophication impact and to establish nutrient targets. A considerable degree of Chl \( a \) variability, however, is not accounted for by TP concentrations or loadings thus diminishing the reliability of this relationship (Carpenter et al., 1985; Phillips et al., 2008). Although there is a number of factors that can potentially affect the Chl \( a \)–TP relationship, submerged vegetation and large zooplankton grazing seem to be the most important ones in the ponds studied as well as in other shallow waterbodies (Lammens et al., 1990; Jeppesen et al., 1997). Both the submerged vegetation and large zooplankters are quite sensitive to the presence of plankti–benthivorous fish that play a central role in ecosystem structuring (Scheffer, 1998; Lammens, 1999). Biomanipulation by fish removal has a cascading effect on phytoplankton biomass owing to large zooplankton release from fish predation that results in more efficient phytoplankton control (Carpenter & Kitchell, 1992). Biomanipulation and continuous monitoring of a large number of ponds characterised by a wide range of TP concentrations within the eutrophic–hypereutrophic part of the trophic spectrum allowed for assessing the effects of submerged vegetation and large cladocerans on Chl \( a \)–TP relationship in a nutrient rich context. All the biomanipulated ponds were very productive ecosystems. Before biomanipulation, they lacked submerged vegetation and large-bodied cladocerans and were prone to persistent phytoplankton blooms often dominated by bloom-forming cyanobacteria. The Chl \( a \)–TP relationship was relatively strong as phytoplankton biomass in these ponds was mostly nutrient driven. Despite the high productivity potential, fish removal led to a marked phytoplankton biomass decrease in the presence of extensive submerged vegetation and/or large-bodied cladocerans. Significant difference in slopes and marked difference in \( R^2 \) in the presence and absence of these factors indicate their strong weakening effect on Chl \( a \)–TP relationship and explain the low Chl \( a \) values at elevated TP concentrations. Data from 13 biomanipulated ponds averaged per pond per year and plotted on log–log scale The negative effect of submerged vegetation on phytoplankton biomass through associated mechanisms, such as increased grazing by large zooplankters finding refuge in plant beds, competition for nutrients, stabilisation of the water column and allelopathy, is well established (Jeppesen et al., 1997; Sondergaard & Moss, 1998; van Donk & van de Bund, 2002; Irfanullah & Moss, 2005). This is supported by the results obtained in this study as indicated by generally lower Chl \( a \) yields per unit of TP in the presence of extensive submerged vegetation as compared to the situation when submerged vegetation was lacking (Fig. 1). It should be noted that the effect of extensive submerged vegetation cover on the Chl \( a \) yield does not seem to depend on the size of large cladocerans suggesting that, when submerged vegetation is restored, phytoplankton can also be controlled by mechanisms other than large zooplankton grazing. The effect of large cladocerans on phytoplankton biomass is less well elucidated. Some controversy exists as to the edibility/grazing resistance of phytoplankton in general and cyanobacteria in particular (e.g. Gliwicz, 1990b; Benndorf et al., 2002). The majority of the studies, however, use number or biomass of large Cladocera or *Daphnia* to assess their effect on phytoplankton. The results of this study indicate that density of large cladocerans has a less straightforward effect on phytoplankton biomass than their size. The non-vegetated ponds, where phytoplankton was mostly controlled by nutrients and zooplankton grazing, often showed markedly lower Chl \( a \) concentrations in association with smaller numbers of large-bodied daphniids than in association with high numbers of small-bodied daphniids. This is clearly reflected on the Chl \( a \) yield per unit of TP that has visibly stronger negative relationship with size than density (Fig. 2). The stronger effect of larger cladocerans on the Chl \( a \) yield is consistent with the idea that smaller individuals have narrower food size spectrum (Burns, 1968); therefore, they rather shift phytoplankton community towards grazing resistant species than effectively control phytoplankton biomass (Cottingham & Schindler, 2000; Benndorf et al., 2002; Steiner, 2002). Apparent biomanipulation success, however, is not necessarily caused by large zooplankton grazing or submerged vegetation presence, but can be caused by a number of other factors related to fish presence (DeMelo et al., 1992). Fish presence contributes to the nutrient pool through excretion, bioturbation, and sediment resuspension (Brabrand et al., 1990; Breukelaar et al., 1994; Vanni, 2002). Changes in zooplankton community structure caused by fish removal can also alter the N/P ratio in a way that would inhibit phytoplankton growth (Sterner et al., 1992). Therefore, fish removal may result in substantial decrease in nutrient availability and subsequently in phytoplankton biomass reduction. The marked increase in SRP and the insignificant change in DIN concentrations after biomanipulation in the ponds where it resulted in phytoplankton biomass decrease show, however, that fish removal did not result in a decrease in nutrient availability in the ponds studied. There are also many reasons why biomanipulation might not work. Insufficient fish removal, phytoplankton composition shift to grazing resistant species, the presence of predator macroinvertebrates and high nutrient concentrations are generally considered as the main reasons of biomanipulation failures to reduce phytoplankton biomass (Meijer et al., 1999; Sierp et al., 2009). The drawdown of the biomanipulated ponds suggests that insufficient fish removal cannot be considered as the cause of the failure. Besides, ponds that were rapidly recolonised by fish could maintain low phytoplankton biomass in the presence of extensive submerged vegetation. When submerged vegetation was lacking, fish recolonisation was often associated with relatively smaller large cladocerans and phytoplankton assemblage bias towards bloom forming cyanobacteria. In the absence of fish, however, large cladocerans alone could control phytoplankton (Fig. 5; Peretyatko et al., 2009) suggesting that when released from predation pressure, large cladocerans can grow big enough (in the fishless ponds the length of large cladocerans exceeded at times 3 mm) to be capable of efficient control of phytoplankton, including bloom-forming cyanobacteria, and thus can prevent bloom formation. This is consistent with the report of Gliwicz (1990b) stating that Daphnia can control bloom-forming cyanobacteria below critical filament concentration. Despite the removal of fish, no marked evidence of large Cladocera control by macroinvertebrates, as reported by Benndorf et al. (2000) and Hosper & Meijer (1993), was observed during the study period. The fluctuations of large Cladocera densities in the three completely fishless ponds seemed to be related to food availability rather than predation. It is possible that macroinvertebrates preyed preferentially on smaller cladocerans and thus biased their size structure towards bigger individuals (Pinel-Alloul, 1995) as cladocerans in these two ponds were the biggest in size. This, however, can also be attributed to the absence of predation by fish as well as low food availability that gives larger filter-feeders a competitive advantage (Gliwicz, 1990a). The significant positive relationship between Chl \( a \) and TP in the biomanipulated ponds with extensive submerged vegetation and large-bodied cladocerans confirmed that the success of biomanipulation depends to a certain degree on nutrient level. Indeed, the capacity of submerged vegetation and large cladocerans to buffer the effects of eutrophication diminished at higher nutrient levels as indicated by the markedly higher Chl \( a \) values corresponding to elevated TP concentrations. This is consistent with the idea that the clear-water state becomes less stable as nutrient levels increase (Scheffer et al., 2001). Therefore, to ensure biomanipulation success in ponds excessively polluted with nutrients, reduction of nutrient loading might be indispensable. In the ponds that are not excessively polluted by nutrients, trophic (large zooplankton) and competitive (submerged vegetation) interactions seem to be more important predictors of phytoplankton biomass than nutrient availability. In the absence of fish, low phytoplankton biomass could be maintained by large Cladocera grazing alone. Because large zooplankters are very susceptible to fish recolonisation, such situation is very unstable and not sustainable in the longer term, except for ponds with recurrent anoxic conditions unsuitable for fish. Conversely, extensive submerged vegetation can withstand some degree of fish recolonisation and thus buffer, to certain extent, the effects of eutrophication. Therefore, submerged vegetation restoration seems to be crucial for the maintenance of low phytoplankton biomass on the longer term. This has important implications for the restoration of ponds affected by eutrophication, as it shows that considerable degree of their ecological quality can be restored by biomanipulation even when nutrient loading reduction is not feasible in the short term, as is often the case because of considerable phosphorus accumulation in the sediment (Jeppesen et al., 2005; Sondergaard et al., 2005a) and surface and ground water contamination by urban pollution. The slopes of the regression lines obtained by the analysis of the data from the Brussels ponds are within the range of the slopes based on the data from temperate lakes (Phillips et al., 2008), suggesting that the ponds studied function in a similar way. Therefore, these results can also be used to get insights into the Chl \( a \)-TP relationship in lakes. Conclusions In ponds lacking submerged vegetation and large-bodied cladocerans, phytoplankton biomass is mainly nutrient driven and therefore the Chl \( a \)-TP relationship is strong. The presence of extensive submerged vegetation and/or intense grazing by large-bodied cladocerans can considerably weaken the Chl \( a \)-TP relationship by inhibiting phytoplankton growth despite high nutrient availability. As biomanipulation of ponds leads to the restoration of submerged vegetation and enhances large zooplankton grazing, it can be used to restore a considerable degree of their ecological quality even when nutrient loading reduction is not feasible. The capacity of submerged vegetation and large zooplankton grazing to buffer eutrophication effects diminishes at higher nutrients levels; therefore, to ensure biomanipulation success in ponds excessively polluted with nutrients, reduction of nutrient loading might be indispensable. Submerged macrophytes as refuges for grazing Cladocera against fish predation: observations on seasonal changes in relation to macrophyte cover and predation pressure Julia H. Stansfield¹, Martin R. Perrow²*, Louise D. Tench¹, Adrian J. D. Jowitt² & Ayesha A. L. Taylor¹ ¹National Rivers Authority, Biology Laboratory, Station Road, St Olaves, Great Yarmouth, NR31 9JA, UK ²ECON, School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich NR4 7TJ, UK (*author for correspondence) Key words: zooplankton, zooplanktivorous fish, macrophyte, refugia, predator/prey interactions, lake restoration Abstract The provision of a refuge from fish predation for large-bodied Cladocera among stands of submerged macrophytes is thought to be an important stabilising mechanism against nutrient-induced phytoplankton increases in clear water shallow lakes. The occurrence of any refuge effect in relation to the seasonal impact of both macrophyte development and recruitment of zooplanktivorous fish was monitored over the summer months (May to September) in three lakes (Cromes Broad, Hoveton Little Broad/Pound End, and Upton Broad) of variable trophic status, fish community structure and nature and extent of macrophyte cover, in the Norfolk Broads in Eastern England. At all sites, Daphnia spp. exhibited a early summer peak of abundance but had declined rapidly by July probably as a result of predation from underyearling fish. In extensive macrophyte stands (Cromes Broad) Daphnia spp. persisted after its elimination in open water, indicating some refuge effect. At sites with macrophyte cover and/or low fish predation pressure, Daphnia spp. was replaced by Ceriodaphnia spp., both with and without Simocephalus sp., thus maintaining large populations of grazing Cladocera, apparently capable of exerting a high grazing pressure on phytoplankton. This occurred, even under high predation pressure from a relatively high density of zooplanktivorous 0+ fish (Cromes Broad), consistent with the refuge hypothesis. In addition, at this site, significant positive associations of cladoceran abundance with increasing macrophyte cover were apparent throughout the summer. From information on the distribution of fish it is suggested that dense macrophytes offer the most suitable refuge through provision of predator-free space. Introduction Eutrophication of shallow freshwater lakes frequently results in increased standing crops of phytoplankton or perhaps filamentous algae. This in turn leads to the decline or loss of submerged macrophytes, typically through shading (Phillips et al., 1978; Scheffer, 1990), with consequent gross changes in biotic structure and function (Moss, 1983; De Nie, 1987; Bronmark & Weisner, 1992). However, there is growing empirical and experimental evidence that stabilising mechanisms associated with the presence of stands of macrophytes, may prevent or reduce increases in algal growth up to a threshold level of nutrient loading (Howard-Williams, 1981; Timms & Moss, 1984; Mitchell et al., 1988; Balls et al., 1989; Andersson et al., 1990; Blindlow et al., 1993; Van Donk et al., 1993; Schriver et al., 1995). Consequently, within a range of nutrient concentration, either macrophytes or phytoplankton may dominate; the alternative stable state hypothesis (Irvine et al., 1989; Scheffer et al., 1993). Several stabilising mechanisms which perpetuate the macrophyte-dominated state have been suggested. These include: allelopathy, the production of com- pounds limiting algal growth by the macrophytes themselves (Wium-Anderson et al., 1982); competition for N, with macrophytes maintaining a competitive advantage over algae through luxury uptake (Balls et al., 1989) and acting as a sink for available nutrients (in both water column and sediments) (Ozimek et al., 1990; Van Donk et al., 1993); prevention of resuspension of sediment and recirculation of fast sinking algae by wind and wave action through calming of the water column (James & Barko, 1990); provision of refuges for grazing zooplankton (Timms & Moss, 1984) and refuges for piscivorous fish acting upon the production (Spencer & King, 1984; Grimm & Backx, 1990) or the distribution (Werner et al., 1983; Persson & Eklov, 1995) of zooplanktivorous fish thereby reducing predation pressure upon the zooplankton (Hambright et al., 1986, Turner & Mittelbach, 1990). Detailed knowledge of the mechanisms responsible for maintaining clear water and low algal populations in lakes dominated by macrophytes is critical for those lake managers concerned with the sustainable restoration (i.e. reversal of anthropogenic eutrophication) of shallow lakes, particularly if this is to be achieved in a predictable and cost-effective manner (Shapiro, 1990). In restoration programmes, the refuge effect for zooplankton is particularly appealing (Shapiro, 1990). This is due to two reasons. First, after nutrient loading has been reduced to the range where macrophyte dominance is likely to be stable (TP<0.15 mg l\(^{-1}\) or higher if N is strongly limiting-Hosper & Jagtman, 1990; Jeppesen et al., 1990), the removal of zooplanktivorous fish, often termed biomanipulation (Lammens et al., 1990), is often required to enhance populations of grazing zooplankton to reduce algal crops to provide a suitable light climate for macrophyte growth. If this mechanism operates, then it is likely that grazing has some importance in maintaining clear water within macrophyte beds. Second, during the development of macrophyte stands following biomanipulation which may or may not be rapid (Meijer et al., 1994; Perrow et al., 1994, Moss et al., 1996), any stabilising mechanism is of increased value if it also preserves water clarity in the open water surrounding macrophyte stands. The diel migration of large-bodied Cladocera from macrophyte stands to open water to feed provides such a mechanism (Timms & Moss, 1984). Although macrophyte stands have been demonstrated to provide refuges for zooplankton (Schriver et al., 1995; Phillips et al., 1996) the timing of such effects relative to the seasonal development of macrophytes and recruitment of 0+ fish is poorly understood. The aim of this study was to describe the seasonal pattern of use of submerged macrophytes by grazing Cladocera in relation to potential predation pressure from fish and to determine whether the refuge effect is plausible as a mechanism in promoting clear water in beds of macrophytes. This adopted a comparative approach by monitoring zooplankton abundance and community structure, fish abundance and biomass, chlorophyll a concentration (as a index of algal abundance) and macrophyte cover during the macrophyte growing season (May–September) in three lakes of varying trophic status, fish community structure and nature and extent of macrophyte cover. Description of study sites The three lakes studied (Hoveton Little/Pound End, Crones and Upton Broads) are among the Norfolk Broads, a series (around 50) of small (1–124 ha), shallow (0.5–2 m) lakes in eastern England, formed from flooded medieval peat diggings. Most may now be classed as hypertrophic and only four retain their original macrophyte populations (Moss, 1983). The study sites represent a continuum from phytoplankton to macrophyte dominance. The first, Hoveton Little Broad, has been divided into two sections as part of a long term management strategy aimed at evaluating the effects of different restorative actions (Table 1). For the purposes of this study, Hoveton Little Broad, acts as a control section with turbid phytoplankton dominated water and few submerged macrophytes, whereas the other biomanipulated section, Pound End, has clear water and some macrophytes, although these are restricted to bird exclosures. The second, Crones Broad, retains a relatively high nutrient loading but has recently developed an extensive cover of Ceratophyllum demersum L. with Potamogeton freisii Rupr. (Perrow et al., 1997). The third, Upton Broad, being isolated from riverine inputs and surrounded by wet woodland, has largely retained its original character and has a large cover of macrophytes, particularly Najas marina L., with Chara spp., P. pectinatus L. and Zannichellia palustris L. (Perrow et al., 1997). The physical characteristics, management measures employed and relevant biological data are shown in Table 1. Table 1. Characteristics of the study sites.

Materials and methods Zooplankton, macrophytes and chlorophyll \( a \) Sampling for zooplankton, macrophytes, and chlorophyll \( a \) was carried out monthly from May to September 1994. At each site, ten zooplankton samples were taken from both open water and from amongst submerged macrophytes, where present. Where macrophytes occurred the density in a 0.25 m\(^2\) quadrat centred on each sampling point was expressed as PVI (per cent volume infested-Canfield et al., 1984). This was estimated by multiplying the estimated % cover by the height of the stand and dividing by the depth of water. At Pound End, five samples were taken from each of the two large (a. 500–1000 m\(^2\)) bird exclosures. In the open water and when macrophyte stands reached the water surface, a tube sampler was used (length 90 cm, diameter 10 cm) in order to sample the whole water column. When macrophyte stands did not reach the water surface a Patalas sampler (10 litre capacity) was used to obtain a sample from among the macrophyte stand. Water was strained through a 64 \( \mu \)m net and the animals retained were preserved in 70% alcohol. Samples were counted under a stereo microscope using 25 \( \times \) magnification. Differences between mean abundance of important cladoceran zooplankton between open water and macrophytes were tested using Mann-Whitney U-tests on each sampling occasion. In addition, the relationships between abundance of particular cladoceran species and % macrophyte cover were explored using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (\( r_s \)). Chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations were determined according to the methods of Moss et al. (1986). Fish Fish populations were sampled on two occasions, in May and September. This corresponded to the period prior to the recruitment of cyprinids and after the late summer period in which 0+ fish are likely to exert a depressive effect on zooplankton (Townsend & Perrow, 1989), respectively. In addition, sampling in May provided a baseline of the adult fish stock prior to the recruitment of underyearlings, whereas sampling in September allowed the relative recruitment strength of the 0+ fish to be estimated. Point abundance sampling (PAS) (Copp & Penáz, 1988) conducted with high frequency (600 Hz) pulsed DC electrofishing equipment was used to sample all habitats in proportion to their abundance. During sampling the 3 m fibreglass dinghy, with one electrofishing operator and one person controlling the boat using ‘push’ (facing the direction of travel) rowing, was rowed systematically along transect lines (8–10 oar strokes apart). At the equivalent distance along the transect line, a point was sampled by rapidly immers- ing the large (45 cm diameter) anode and swinging it through a 2 m arc in one motion. Any stunned fish were removed and transferred to individual buckets. The area sampled was quantified as 2.4 m\(^2\). This was achieved by using a voltmeter to determine the distance at which the voltage gradient was reduced to 0.12 V which may be used as the threshold limit for effective electrofishing (Copp & Penáz, 1988). At the end of each transect all fish were identified, counted, measured to the nearest mm fork length and weighed to the nearest gram, before being returned to a stretch of water that had been sampled previously. In addition, the % of the water column occupied by submerged macrophytes was estimated visually at each sampling point. The entire area of Pound End, Upton and Cromes Broads were sampled, whereas only part of Hoveton Little Broad (c. 6 ha-comparable to the size of Pound End) was covered. Results Fish The spring biomass of adult cyprinid and percid fishes was variable but low (up to 110 kg ha\(^{-1}\) but typically <15 kg ha\(^{-1}\)) (Table 2). The increase in biomass and especially, density, of potentially zooplanktivorous fish (all except pike, *Esox lucius* L. and eel, *Anguilla anguilla* (L.)) over the sampling period underlines the important contribution the recruitment of 0+ fish makes to fish production in the study lakes (Table 2). The relative recruitment strength of the different species in the different lakes is illustrated in Figure 1. Zooplankton Three genera of large-bodied grazing Cladocera zooplankton were found at significant density (>50 l\(^{-1}\)) in some or all of the study sites. These were *Daphnia hyalina/longispina* (Leydig/O.F.M.) *Ceriodaphnia reticulata/quadrangula* (Jurine/O.F. M.) and *Simocephalus vetulus* (O.F.M.). *Daphnia* spp. had an early summer peak of abundance, albeit of varying magnitude, at all sites, but had declined to low populations by July. At Cromes Broad, where extensive macrophyte stands developed from June onwards (Figure 1), *Daphnia* spp. persisted amongst the macrophytes after its elimination in open water (Figure 2). At Cromes and Pound End *Daphnia* spp. was replaced by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. both with (Cromes and Pound End) and without (Upton) *Simocephalus* sp., thus maintaining large populations of grazing Cladocera. This was not the case in Hoveton Little Broad, where cladoceran populations remained extremely low throughout the summer. The patterns of habitat use by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. varied between the different sites (Figure 2). At Pound End, macrophyte beds were favoured in early season, although once populations had built up by mid-summer, significant numbers (>100 l\(^{-1}\)) were found in open water. At Upton, prior to the peak in macrophyte populations, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was more abundant in open water, thereafter there was no significant difference between the different habitats. In contrast, in Cromes, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds compared to open water on all occasions (Figure 2). A similar pattern was shown by *Simocephalus* sp. where it occurred, as it was virtually always significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds (Figure 2). For sites with macrophytes, the relationships between PVI and the abundance of the different genera as well as all grazing Cladocera combined are shown in Table 3. At Cromes, there is a consistent pattern of increasing abundance of all genera, including *Daphnia* spp. while it was still present, with increasing PVI. At Upton no such pattern was found, with either no significant relationships, or in July, a significant negative relationship with *Ceriodaphnia* spp. Pound End represented an intermediate situation, with different species exerting different preferences: *Daphnia* spp. tended to be negatively associated with macrophytes; *Ceriodaphnia* spp. displayed positive associations early in the summer but no relationship in subsequent samples and *Simocephalus* sp. showed significant positive correlations with PVI on all occasions. Discussion Seasonal interactions between macrophytes, fish, zooplankton and phytoplankton There is clearly some interaction between extent of macrophyte development, intensity of predation by 0+ fish measured simply as a function of density and the structure and abundance of the cladoceran community and its potential impact on algal abundance (measured as chlorophyll *a*) (Figure 1). Indeed, where fish recruitment is poor or absent, *Daphnia* spp. populations typically persist throughout the summer months (Perrow et al., 1994). Conversely, it is clear that the relatively low overwintering stock of older fish exerted little influence on the development of the *Daphnia* spp. population. Second, in all sites, *Daphnia* spp. was quickly replaced by high densities of other species which is not consistent with food limitation and indeed at no site was the abundance of edible algae (expressed as chlorophyll *a*) apparently limiting. It therefore seems reasonable to conclude that predation by 0+ fish is responsible for the decline in *Daphnia* spp. Moreover, this appears to be readily achieved by a relatively low number of 0+ fish in Upton (prior to the development of macrophytes) and relatively moderate recruitment in Pound End and Hoveton Little Broads. However, *Daphnia* spp. persisted in Cromes Broad for a further month even in the presence of a suite of zooplanktivorous fish at relatively high density. This seems related to the early development of an extensive cover of macrophytes at this site. *Daphnia* spp. showed a positive association with macrophytes (Figure 2) and increasing macrophyte cover (Table 3) at this time, quite unlike the situation in any other site. Such use of macrophytes is consistent with the refuge hypothesis. However, *Daphnia* spp. appeared unable to exploit macrophytes as a refuge over an extensive period. This is in keeping with the behavioural ecology of the group which are typically pelagic and have been shown to avoid macrophytes (Pennak, 1973; Dorgelo & Heykoop, 1985). Recent experiments in the laboratory have shown that a clear trade-off exists, *Daphnia magna* Straus preferring to stay in open water until exposed to the risk of predation from zooplanktivorous fish whereupon it migrates to macrophytes, predation risk clearly outweighing repellency (Lauridsen & Lodge, 1996). However, many common fish species, particularly 0+ cyprinids, are capable of feeding in darkness (Townsend & Risebrow, 1982) and so the risk of predation, although reduced, is still evident. In addition, Daphnia spp. populations may suffer some predation from the fish concentrated in a low density of macrophytes (Figure 3). Therefore, in the face of intense predation pressure from a high density of zooplanktivorous fish, as at Cromes Broad, Daphnia spp. may not be able to persist through time, even with the provision of suitable refuges. Following the decline of Daphnia spp., at those sites retaining at least some macrophyte cover Ceriodaphnia spp. dominated, both with (Pound End) and without Simocephalus sp. (Upton). At Pound End, there was even some partial recovery of Daphnia populations in late summer. In contrast, the connected Hoveton Little Broad, with relatively high numbers of 0+ roach, displayed no replacement of Daphnia spp. with other species or any recovery of populations. The consequence of the presence of Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus was the maintenance of large populations (typically >50 l\(^{-1}\), Figure 1) of grazing Cladocera throughout the summer months in Cromes and Pound End. The patterns of habitat use of these species also appeared to be related to the potential predation pressure from fish, thus also consistent with the refuge hypothesis. For example, where predation pressure was presumably low from a low density of 0+ perch as in Upton, Ceriodaphnia spp. was present in both open water and macrophyte beds (Figure 2). Under moderate fish predation pressure in Pound End (0.45 m\(^{-2}\) of 0+ perch and roach), Ceriodaphnia spp. and particularly Simocephalus sp. were more abundant in macrophytes, although Ceriodaphnia spp. also occurred at high density in open water (Figure 2). In contrast, where predation pressure was likely to be intense from a suite of 0+ fish at high density (0.8 m\(^{-2}\)) in Cromes, large populations of both Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. were only maintained through association with macrophytes. Furthermore, under intense predation pressure the abundance of cladocerans was almost always positively correlated with increasing PVI suggesting that increasing cover offered a better refuge (Table 3). What is the mechanism behind the refuge effect? Schriver et al. (1995) demonstrate that a refuge effect may exist at low macrophyte density (15–20% of volume) but that this is dependent on fish density. In the current study, it is suggested that macrophytes may act as refuges for zooplankton at relatively high fish ![Bar chart showing the relative distribution of all fish species in different levels of macrophyte PVI in Cromes Broad in September.](page_320_370_1047_482.png) Figure 3. However, the situation at Pound End suggests that even where the distribution of macrophytes is limited, providing patches of dense macrophytes are available (Table 1), a refuge against moderate predation pressure may be provided. The reasons for this may be that dense macrophyte stands contain relatively few fish (Figure 3). By implication, this suggests that predation risk for Cladocera declines with increasing macrophyte cover. Evidence for this is provided by Phillips et al. (1996), who demonstrated that predation pressure, derived from known numbers of fish with known diet, upon zooplankton declined with increasing macrophyte cover. It is therefore suggested that the formation of predator-free space is the mechanism responsible for the refuge effect. The question is, why do zooplanktivorous fish avoid dense macrophytes? (Engel, 1988). Several plausible mechanisms exist. First, oxygen concentrations (Davis, 1975) and pH (Beklioglu & Moss, 1995) may be unsuitable in macrophyte stands, although there is no evidence that either was limiting in the samples collected during routine monitoring of the study sites. Second, and perhaps more applicable, the foraging efficiency of some fish may decline with increasing habitat complexity (Winfield, 1986; Diehl, 1988). However, when foraging on zooplankton, this is clearly species and size dependent. For example, 0+ perch (Perca fluviatilis L.) may show high feeding efficiency in structured environments unlike 0+ roach (Rutilus rutilus (L.)) (Winfield, 1986), and vegetation may serve as a competitive refuge for perch (Persson, 1993). In support of this, several authors (Hall & Werner 1977; Carpenter et al., 1987; Venugopal & Winfield, 1993) have demonstrated that small fish may associate with macrophytes. However, this is typically a behavioural response to potential predation risk (Savino & Stein, 1982; Werner et al., 1983; Persson & Eklov, 1995) and not because of enhanced foraging opportunity. Whether small fish take refuge in macrophytes in response to predation risk is dependent on a number of factors including the functional type of predator and prey (Jacobsen et al., 1997). It is perhaps significant that in this study the relative proportion of piscivorous pike increased with increasing macrophyte cover (Figure 3). In addition, the individuals present in these habitats were 0+, the size class most likely to consume 0+ zooplanktivores (Van Densen, 1994). Therefore, a third explanation for the avoidance of dense macrophytes by fish in this study may be that they were exposed to a greater risk of predation in these habitats. This in turn may have led to a reduced predation risk for zooplankton (Turner & Mittelbach, 1990) thereby enhancing the refuge effect. Are refuging Cladocera able to control phytoplankton populations? The presence of large numbers of cladoceran grazers exerting an influence on phytoplankton populations is essential to the value of any refuge effect in explaining the presence of clear water in macrophyte-dominated lakes. Particularly to species other than Daphnia spp.? The relationship between grazing rate and body length are very similar for Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. compared to Daphnia spp. (Peters & Downing, 1984; Knoechel & Holtby, 1986; Bern, 1987; Mourelatos & Lacroix, 1990) and if at high enough density it seems reasonable to conclude that these species may be able to graze out phytoplankton crops, as observed by Turner & Mittelbach (1992). The interconnected Pound End and Hoveton Little Broads, with the same nutrient concentration, but radically different chlorophyll \(a\) values, appear to provide a convincing example of the grazing potential of these Cladocera (Figure 1). Moreover, in Cromes Broad, the filtering capacity of Simocephalus spp. and Ceriodaphnia spp., which are maintained at densities in excess of 50 l\(^{-1}\) throughout the summer months, appears to more than compensate for that of Daphnia spp. (Table 4). In Upton, the situation is less clear, where Simocephalus sp. is absent and the filtering rate of Ceriodaphnia spp. in midsummer does not compensate the loss of Daphnia spp. However, it is still comparable with that of Daphnia spp. at Cromes in early season, before the development of macrophytes when the only likely explanation for the control of phytoplankton populations is grazing. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that grazing by Ceriodaphnia spp. is at least a contributory factor in limiting phytoplankton development in Upton in mid- to late summer. From the patterns of habitat use of Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp., it is likely that only Ceriodaphnia spp. may have the potential to graze in the open water between stands of macrophytes, Simocephalus sp. always being limited to the macrophytes themselves (Lauridsen et al., in press). Thus in developing macrophyte populations at the beginning of the growing season or following a restoration attempt using control of zooplanktivorous fish, it seems that large populations of Daphnia spp. are required to provide the clear water necessary for macrophyte development. Following the establishment of macrophyte cover and/or recruitment of 0+ fish, Daphnia may be expected to decline, with Ceriodaphnia assuming the role of grazing in open water between as well as within macrophyte stands, with Simocephalus contributing to control of phytoplankton standing crop in the macrophyte beds themselves (Table 4). Conclusions Several results of the study are consistent with the refuge hypothesis: • The elimination of Daphnia spp. by 0+ fish is delayed where extensive stands of macrophytes are present in early summer. • Large populations (\(>50\ l^{-1}\)) of grazing Cladocera may be maintained throughout the summer at relatively high fish density. • The level of use of macrophyte stands is linked to fish predation pressure. • Cladoceran abundance is positively associated with increasing macrophyte cover. Essential to the value of the refuge effect as a mechanism promoting the stability of submerged macrophyte populations in shallow lakes, the presence of significant populations of grazing Cladocera seems to contribute to the maintenance of a low phytoplankton standing crop and the attainment of clear water. Moreover, macrophyte-associated species such as Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. appear to make an important contribution to this effect where Daphnia spp. is reduced by fish predation and/or disfavoured by extensive macrophyte cover. The mechanism for the refuge effect in this study appears to be the provision of predator-free space as zooplanktivorous fish appear to avoid dense macrophytes. Particularly to species other than Daphnia spp.? The relationship between grazing rate and body length are very similar for Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. compared to Daphnia spp. (Peters & Downing, 1984; Knoechel & Holtby, 1986; Bern, 1987; Mourelatos & Lacroix, 1990) and if at high enough density it seems reasonable to conclude that these species may be able to graze out phytoplankton crops, as observed by Turner & Mittelbach (1992). The interconnected Pound End and Hoveton Little Broads, with the same nutrient concentration, but radically different chlorophyll \(a\) values, appear to provide a convincing example of the grazing potential of these Cladocera (Figure 1). Moreover, in Cromes Broad, the filtering capacity of Simocephalus spp. and Ceriodaphnia spp., which are maintained at densities in excess of 50 l\(^{-1}\) throughout the summer months, appears to more than compensate for that of Daphnia spp. (Table 4). In Upton, the situation is less clear, where Simocephalus sp. is absent and the filtering rate of Ceriodaphnia spp. in midsummer does not compensate the loss of Daphnia spp. However, it is still comparable with that of Daphnia spp. at Cromes in early season, before the development of macrophytes when the only likely explanation for the control of phytoplankton populations is grazing. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that grazing by Ceriodaphnia spp. is at least a contributory factor in limiting phytoplankton development in Upton in mid- to late summer. From the patterns of habitat use of Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp., it is likely that only Ceriodaphnia spp. may have the potential to graze in the open water between stands of macrophytes, Simocephalus sp. always being limited to the macrophytes themselves (Lauridsen et al., in press). Thus in developing macrophyte populations at the beginning of the growing season or following a restoration attempt using control of zooplanktivorous fish, it seems that large populations of Daphnia spp. are required to provide the clear water necessary for macrophyte development. Following the establishment of macrophyte cover and/or recruitment of 0+ fish, Daphnia may be expected to decline, with Ceriodaphnia assuming the role of grazing in open water between as well as within macrophyte stands, with Simocephalus contributing to control of phytoplankton standing crop in the macrophyte beds themselves (Table 4). Conclusions Several results of the study are consistent with the refuge hypothesis: • The elimination of Daphnia spp. by 0+ fish is delayed where extensive stands of macrophytes are present in early summer. • Large populations (\(>50\ l^{-1}\)) of grazing Cladocera may be maintained throughout the summer at relatively high fish density. • The level of use of macrophyte stands is linked to fish predation pressure. • Cladoceran abundance is positively associated with increasing macrophyte cover. The diversity of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte communities in ponds LAURIE E. FRIDAY Department of Biological Sciences, University of Exeter SUMMARY. 1. The range of factors which may influence the wide variation in the structure of pond communities is reviewed. 2. Factors explaining the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte taxa are investigated, using multiple regression analysis, for a group of ponds in which biogeographical effects are likely to be minimal. 3. Numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa in these ponds are highly correlated with pH and probably, therefore, with other associated aspects of water chemistry. 4. Many invertebrate taxa, from species to entire phyla, were not found below pH 5.5, but few characteristically 'acidophilic' taxa were apparent. 5. Details of species composition of the macroinvertebrate fauna differ widely even between ponds of similar pH. 6. The diversity and composition of macrophyte communities are not adequately predicted by any of the factors investigated. Introduction Ponds and other small water bodies are highly individual habitats: the fauna and flora usually vary widely, and often unpredictably, between ponds even within a small geographical area. While it is sometimes possible to find correlations between observed faunal or floral diversity and various factors, it is rarely possible, except by rigorous experimental treatment, to establish the causes of inter-pond variation. A wide variety of explanatory factors has been put forward, as a result of field studies of small water bodies or on theoretical grounds, as possible influences on the diversity and composition of pond communities. These factors may be grouped together under two broad headings: 'biogeographical' factors, operating via the dispersal of organisms to essentially insular habitats, and 'habitat' characteristics, both physico-chemical and biotic, influencing the establishment and persistence of colonizing species. These categories are not mutually exclusive, but form a useful basis for reviewing the wide range of factors which might explain inter-pond variation in the number and identities of species. Correspondence: Dr L. E. Friday, Department of Applied Biology, Pembroke Street, Cambridge CB2 3DX. (i) Biogeographical factors (a) Pond age. Studies of the initial colonization of newly created ponds show a general increase in the numbers of species of invertebrates and macrophytes (Gates, 1927; Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). Where dispersal distances are short, the rate of acquisition of new species has been observed to decline within a few years (Barnes, 1983), suggesting an approach to an 'equilibrium number of species', as predicted by MacArthur & Wilson's (1967) theory of island biogeography. However, Godwin's (1923) observations on the flora of much older ponds suggest that numbers of less vagile species (i.e. those with weak or passive dispersal) may continue to rise over many decades. As a pond ages, so the habitat it presents to colonists changes, partly due to increases in the extent and diversity of aquatic vegetation and in the production of autochthonous detritus. These changes are accompanied by changes in the identity of the dominant invertebrate taxa (Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). While it is possible to fit a model to the observed rise in numbers of taxa with age, the order in which individual colonists establish is not easy to predict. Invasion by an individual species depends on the availability of suitable propagules in 'source' habitats, the species' dispersal mechanisms, and the distance over which it has to disperse, but is also subject to chance (Talling, 1951). (b) Isolation. MacArthur & Wilson's model predicts a decrease in the equilibrium number of species on an island, and changes in the species represented, with increasing isolation from the source of colonists. Aho (1978a) found a significant correlation between isolation of small, productive Finnish lakes and the diversity of their molluscan faunas. Several authors have suggested that changes in isolation over historical or geological time (due to flooding, changes in river courses, creation or destruction of source habitats) have influenced the diversity of less vagile organisms in lakes (e.g. Boycott, 1919; Godwin, 1923; Aho, 1978b; Barbour & Brown, 1974). The immediate surroundings of ponds may also influence their chances of discovery by actively dispersing organisms, but surrounding vegetation and land use are likely to be of greater importance in their effect on aspects of the pond habitat, namely hydrology, water chemistry and allochthonous organic inputs. (c) Pond area. Connor & McCoy (1979), in their review of the species–area relationship, point out that the possible effects of area on community diversity have both biogeographical and biotic elements: as area increases, so the number of habitat types, with their associated species, is likely to increase; population sizes should also increase with area, thus reducing the extinction rate of resident species (MacArthur & Wilson, 1967); and large 'target' areas may simply receive a larger number of colonizing propagules, and therefore a chance of a greater variety of species, than smaller ones. Lassen (1975), Aho (1978a), Driver (1977) and Fryer (1985) found correlations between area (or log area) and the numbers of species of molluscs, chironomids and crustaceans respectively. Which of these aspects may account for the observed relationships is not possible to determine from diversity data alone, but Fryer (1985) suggests that the types of habitats found in different sized water bodies ('pond' as opposed to 'lake' habitats) may partly explain the composition of the crustacean faunas in his study area. Area, as an expression of the size of a water body, is also related to its persistence. Small ponds tend to be less permanent than larger ones, may show greater fluctuations in physical and chemical conditions, and so present quite a different type of habitat. Macan (1954, 1962) discusses the probable influence of habitat stability on the identity, and possibly on the diversity, of corixid species in a water body. (ii) Characteristics of the habitat (a) Habitat diversity. Factors contributing to the diversity of habitat for pond macrophytes include details of the bank topography and changes in substratum associated with irregularities in the shoreline. For the macroinvertebrate fauna, the diversity of macrophytic vegetation and local changes in substratum may be major factors. Observations by several authors on invertebrate communities associated with different species of macrophytes (e.g. Soszka, 1975; Dvorak & Best, 1982; Lodge, 1985), suggest that a correlation might be expected between macrophyte and macroinvertebrate numbers of species. Palmer (1981) found a close relationship between macrophyte species diversity and the number of species of Coleoptera and Hemiptera in a survey of base-rich ponds in Norfolk. (b) Competition and predation. Little direct evidence has been put forward to show that biotic interactions are major determinants of pond biotic diversity. However, changes in fish populations are often accompanied by changes in the plant and invertebrate communities (Macan, 1965, 1977b; Korinkova, 1967; Henrickson & Oscarson, 1985) and the effect of fish predation on zooplankton community structure is well documented (see Zaret, 1980). Biotic interactions might possibly be a major influence from the very earliest stages of pond colonization. In new ponds, extensive pure stands of emergent or floating-leaved macrophytes may establish within a few years (Barnes, 1983) and preclude other species by competition for light or space. They may constitute very distinctive habitats for invertebrates and if, by chance, different aggressive species colonize neighbouring ponds, then quite different communities may result. (c) Water chemistry. Many workers have found a correlation between pond biotic diversity and water chemistry. Scandinavian studies of molluscan communities (e.g. Aho, 1987a; Økland, 1980) link species diversity to a combination of pH and calcium levels. Strong positive correlations between pH and numbers of species of Crustacea have been reported from acidic, low-calcium ponds and lakes in Northern Britain (Fryer, 1980) and Norway (Økland & Økland, 1980). The composition of macrophytic communities may also be changed during lake acidification (Grahn, 1975). Green (1986) found a non-linear relationship between conductivity and zooplankton diversity in crater lakes. Several authors stress the importance of the general level of productivity of a water body (usually gauged by concentrations of nutrient ions) in determining the assortment of species found there, e.g. Saether (1975). In the present study, the distribution of littoral macroinvertebrates and macrophytes in a group of ponds within a small geographical area were investigated to discover which factors best predict the numbers of taxa and the types of communities found in each pond. In view of the difficulties inherent in distinguishing the confounding effects of different types of variables, the ponds were chosen to minimize the possible influence of pond age and isolation. Sites Sixteen ponds were chosen from among the large number of water bodies created by open-cast extraction of ball-clay in the Isle of Purbeck, Dorset, U.K. The study ponds all lie within an area of heath, woodland and pasture, 5×2 km, centred on National Grid Reference SY935835, just north of the chalk escarpment (Fig. 1). The ponds were chosen to represent as wide a range of physico-chemical and habitat conditions (as judged from terrestrial and aquatic vegetation) as possible. The exact ages of individual ponds are not known, but all date from the nineteenth century, with the exception of pond Q, which was formed in the eighteenth century (English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd, pers. comm.). From a study of the rate of colonization of newly created ball-clay ponds in the area (Barnes, 1983), it appears that the equilibrium number of macroinvertebrate taxa for small ponds is approached within 20 years of the first appearance of the water body. It is expected, therefore, that the ponds chosen for this study have attained the colonization asymptote, at least as far as macroinvertebrates are concerned, and any differences in age between them are not likely to be of importance. Dispersal distances between the ponds are small, the greatest nearest-neighbour distance being <1 km. No discrete source of colonizing propagules is recognizable, there being numerous small water bodies (ball-clay ponds, bomb craters and streams) in the area as well as the Corfe River to the east and the River Stour to the north-west. It is therefore assumed that the source pool of colonists is diffuse, so that no pond is substantially more isolated than any other. All the ponds contain at least 1 m depth of water throughout the year and none is connected, at any time, to any other water body. Methods (i) Morphometry Pond areas and shore lengths were estimated from large-scale maps produced by English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd surveyors. For the larger ponds, maximum depths and basin profiles were obtained from depth measure- FIG. 1. Location of the study site and map of the sixteen ball-clay ponds, labelled A–R. ments taken at 5 m intervals along transects; depths of smaller ponds were measured using a lead line from the bank. (ii) Chemistry Water samples were taken from 20 cm below the surface, 2 m from the shore, away from dense vegetation. All ponds were sampled within 2 h around noon on 12 April 1979 and again on 8 August 1979. Temperature and dissolved oxygen were recorded in situ and samples were analysed the same day by the Wessex Water Authority chemical laboratory, Poole, using standard methods (see Barnes, 1981; for details). For each sample, pH, electrical conductivity, turbidity, total hardness, alkalinity, nitrate, ammonium, orthophosphate, and 5-day B.O.D. were determined. Seven samples were later analysed for calcium and two for total aluminium, using an atomic absorption spectrophotometer at the University of Exeter. (iii) Macrophytes All ponds were surveyed during a 2-week period in August 1979 to determine the total area vegetated, the number of species, and their relative abundance, expressed as cover abundance scores as follows: 1 = 0.1–5% of vegetated area 2 = 6–25% of vegetated area 3 = 26–50% of vegetated area 4 = 51–75% of vegetated area 5 = 76–100% of vegetated area (iv) Macroinvertebrates The macroinvertebrate communities of the shallow littoral were sampled using standard sampling units, each consisting of five separate 2 m sweeps with an F.B.A. pond net (mesh aperture 1 mm). Trials showed that five sweeps obtained at least 85% of the species to be discovered by repeated sweeping within a given weed bed. Pond nets tend to under-sample certain elements of the fauna (see Macan, 1977a, for a critique), and the species lists obtained from one period of sampling will not be complete. However, such samples, taken in a standard manner and within a short space of time, may be used to compare communities between ponds. All sixteen ponds were sampled in a 3-day period in early April 1979. All were sampled with equal intensity, that is the number of sampling units employed in each pond was proportional to the extent of the shallow littoral habitat. An increase in the number of samples as pond size increased was deemed necessary to incorporate the apparent greater diversity of littoral habitats in larger ponds. The shoreline of each pond was divided arbitrarily into 100 m stretches and one sampling unit was taken in each 100 m stretch. The positions of the five individual sweeps in each sampling unit were determined by possibility of access to the water. Identification was taken to species wherever possible, but chironomid larvae were identified only to genus, and some members of other groups could be identified only to family. The relative numerical abundance of taxa were expressed as abundance scores as follows: 1 = present, but a mean of <1 individual per sampling unit 2 = 1–10 individuals per sampling unit 3 = 11–100 individuals per sampling unit 4 = >100 individuals per sampling unit The use of approximately logarithmic abundance categories to some extent overcomes the problem of comparing relative abundance of taxa of very different body size and reduces the dominating effect of seasonal swarms of small individuals. Results Numbers of taxa The numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa and macrophyte species found in each pond are shown in Table 1, together with values for selected physical and chemical parameters. The wide range of all these parameters over the sixteen ponds is apparent: for example, the number of macroinvertebrate taxa ranges from twenty-four to eighty-eight; pH from 3.8 to 7.5; and pond area from 0.023 to 2.0 ha. The total number of macroinvertebrate taxa found was 174 and the total number of macrophyte species thirty-one. The relationships between numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa (INVERTS) and macrophyte species (PLANTS) and physical and chemical characteristics of the ponds were investigated by correlation and regression analyses carried out using the statistical package MINITAB 81.1 (Ryan, 1981). Regression analyses were used to discover which, if any, of the biotic, physical and chemical factors might adequately explain the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa or macrophyte species found in these ponds. Preliminary analyses suggested that regression analysis would not be inappropriate, since the measurement errors in the y-variables (INVERTS or PLANTS) are great relative to those in the x-variables (predictors), and the individual variables are approximately normally distributed. Bivariate plots suggested the need to log-transform INVERTS, PLANTS, area and vegetated area for regression analysis (i.e. LINVERTS, LPLANTS, LAREA, LVAREA); this gave an acceptable degree of homoscedasticity in the residuals (Draper & Smith, 1981). Regression analyses proceeded by using predicator variables in turn, and, for multiple regression, adding them one at a time, using a correlation matrix as a guide and inspecting residuals and coefficients at each stage. The effectiveness of the various regression equations for predicting numbers of taxa in individual ponds was assessed by plotting the number of taxa predicted v. the number observed for each pond ('predicted-y v. observed-y' plots). Points falling above the line of equality indicate an over-estimation by the equation, those below an under-estimation (see Fig. 3). As a first step, Pearson correlation coefficients were computed between all pairs of the fourteen variables given in Table 1, log-transformed as appropriate. Sixteen pairs of observations were used in each case, except those involving calcium, for which only seven pairs could be used. Table 2, the correlation half-matrix, shows a number of distinct patterns: (i) LINVERTS is positively correlated with calcium and pH (\( P < 0.01 \)) and with LPLANTS, alkalinity, and LVAREA (\( P < 0.05 \)). (ii) All pairwise correlations between pH, conductivity, B.O.D., total hardness, alkalinity and calcium are significant at the 1% level. (iii) LAREA and LVAREA are correlated (\( P < 0.05 \)), depth is correlated with LAREA (\( P < 0.01 \)), and LVAREA with LINVERTS (\( P < 0.05 \)) but none of these morphometric variables is correlated with any chemical factor. Discussion For the majority of the Purbeck ball-clay ponds considered here, the numbers of littoral macroinvertebrate taxa present are closely predicted by a single environmental variable, namely pH. Below pH 5.5, Mollusca, Malacostraca and Ephemeroptera are completely absent, while other taxa, notably the Trichoptera and Chironomini (Diptera), show a reduction in the numbers of taxa present. These patterns concur well with those reported from Scandinavian acidified lakes and North American dystrophic waters, where Gastropoda, Malacostraca and Ephemeroptera are characteristically absent at low pH (Wetzel, 1975; Økland, 1980; Stenson, 1985). In terms of the identities of taxa present, faunal similarities are greatest between ponds of similar pH (Fig. 5a), which suggests that successful colonization of at least some ponds is restricted to a subset of the total Purbeck species pool by chemical, or associated, factors. Marked faunal differences between acid and circum-neutral ball-clay ponds are apparent from the earliest stages of colonization of new ponds in the Isle of Purbeck (Barnes, 1983) so that differences between acid and circum-neutral 'mature' pond faunas are not the result of successional changes or differential dispersal rates between acid-sensitive and acid-tolerant species. Absence of taxa from ponds of low pH is probably due to a suite of factors, both chemical and biotic, which are directly or indirectly consequential on pH. The adverse effects of high hydrogen ion concentrations per se are exacerbated where calcium concentrations are low and levels of toxic metal ions, notably Al^{3+}, are high (Howells, 1984). The toxic effects of low pH have been demonstrated experimentally for a number of freshwater invertebrate groups, notably Crustacea (e.g. Steigen & Raddum, 1981), Ephemeroptera (Bell, 1971), and some Plecoptera and Trichoptera (Raddum & Steigen, 1981). In the Purbeck ponds, calcium levels are very highly correlated with pH, and although total aluminium levels were not measured systematically, two measurements of 70 \( \mu \)g l^{-1} in pond J and 570 \( \mu \)g l^{-1} in pond Q indicate that some of the acid ponds are probably well within the range of Al^{3+} concentrations known to be toxic to fish (Howells, 1984). The water chemistry in acid ponds E, J, P, Q and R is likely to cause severe physiological stress and prevent completion of the life-cycle in sensitive groups and thus ensure that any incoming propagules of these species cannot colonize. Furthermore, changes in certain biotic elements brought about by physiological stress may so change the habitat as to preclude colonization by species which are not themselves acid-sensitive. Stenson (1985) suggests that a loss of grazers (gastropods) and shredders (malacostracans) may have a major influence on littoral feeding relationships in the acidified Lake Gårdsjön. In the present study the macroinvertebrate faunas of acid ponds are characterized by what is absent, rather than what is present. Few taxa are recognizably 'acidophilic' in their distribution, with the possible exceptions of the chironomid Acamptocladius ?submontanus and the mayfly Leptophlebia marginata. The Odonata also appear to be better represented in ponds of pH<6.8. There is no evidence in these data of the biologically mediated pH effect reported by Hendrikson & Oscarson (1985), namely that loss of fish, the major visual predators, during lake acidification results in increased abundance of large, active invertebrates such as corixids and Notonecta (Hemiptera) and dytiscids (Coleoptera). Fish are absent from most of the ponds below pH 6.5 (A, B, C, D, E, J, P, Q and R), but there is no indication of a greater relative abundance of Hemiptera or Coleoptera in these ponds. This lack of agreement may be because the open water ('limnetic') species included by Hendrikson & Oscarson were not specifically sampled here. Over the wide range of pH represented in the study ponds, then, differences in faunal composition and diversity between the opposite ends of the pH spectrum may be due to a number of factors, probably acting in combina- tion. Many of these are themselves a direct or indirect consequence of hydrogen ion concentration, and pH alone would seem to provide a convenient index of the macroinvertebrate diversity to be expected in a pond. However, spot pH measurements from different water bodies can meaningfully be compared only if all are taken at approximately the same time and in a comparable way, since the pH of a given water body may vary both spatially and temporally, and with different methods of measurement. Although the general character of the macroinvertebrate communities of the Purbeck ponds is set by water chemistry, there is considerable variation in the details of the assemblages, even in ponds of similar pH. In general, ponds which fall within a narrow range of water chemistry, and not affected by any other overwhelmingly influential factor, may be expected to display a considerable diversity of assemblages, each created by a multiplicity of abiotic and biotic factors acting in unique combinations. Two ponds, F and L, clearly do not fit the linear model relating numbers of taxa to pH. Their faunal impoverishment may be linked to the lack of extensive weed beds in both ponds. The paucity of macrophytes may, in turn, be due to a number of factors, such as dense phytoplankton in the summer, supported by high nitrate and phosphate levels (Table 1), unbroken tree-shade round the margins and disturbance of the littoral sediment by bottom-feeding carp and tench. (The latter two points apply equally well to the richly-vegetated pond H, however.) Ponds F and L both have highly organic littoral substrata which support some distinctive faunal elements: pond F, in common with the other woodland ponds H and K, is dominated by shredders (mainly Trichoptera), while pond L, which also receives run-off from a nearby pig-farm, is dominated by organisms typical of organically enriched habitats, such as Tubificidae (Oligochaeta) and Chironomus spp. (Diptera). The number of species of macrophyte found in the Purbeck ponds bears no clear relationship with any of the factors considered. Some of the species distributions are clearly linked with pH: Sphagnum cuspidatum and Juncus bulbosus, in particular, are typical of the acid ponds. Grahn (1975) shows that Sphagnum species rapidly dominate acidified Swedish lakes, and this creates a characteristic biotope for invertebrates quite different from the habitat provided by aquatic angiosperms. The tenuous link observed here between macrophyte assemblages and water chemistry is in sharp contrast to the close relationship known to occur between lake diatom assemblages and pH (e.g. Battarbee, 1984). It remains to ask why such a wide range of pH occurs in the Purbeck ball-clay ponds. Two main sources of possible variation can be identified: local variations in geology, and differences in the land-use and vegetation immediately surrounding the ponds. Ball-clays are themselves chemically inert, but some clay sequences contain pyritic plant remains, which may be oxidized during changes in the water-table and cause acidification. The incidence of acid and neutral ponds is, however, independent of the oxidation state of the clays in this study area. A far greater influence on water chemistry would appear to be the use and vegetation of the surrounding land. The ponds all lie within the Bagshot Beds sandy deposits, which support Calluna heathland over much of the area (Fig. 1). Water passing through these heathland soils is likely to be acidic and low in nutrient ions. The ecology of littoral zone Chironomidae in four artificial, urban, tropical Malaysian lakes Jin-Min Lee1 · Jing-Ye Gan1 · Catherine Mary Yule1,2 Published online: 14 September 2018 © Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2018 Abstract Urbanization is increasingly compromising lakes in the rapidly developing countries of tropical Southeast Asia. Greater understanding of the ecology of tropical lakes is essential in order to determine the best ways to protect and manage them. A comparison was made of the species richness, abundance and diets of Chironomidae in two forest lakes (both created by damming rivers - one in an urban forest reserve, one adjacent to an urban area) and two urban park lakes (ex- tin mine lakes) in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. 19 species of chironomids were recorded (10 collector-gatherers, one collector-filterer, one shredder, 3 predators and 4 predators/grazers). The most abundant species were Polypedilum leei, Tanytarsus formosanus, Zavreliella marmorata and Procladius sp.. Conductivity was highest in the urban park lakes due to pollution. Temperature was also highest in the urban park lakes due to lower riparian canopy cover and lower macrophyte abundance. Larval abundance (mostly collector-gathering Chironominae) was significantly higher in the forest lakes compared to the urban park lakes, which could be related to cleaner water and higher vegetation cover which provided more food resources (leaf litter and periphyton) and more microhabitats. Predatory tanypods were most abundant in forest lakes which also had the highest numbers of their prey (Chironominae). Four predatory species of Tanypodinae supplemented their diet with blue-green algae in two of the urban lakes. Only one collector-filterer (Corynoneura sp.) was recorded (only in the forest lakes). Keywords Community structure · Species richness · Functional feeding groups Introduction Globally only 0.01% of the world’s water is freshwater covering 0.8% of the land surface yet freshwater ecosystems are particularly vulnerable to human impacts (Dudgeon et al. 2006). Lakes and ponds comprise about 3% of the world’s freshwater bodies with a huge number being small and undervalued (Downing et al. 2006). The contribution of these small lakes is increasingly becoming recognized to be important and different from larger lakes in several aspects such as nutrient and carbon cycling (Hanson et al. 2007; Downing 2010; Read and Rose 2013) as well as responses to climate change (Winslow et al. 2015). Most of the research has been in temperate regions and little is known of small tropical lakes, yet these differ from temperate lakes in many aspects (Lewis 1996, 2000; Danger et al. 2009), including threats and management (Jeppesen et al. 2005). As with other natural ecosystems such as rivers and streams, lakes are also negatively impacted by urbanization. The effects of urbanization on streams – the “urban stream syndrome” – is well known and results in distinctive changes to the physico-chemistry and ecology of urban streams (Walsh et al. 2005). The urban stream syndrome has frequently been observed in temperate regions and is also applicable in tropical streams (Yule et al. 2015). Although less is known regarding the impacts of urbanization on lakes and even less is known about tropical lakes, urbanization has been shown to cause similar problems in lakes as in streams due to increases in sedimentation, nutrients, and heavy metals and loss of biodiversity (Naselli-Flores 2008; Sharip and Zakaria 2008). Tropical Malaysia has very few natural lakes (e.g. Tasik Bera and Tasik Cini – both floodplain lakes) but they have received more extensive research due to their environmental and socio-economic importance compared to artificial lakes (Sharip and Zakaria 2008). Thousands of small artificial lakes have arisen in the past century due to previous tin mining activities (Yule 2004). Many of these ex-mining pools have simply been abandoned, while some are now used for recreation, the focus of housing estates, dumping industrial and domestic waste, and flood control. Several public parks have been built around rehabilitated ex-mining pools in urban areas such as Kuala Lumpur. Such urban lakes have been shown to offer many benefits such as recreation, aesthetic values and provision of an aquatic ecosystem for flora and fauna (Elmqvist et al. 2004; Shojaei et al. 2013). In particular they are potential refuges for fish and wildlife in an urban environment. Given the paucity of natural lakes in Malaysia, these artificial lakes are highly valuable thus it is important that management of these lakes includes consideration of societal and ecological needs (Baron et al. 2002; Chester and Robson 2013). Despite the ease of accessibility and high public contact with urban lakes, there have been very few studies of Malaysia’s urban lakes. Although a basic water quality assessment of two urban lakes has been undertaken (Said et al. 2012a, b), there have been no published biological studies. This information is valuable as the littoral zones of urban lakes are teeming with organisms and are also the forefront of exposure to urbanization, which could lead to changes in the lake communities. This study investigates factors affecting the biodiversity and distribution of a common group of littoral residents – Chironomidae (Insecta, Diptera) in four artificial lakes in Kuala Lumpur – two ex-tin mining lakes in urban parks, and two forested lakes (one in an urban forest park dominated by secondary forest, one in a primary forest reserve to the east of the city) which were created by the damming of small rivers. We chose to study chironomids because they have a worldwide distribution and they are valuable indicators of aquatic-ecosystem responses to environmental and anthropogenic changes (Armitage et al. 1995; Langdon et al. 2006). We hypothesized that the species composition, species richness and abundance of chironomids in the forested lakes would be different from the urban park lakes due to variations in environmental factors and food availability. We predicted that the chironomids in the forested lakes with high allochthonous input and less impact from urbanization (particularly with respect to pollutants) would be (1) higher in abundance and (2) more diverse than in the urban park lakes. We also predicted that (3) due to the availability of different food resources in forested and park lakes, chironomids of the same species might have different diets. We tested this prediction by examining the gut contents of the chironomids. Methods We studied two forested and two park lakes in Kuala Lumpur (Fig. 1, Table 1), all located in a lowland environment (<200 m). Four different sites around the littoral zones of each lake were chosen to represent diverse habitats. Kuala Lumpur has a warm, humid tropical climate with an annual temperature range of 23-33 °C. It typically experiences lower rainfall in the middle of the year (May to August) and higher rainfall at the end of the year (October to January). Forested Lakes We studied two lakes in forest reserves: a lake in primary forest in the Ampang Forest Reserve (on the edge of the suburb of Ampang) and another in secondary forest in the Kota Damansara Community Forest Park. The lake in Ampang Forest Reserve (Fig. 1a) was originally a reservoir supplying water to Kuala Lumpur which was constructed in 1892 by damming a tributary of the Ampang River. Its entire catchment lies within primary lowland dipterocarp forest. It receives water inflow from three pristine streams and it flows out into the Ampang River. In contrast, the lake in the Kota Damansara Community Forest Park (Fig. 1b) is an artificial urban lake created by damming a small stream in the early 2000s. Apart from the dam wall, the lake is surrounded by secondary dipterocarp forest. It flows out into a drainage channel and it receives runoff from a road which runs beside the dam wall. Urban Park lakes Two urban park lakes were also studied: Subang Jaya Lake (Fig. 1c) and Shah Alam Lake (Fig. 1d). Both are former tin mining lakes which have been turned into public parks with sparse trees and drainage channels into and out of the lakes – so they receive road runoff and other pollutants. These two lakes are managed and maintained by the local municipal councils who occasionally remove vegetation from around the banks such as tall grasses and macrophytes. Subang Jaya Lake was officially opened to the public in 1990. Shah Alam Lake lies in Shah Alam Lake Gardens which was developed around seven ex-tin mine lakes. It has a raised wooden platform to observe wildlife such as tortoises, fish and storks. All four lakes are sites for recreation and fishing. Environmental factors Environmental factors at each of the four sampling sites of the lakes were measured as follows: air temperature (Kestral 3500), water temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, and conductivity (EUTECH CyberScan PD650), and light intensity (Lutron LX-103). Spot measurements were taken at each site. Fig. 1 The study sites: (a) Ampang lake, (b) Kota Damansara lake, (c) Subang Jaya lake and (d) Shah Alam lake The percentage of canopy cover, leaf litter cover, vegetation cover at bank (e.g. grasses and shrubs), macrophytes and wood in the water were estimated qualitatively by observation with the aid of a grid depicting % cover. The substrate composition of the lakes was classified into mud/silt (<0.5 mm), sand (0.5–2 mm), gravel (2–64 mm), cobbles (65–256 mm) and boulders (>256 mm) and these data were computed into a substrate index (Suren 1996): \[ \text{Substrate index (SI)} = 0.07 \times \% \text{boulder} + 0.06 \times \% \text{cobble} \\ + 0.05 \times \% \text{gravel} + 0.04 \times \% \text{sand} \\ + 0.03 \times \% \text{mud/silt} \] Sample collection and processing Macroinvertebrates were haphazardly collected by kick sampling using a 250 μm mesh dip net at four sites around each lake for 2 min per site. Each sample covered about 5 m along the banks with care taken to dislodge fauna from within the substrate and among the macrophytes in the littoral zone. Dip-net sampling has been shown to be suitable for macroinvertebrate sampling in the littoral zone of lakes (e.g. Kashian and Burton 2000; García-Criado and Trigal 2005; Heatherly et al. 2005). The samples were placed in a tray of water and the net was rinsed to remove debris and fauna. The samples were then sorted to remove large macroinvertebrate predators (e.g. water scorpions and dragonfly larvae) and debris such as twigs and leaf litter. The samples were then preserved in 70% alcohol for sorting in the laboratory using a stereo microscope (Zeiss Stemi DV4). Chironomids were removed and placed in vials with 70% alcohol for taxonomic identification, determination of abundance and gut analysis. Sampling was performed once for each lake between January to March 2014. Chironomidae communities and diets Preserved Chironomidae larvae were mounted on slides in polyvinyl alcohol lactophenol mountant and examined under a Zeiss AXIO Lab. AI compound microscope. The identity of each larva was determined to the lowest taxonomic level possible (keys by Cranston 2004, 2007, 2010). The species richness and abundance of each chironomid species at each site was determined. The gut contents of the mounted chironomids with at least partially filled guts were assessed using a compound microscope to determine their diets. Gut contents were categorized as: 1) fine particulate organic matter (FPOM, particles <500 μm), 2) coarse particulate organic matter (CPOM, particles 500 μm–1 mm), 3) fungal hyphae, 4) leaf-litter fragments, 5) algae, and 6) animal tissue. The larvae were then assigned to functional feeding groups, i.e. shredders, collector-filterers, collector-gatherers, grazers, or predators following Merritt and Cummins (1996). Collector-gatherers were distinguished from collector-filterers based on field and laboratory observations of their mode of feeding. Table 1 Comparison of the environmental factors of the four lakes
