It is necessary to point out that when \( \Delta WF > 0 \), WI predominates in a pond and \( \Delta WF \) is a gain (on the left side in Fig. 5). When \( \Delta WF < 0 \), WO predominates and \( \Delta WF \) is a loss (on the right side in Fig. 5). When \( \Delta S > 0 \), storage is in fact a loss, because the pond makes up its water deficit with water from \( P \) and WI. When \( \Delta S < 0 \), it is a gain, because the pond feeds its water to WO. In the second type of pond (Ponds 6, 10 and 13), storage and supplying functions predominated. In these ponds, 100% of the gain was due to \( P - E \), while WO and \( \Delta S \) were responsible for 52% and 48% of the loss, respectively. The third type of ponds, supplying ponds, was the most numerous (Ponds 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 12 and 14). In these ponds, 100% of WO was made up of \( P - E \) and \( \Delta S \). Between 28% (Pond 12) and 89% (Ponds 4 and 14) of the water gain was due to \( P - E \), and between 11% (Ponds 4 and 14) and 72% (Pond 12) was due to \( \Delta S \). The total annual amount of water determining water circulation in the ponds ranged from 83 mm (Ponds 6, 10 and 13) to 293 mm (Pond 12) with an average of 124 mm. Assuming that the average area of the pond in our material was 1,719.7 m\(^2\), the 124-mm layer corresponded to 213 m\(^3\) of water. During the wet season (early spring), the ponds were connected to the river network, so we used Eqs. 4 and 5 to calculate the water balance components for these water bodies. The role of \( P - E \) lost its significance. We found that only two ponds (Ponds 3 and 14) still maintained their storage and evaporative functions (Fig. 6). In these ponds, the contribution of \( P - E \) to the water gain ranged from 60% (Pond 3) to 89% (Pond 14). In these ponds, precipitation was responsible for 89% (Pond 14) to 100% (Pond 3) of SWO. In the other ponds, \( \Delta SWF \) and \( \Delta GWF \) were the predominant water balance components. These ponds differed from each other in terms of water circulation. In the first group (Ponds 1, 2, 7, 9, 11 and 13), the groundwater influence predominated. These ponds drained aquifers, as indicated by the sign of \( \Delta GWF \). Here, GWI comprised between 91% (Pond 2) and nearly 100% (Pond 9) of the water gain. The water surplus originating mainly from GWI activated SWO from these ponds. GWI comprised from 86% (Pond 2) to 100% (Pond 7) of the gain, while SWO accounted for 91% of the loss in Pond 2 and 100% of the loss in Pond 7. These were, therefore, ponds that drained groundwater reservoirs, redirecting water to the surface, as SWO. The remaining ponds (Ponds 4, 5, 6, 8, 10 and 12) were supplied by river water, as indicated by the sign of \( \Delta SWF \). The contribution of SWI in water inflow in these ponds was 82% in Pond 8 and 98% in Pond 6. The water that supplied to these ponds was “redirected” to groundwater reservoirs in the amounts ranging from 94% in Pond 10 to 100% in Ponds 4, 5, 8 and 12. These ponds, therefore, supply SWI into groundwater. When we included \( \Delta SWF \) and \( \Delta GWF \) in the water balance of these ponds, it turned out that the total amount of water involved in water circulation was in fact greater and ranged from 93 mm in Pond 14 to 27,431 mm in Pond 9. As mentioned before, two phases may be distinguished in the functioning of moraine ponds in northern Poland: the dry and the wet phase. The duration of the dry phase ranges from 3 months (Pond 12) to 10 months (Ponds 1, 3, 5 and 6), while the wet phase lasts from 2 months (Ponds 1, 3, 5 and 6) to 9 months (Pond 12) (Fig. 7). Limitations Calculation of a pond’s water balance (but also that of a lake, a wetland, etc.) involves a number of restrictions. The first issue is, of course, the accuracy of measurement of each element of the water balance. While it is possible to quantitatively determine streamwater inflow, streamwater outflow, precipitation and storage of a pond, evaporation and groundwater flow are very difficult to measure. Evaporation is therefore often calculated from empirical formulas. Evaporation is influenced by many factors, such as water temperature, water mixing, wind velocity, plant overgrowth and water colour. When calculating the water balance we found, however, that the amount of evaporation had a much smaller impact on the water balance of a pond than streamwater and groundwater flow, hence we decided to omit these factors. Exact measurements of streamwater flow and water level changes are another limitation. While it is possible to determine these two parameters using specialised measuring equipment (automatic flow meters and limnigraphs), it is also very expensive. Due to financial constraints, we had to limit the frequency of measurements to monthly intervals. Additionally, the ponds were private property of farmers, who are very suspicious and reluctant to allow researchers on their land. Another limitation is the exclusion of subsurface flow from the water balance equations. Subsurface flow depends on many factors, including the shape and size of the direct catchment, surface deposits, land use and many more. Subsurface flow seems to be particularly important during the dry phase. It has a significantly lower impact on ponds connected to the river system. In this case, almost the entire subsurface flow is included in the streamwater inflow (SWI) and groundwater inflow (GWI). Discussion Ponds in Poland are considered almost invisible. The assumption that ponds have no connection with groundwater and streamwater results in that they are considered wastelands. Some researchers do not regard then as a part of the river network and refer to them as small water-filled depressions (Pieńkowski, 2006). In terms of water circulation, ponds are no different from larger water bodies. Our study has shown that ponds situated within the same catchment, not uncommonly in close vicinity to each other, may each have a different hydrological function in water circulation. In contrast to the established view, ponds do not only have storage and evaporative functions modified by groundwater flow (Lehsten et al., 2011), but their water circulation is almost entirely dominated by streamwater flow (\( \Delta \mathrm{SWF} \)) and groundwater flow (\( \Delta \mathrm{GWF} \)). These functions may, however, vary from pond to pond. It may be a result of their high hydrogeomorphological diversity (Kalettká & Rudat, 2006). A given pond may drain groundwater during one period and supply groundwater aquifers in another. The connectivity of ponds with groundwater is of enormous significance for the stability of runoff from the moraine plateaus of northern Poland (Bajkiewicz-Grabowska & Golus, 2009). Ponds are even more diverse than larger lakes and rivers (Williams et al., 2004; Biggs et al., 2005; De Meester et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2005; Davis et al., 2008; Oertli et al., 2009; Céréghino et al., 2012). The interconnection of ponds by streams is also of great importance for the movement of animals and plants. The seasonal intermittent streams that connect the ponds form pathways along which living organisms can migrate. These ponds, during the dry phase, may be used as a “stopover” by these organisms to “take shelter” until the wet season arrives. The capability of ponds to join the river system during the wet phase has an important bearing on determining the external boundaries of endorheic areas. The ranges of endorheic areas are taken into account when calculating the runoff in a given catchment and when assessing the input of the catchment’s biogenic elements in a stream or lake (Vollenweider, 1976). Ponds may release stored loads of nutrients from endorheic areas during the wet phase. They may therefore have a great impact on the quality of water in rivers and lakes that are their recipients. The contact of pond water with groundwater and river water also has great implications for their use. The common belief in Poland is that ponds are devoid of surface outflow and connection with groundwater has so far given us, humans, an unrestricted moral (but also legal) right to do with these bodies of water whatever we pleased. Ponds in Poland are still considered part of wasteland and pond owners believe that anything you do with the ponds will be better than just leaving these water bodies alone. They therefore drain the ponds and fill them in, convert them into fish ponds, use them for disposing of sewage and waste. And it is important that we change this way of thinking sooner better than later. Conclusion Ponds are small objects and despite their omnipresence, it is easy to overlook them when calculating water circulation of larger lakes, rivers, or basins. Our relatively simple method using the water balance equation shows that ponds are not only connected with groundwater but also shape and “control” runoff from the catchment. They are dynamic objects that affect whole water cycle in the region. Our results indicate that ponds play more important role in the environment of moraine plateaus than was previously thought. The hydrological functions of ponds situated on the moraine plateaus of northern Poland vary from pond to pond, but it is dependent almost entirely on streamwater flow and groundwater flow. The ponds we studied displayed a wet–dry cycle. During the dry cycle, when the ponds became water bodies without surface outflow, they exist because they are a drainage base for the shallow groundwater. As the amount of water in the cycle increases (the spring melt), the ponds become connected with the river network and initiate stream water outflow. Streamwater outflow results in water surplus within the catchment, as ponds are a storage base for catchment water. As the result of their connectivity with groundwater, ponds rarely dry up. The wet phase of the ponds lasts from 3 to 10 months, depending on the topographic location of each pond. The main hydrological function of the moraine plateau ponds in the dry phase is to retain water surplus originating from atmospheric exchange (\( P - E \)) and to retain water from underground drainage and surface inflow. During the wet phase, ponds activate stream- and groundwater outflow (SWO + GWO). Even neighbouring ponds may have opposite hydrological functions within a catchment. Some of them may drain groundwater and shape streamwater outflow, while the neighbouring ponds may “convert” streamwater into groundwater outflow. The ponds located on the moraine plateaus of northern Poland, therefore, deserve a greater interest on the part of researchers, regulation of their legal status and provision of legal protection. Zooplankton body size versus taxonomy in Mediterranean wetlands: implications for aquatic ecosystem evaluation Juan Diego Gilbert1,2,4, Inmaculada de Vicente3,5, Raquel Jiménez-Melero1,2,6, and Francisco Guerrero1,2,7 1Departamento de Biología Animal, Biología Vegetal y Ecología, Universidad de Jaén, Campus de Las Lagunillas, s/n. E–23071, Jaén, Spain 2Centro de Estudios Avanzados en Ciencias de la Tierra CEACTierra, Universidad de Jaén, Campus de Las Lagunillas, s/n. E–23071, Jaén, Spain 3Departamento de Ecología, Universidad de Granada, Campus de Fuentenueva, s/n. E–18071, Granada, Spain Abstract: Intrinsic ecological characteristics of Mediterranean wetlands make them excellent sites for studying biodiversity, but these wetlands have been studied much less frequently than temperate lakes. The invertebrates that inhabit them, and zooplankton specifically, play important roles in these wetlands. We compared the ability of taxon- and size-based analyses of the zooplankton community to predict the influence of environmental variables. We sampled environmental variables and zooplankton at 7 Mediterranean wetlands in the Iberian Peninsula (southern Spain) monthly along 1 hydroperiod cycle (2009–2010). We used 3 arrays for classifying the zooplankton community: 1) species occurring in >5% of the samples, 2) coarse-level taxa easily identified by a nonexpert (large branchiopods, small branchiopods, calanoid copepods, cyclopoid copepods, and harpacticoid copepods), and 3) 4 body-size classes (<1, 1–2.5, 2.5–10, and >10 mm in length). We used permutational analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) and canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) to test our hypotheses. Communities differed significantly among wetlands, and body size (55.8% of explained variance) was more useful than taxonomic composition (common taxa: 24.4%, coarse-level taxa: 26.5% of explained variance) for rapid assessment of the influence of the environmental variables on zooplankton community in temporary wetlands. Key words: zooplankton, Mediterranean wetlands, body size, eutrophication, wetland evaluation Wetlands are accepted globally as singular ecosystems (Mitsch and Gosselink 2000 and references therein). Nevertheless, small lentic ecosystems, and more specifically Mediterranean wetlands, have received much less attention than other aquatic ecosystems, such as large temperate lakes (Álvarez-Cobelas et al. 2005, Downing 2010). Mediterranean wetlands are unique because of their ecological characteristics. Most of them are very small with catchment area much larger than wetland surface area, and they experience a long vegetation period and strong seasonality in water supply (Álvarez-Cobelas et al. 2005). They are excellent repositories of biodiversity, frequently hold exclusive communities of aquatic organisms, and play an important role in the maintenance of regional biodiversity (Williams 1999, De Meester et al. 2005, Céréghino et al. 2008, Kagalou et al. 2010, Gilbert et al. 2014a, 2015a). They are recognized as essential hot spots of aquatic biodiversity, but the scarcity of research done in these ecosystems has made possible strongly detrimental human disturbance leading to the disappearance of many of them (Brinson and Malvárez 2002). A great fraction of Mediterranean wetlands are temporary and fishless (Conlon 2002). Thus, knowledge of the invertebrate communities that inhabit them is essential for modeling their trophic web structure (Wellborn et al. 1996, Quintana et al. 2006). Among invertebrates, the zooplankton assemblage is a good indicator for wetland assessment because zooplankton are easy to identify, play a key role in food webs, respond to environmental gradients (Jeppesen et al. 2000), and, in some cases, act as keystone species (Badosa et al. 2007). Aquatic assemblages can be analyzed on the basis of taxonomic identity or size of the individuals inhabiting them. The taxon-based approach is commonly used for analyzing the abundance or biomass of taxa in response to different experimental treatments or environmental variables (e.g., Quintana et al. 2006, Bagella et al. 2010). In contrast, the body-size approach is used to consider the distribution of biomass among size classes independently of taxonomic affiliation (e.g., Rojo and Rodríguez 1994, Blanco et al. 1998, Havens and Beaver 2011a, b). These approaches are complementary, but most studies of zooplankton assemblages, particularly in Mediterranean wetlands, have been based on the taxonomic approach. However, information about the size structure of zooplankton assemblages in wetlands is very useful for making management decisions because the body-size approach is simpler and less costly than the taxonomic approach (Havens and Beaver 2011a). The body-size approach has been used widely in oceanographic studies, in which investigators have used various optical techniques ranging from the more ancient Kontron, IBAS-I Image Analyzer (Rodríguez et al. 1987) or the semi-automatic image analyzer (AMS-VIDS 4; Guerrero and Rodríguez 1997) to more novel technologies, such as ZooScan (Gorsky et al. 2010), to obtain different biometric measures. We focused our study on the use of taxon- and size-based methods to explore whether taxonomic structure or body-size are good predictors of zooplankton responses to environmental influences in 7 Mediterranean wetlands located in the southern Iberian Peninsula. First, we analyzed zooplankton taxon abundance and size distribution. Second, we assessed the effect of environmental variables on zooplankton assemblages with the aid of permutational analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) and canonical correspondence analysis (CCA). METHODS Study site We worked in 7 wetlands (Fig. 1) in the Alto Guadalquivir region of the southeastern Iberian Peninsula. The study ![Geographical location of the study area in southern Spain and the 7 wetlands in the Alto Guadalquivir region.](page_1012_1342_1047_482.png) Figure 1. Geographical location of the study area in southern Spain and the 7 wetlands in the Alto Guadalquivir region. wetlands were classified based on the definition reported by Montes et al. (2004) and typology described by Rodríguez-Rodríguez and Benavente (2008) as playa-lake water bodies. The region has a Mediterranean climate, with 2 strongly marked seasons, a wet autumn–winter during which most of the annual rainfall occurs and a dry summer without precipitation (Álvarez-Cobelas et al. 2005). These climatic conditions are responsible for drastic water-level fluctuations, and most of the wetlands dry during the summer season. As a result of these water-level fluctuations, biotic and abiotic variables typically undergo dramatic temporal changes (Gilbert et al. 2014a, b, 2015a, b). We sampled wetlands periodically over 1 y. As is usual in Mediterranean regions, the wetlands were dry at the beginning of the hydrologic cycle in October and November 2009, except Castillo wetland, which filled in November. Therefore, the sampling period started in January 2010 except for Castillo (December 2009) and extended through December 2010. Zooplankton samples We collected zooplankton samples (plankton-net mesh size = 63 μm) monthly along 2 longitudinal transects, one from the shoreline to the open water and another along the shoreline. We combined the samples to obtain an integrated sample. We estimated the volume of filtered water as the distance of the haul multiplied by the mouth diameter of the net (27.5-cm mouth diameter). This sampling strategy allowed us to include all spatial and temporal heterogeneity characterizing the studied wetlands (Gilbert et al. 2015a). We preserved all samples in situ with 4% formalin (final concentration). In the laboratory, we counted crustacean zooplankton in the whole sample and identified individuals at the species level with the aid of keys published by Dussart (1967, 1969), Dussart and Defaye (1995), Einsle (1996), and Ranga-Reddy (1994) for copepods and Alonso (1996) for branchiopods. Later, we classified the zooplankton in 3 assemblages (Havens and Beaver 2011a) that corresponded to 3 matrices: 1) species matrix: species present in >5% of the total samples collected; 2) coarser-taxa matrix: taxa easily identified by a nonexpert after some training, including large branchiopods (LB; Anostraca, Conchostraca, Notostraca, Spinicaudata, and large Cladocera [Daphnia spp. and Simocephalus spp.]), small branchiopods (SB; small cladocerans), calanoid copepods (C), cyclopoid copepods (CY), and harpacticoid copepods (H); and 3) body-size matrix: 4 body-size classes that encompassed the observed range of sizes in the sampled zooplankton (S1: <1 mm, S2: 1–2.5 mm, S3: 2.5–10 mm, and S4: >10 mm). We estimated the abundance of each body-size class based on the average size of each taxon reported in the literature (Alonso 1996, Dussart 1967, 1969, Ranga-Reddy 1994, Dussart and Defaye 1995, Einsle 1996). Environmental variables We measured maximum depth (cm), Secchi disk depth (cm), temperature (°C), pH, and conductivity (μS/cm) monthly at the deepest point in each wetland. We measured temperature, conductivity, and pH in situ with a multiparameter YSI 556 MPS probe (Yellow Springs Instruments, Yellow Springs, Ohio). We measured turbidity (nephelometric turbidity units [NTU]) in situ with a Hanna HI93703 probe (Hanna Instruments, Woonsocket, Rhode Island) and fluorescence in situ with a field fluorometer (Aquafluor Handheld; Turner Design, San Jose, California) on an integrated sample from the 2 longitudinal transects (similar to the sampling design used for zooplankton samples). We estimated chlorophyll \( a \) (Chl \( a \)) concentration based on a fluorometry calibration curve (fluorescence = 16.584[Chl \( a \)] – 2.3616; \( R^2 = 0.998 \)) obtained in the laboratory based on Chl \( a \) standard solutions. We transported unfiltered integrated water samples to the laboratory within 3 h of collection and stored them in darkness and frozen at –20°C for <3 mo before analysis. In the laboratory, we digested unfiltered 50-mL aliquots with potassium persulfate for analysis of total P (TP) or sulfuric acid for analysis of total N (TN) (APHA 1995). We quantified TP and TN in the digested samples spectrophotometrically (HALO RB-10; Dynamica Scientific, Newport Pagnell, UK) by the molybdenum-blue method (Murphy and Riley 1962) or by ultraviolet spectrophotometric screening (APHA 1995), respectively. Detection limits were 1 μg P/L and 40 μg N/L for TP and TN, respectively. We measured the length of the aquatic phase or days of water inundation (DWI) as the presence of a taxon in relation to the day of the initial wetland inundation (the day on which a wetland basin was waterlogged) and wetland surface area (ha) as other explanatory variables. We estimated wetland surface area based on its length and width and formulae for the areas of simple shapes (ellipse or circle) fitted to the geometric form of the wetland on each sampling date. Statistical analysis We used PERMANOVA (PAST, version 3.06; Hammer et al. 2001) to conduct multivariate analysis of zooplankton species, coarser-taxa, and body-size assemblages. PERMANOVA was performed with 9999 permutations on Bray–Curtis distances among log(x + 1)-transformed abundances for each of the 3 matrices to test for differences in the assemblages among wetlands. PERMANOVA is not affected by unbalanced data sets (Alfonso et al. 2010). Significant differences were inferred at \( \alpha = 0.05 \). We used detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) to select the most appropriate direct statistical analysis to relate the 3 zooplankton matrices to environmental variables. The length of the DCA gradient was >3, indicating that a CCA was the most appropriate unimodal analysis (Iturron- dobeitia et al. 2004). CCA is a multivariate statistical ordination method that finds the maximum correlation between environmental and biological data sets (ter Braak 1987). Prior to analysis, we log(\( x + 1 \))-transformed data (except pH) from the zooplankton and environmental variable matrices to reduce the effect of different measurement scales of variables (Havens and Beaver 2011a). We removed species that were present in <5% of the samples from the species matrix. This step could be considered as a loss of information, but CCA is highly sensitive to low-abundance species (Zuur et al. 2010). We ran the CCAs with 499 Monte–Carlo permutations with significance set at \( p < 0.05 \). Multivariate analysis of ecological data was run with CANOCO (version 5; Microcomputer Software, Ithaca, New York). RESULTS Mean (±SE) values of the environmental variables in each wetland are presented in Table 1. Thirty-five zooplankton species were recorded during the sampling period. Of these species, 26 were present in >5% of the samples and constituted the species matrix. The most abundant common taxa were SB (35%) and CY (26%). The size classes S1 and S2 accounted for 38 and 35%, respectively, of the size-class matrix. Zooplankton assemblages described by all 3 matrices differed among wetlands (PERMANOVA, species matrix: Pseudo-\( F = 10.69, p < 0.01 \); coarse-taxa matrix: Pseudo-\( F = 6.40, p < 0.01 \); size-class matrix: Pseudo-\( F = 6.54, p < 0.01 \)). The CCA of the species matrix and environmental variables produced 3 significant axes (CCAs; Monte–Carlo tests, \( p < 0.05 \)). CCA1 (10.2% of explained variance) was correlated with turbidity, TP, and DWI; CCA2 (9%) was correlated with pH, area, maximum depth, TN, and Secchi-disk depth; and CCA3 (5.2%) was correlated with conductivity and Chl \( a \) (Table 2). Abundances of 13, 12, and 5 zooplankton species were correlated with CCA1, CCA2, and CCA3, respectively (Table 3). The CCA of the coarse-taxa matrix and environmental variable also produced 3 significant axes (Monte–Carlo tests, \( p < 0.05 \)). CCA1 (14.1%) was correlated with pH, Chl \( a \), area, maximum depth, Secchi-disk depth, and TN; CCA2 (10.0%) was correlated with conductivity and turbidity; and CCA3 (2.4%) was correlated with temperature, TP, and DWI (Table 2). Abundances of 3 (LC, C, and CY), 3 (LC, SC, and H), and 2 (LC and SC) coarse taxa were correlated with CCA1, CCA2, and CCA3, respectively (Table 3). The CCA of the body-size matrix and environmental variables yielded 3 significant axes (Monte–Carlo test, \( p < 0.05 \)). CCA1 (37.5%) was correlated with pH, maximum depth, Secchi-disk depth, TP, and TN; CCA2 (14.6%) was correlated with area and temperature; and CCA3 (3.7%) was correlated with turbidity, Chl \( a \), and DWI (Table 2). Abundances of size classes S1, S2, and S3 were correlated with CCA1; size class S4 was correlated with CCA2; and size class S1 was correlated with CCA3 (Table 3). DISCUSSION Taxon- and size-based analyses are 2 frequently used methods for assessing the effect of environmental variables on plankton community. Our results suggest that body size (55.8%) of explained variance is more informative than species (24.4%) or coarse taxa (26.5%) about the influence of the environmental variables on zooplankton community. Nevertheless, the combination of both approaches led us to a better understanding of the ecological functioning of aquatic systems (Strayer 1991, Rodríguez and Magnan 1993). Our results suggest that the zooplankton assemblages differ in species, coarse-level-taxa, and body-size composition among wetlands, and thus, reflect the extreme variability among Mediterranean wetlands and their key role for the maintenance of regional biodiversity (Williams 1997, Kagalou et al. 2010). Many investigators have found that zooplankton composition and body size are affected by factors, such as fish predation, food availability, temperature, and generation time (Brooks and Dodson 1965, Gillooly 2000, Hambright 2008, Fernández et al. 2009, Castellani et al. 2013, Lin et al. 2013, Quintana et al. 2015). All environmental variables in our study had a significant correlation with \( \geq 1 \) CCA of each analysis, a result indicating that all environmental variables in our study significantly affected the zooplankton assemblage. Maximum depth, Secchi-disk depth, TN, and DWI were more strongly correlated with the CCAs than other environmental variables (high Pearson \( r \) values; Table 2). The environmental variables that contributed to CCA1 of the CCAs based on coarse-taxa and size-class matrices were very similar to those that contributed to CCA2 of the CCA based on the species matrix. These axes might be linked to eutrophication level (see the opposite correlation between Secchi disk and TN in Table 2). The Chl \( a \) concentration supports this notion only for coarse taxonomic groups. However, the lack of a relationship between Chl \( a \) and eutrophication has been explained in these ecosystems as being a result of the presence of well-developed macrophyte beds, which negatively affect phytoplankton biomass and, consequently, Chl \( a \) concentration. Gilbert et al. (2015b) suggested competitive interactions between macrophytes and phytoplankton for inorganic nutrients and the release of allelopathic substances by macrophytes as main reasons for this negative relationship in these wetlands. They also pointed out a discrepancy between the trophic levels estimated based on the chlorophyll trophic state index (Carlson 1977) and the bioproduction number (BPN; Håkanson 1984), which is related to N and organic matter concentration in wetland sediments. The greater importance of TN than TP in our analyses is consistent with previous reports by Badosa et al. (2008), who found that N acts as a limiting nutrient and is more appropriate than P as an indicator of eutrophication in shallow Mediterranean wetlands. Eutrophication is a key process in wetlands and determines biological composition and community structure

(Maier 1996). Our results indicate that 12 species, 3 coarse taxa (LC, C, and CY), and 3 size classes (S1, S2, and S3) are affected by eutrophication. Eight of the 12 species were negatively and 4 were positively correlated with factors indicative of eutrophication (Table 3). These results are consistent with the biology of these species described by Margalef (1953), Armengol (1978), and Alonso (1996) for the Iberian Peninsula. The positive relationship of LC and CY with factors related to eutrophication also has been reported in the literature. Vijverberg and Boersma (1997) indicated that LC (Daphnia) have a better response to the increase in detritus and filaments of Cyanobacteria than do SC, but are more vulnerable to fish predation. Our study wetlands are fishless ecosystems, which may reinforce the tendency for LC to increase as eutrophication increases. The tendency of CY to increase with eutrophication also is well known (Marques and Boavida 1997, Parra et al. 2009). Last, a shift in the body-size distribution toward smaller individuals as eutrophication progresses is in accordance with the general pattern of reduced size in stressed communities described by Kerr (1974). The 2\textsuperscript{nd} interesting idea that can be extracted from environmental variables associated with CCA1 obtained with species matrix and CCA3 obtained with coarse-taxa and size-class matrices is related primarily to DWI and secondarily to light limitation associated with turbidity and P concentration in shallow ecosystems. Thus, these axes, which are associated with 13 species, 2 coarse-level taxa (LC and SC) and 1 size class (S1), are indirectly related to the eutrophication process. DWI or length of the aquatic phase is one of the most important variables that influence the biota of temporary ponds (Williams 1997). Our results suggest that it is a key variable for zooplankton assemblage composition (correlation with CCA1; Table 2), but is less important for coarse-taxa or size-class composition. Rewetting induces sediment resuspension, but the initial turbidity decreases with time since initiation of inundation (Scheffer 1998). Sediment desiccation drastically affects nutrient cycling in Mediterranean wetlands. Rewetting of dry surface sediment increases P concentration in the water column, thereby affecting the trophic state of the system (Gilbert et al. 2014b). The correlation between CCA1 and the 13 zooplankton species is in accord with the pattern of occurrence of those species in the water column from the start of the inundation period. The relationship with LC is explained by the prevalence of this group in temporary waters (Williams 1997). In contrast, SC and C have longer generation times (Allan 1976), and their occurrence in wetlands is later in the period of inundation. The relationship obtained with S1 is related to the idea that invertebrates of temporary ponds exhibit traits of r-selected species (sensu MacArthur and Wilson 1967), especially rapid growth, short life span, and small size (Williams 1997). The combined use of taxon- and body-size approaches allowed us to identify successional phases, according to the Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis (Connell 1978). High diversity of species and body-size classes is achieved after inundation. Water inputs cause an input of nutrients to the ecosystem (Brucet et al. 2006), thereby increasing resource availability to a large number of species (Denslow 1985). As soon as water input ceases, resource scarcity begins and the assemblage moves to a competitive equilibrium characterized by low taxonomic and body-size diversity. Only CCA3 obtained with the species matrix, CCA2 obtained with the coarse-taxa and size-class matrices, the cyclopoid species *Acanthocyclops kieferi*, the Harpacticoida taxa group, and the largest body-size class (>10 mm) appear to be excluded from the influence of eutrophication. *Acanthocyclops kieferi* had low abundance and was present in Table 3. only 1 wetland. Harpacticoida is a benthic group, and our sampling was designed to capture species in the water column. Thus, our abundance estimates for this taxon are suspect. The individuals in the S4 body-size class belong to the Anostraca, which are regarded as ‘nexus species’ and transient in assemblage development (Angeler et al. 2008). In conclusion, our results suggest that body size might be better than taxonomic composition for rapid assessment of the influence of the environmental variables on zooplankton assemblages in temporary wetlands. We do not recommend a general move away from taxonomic studies because they provide fundamental information, e.g., for colonization processes or the appearance of new species. However, future investigators should test our conclusion in other aquatic systems, such as permanent or temperate wetlands. Moreover, our conclusions should be tested in relation to climate change, which could modify the size structure of the zooplankton favoring the small-sized species (Molinero et al. 2006). In this future scenario, temporary wetlands would suffer a drastic reduction in hydroperiod length, and therefore, pioneer species of the annual zooplankton succession could be favored over those that appear at the end of the hydrological cycle. This idea has been studied in relation to other alterations of wetlands, such as agricultural effects (Ruhí et al. 2009, Gilbert et al. 2017). Last, the 3 approaches have ecological and practical considerations for limnological monitoring programs. The species identification requires laborious analytical procedures and human and financial resources (Carignan and Villard 2002), whereas coarse-taxonomic and body-size approaches could be cost-effective tools for monitoring Mediterranean wetlands. This idea complements the approach taken by other authors (Rodríguez and Magnan 1993, Boix et al. 2004, Brucet et al. 2006) who recommend use of simultaneous methods in future limnological studies. Our approach provides a wider interpretation of the concept of diversity proposed by Margalef (1980, 1991), who pointed out the importance of the body size and taxonomic diversity and their relationships with some ecological factors (Rodríguez 2005, Quintana et al. 2006). (Maier 1996). Our results indicate that 12 species, 3 coarse taxa (LC, C, and CY), and 3 size classes (S1, S2, and S3) are affected by eutrophication. Eight of the 12 species were negatively and 4 were positively correlated with factors indicative of eutrophication (Table 3). These results are consistent with the biology of these species described by Margalef (1953), Armengol (1978), and Alonso (1996) for the Iberian Peninsula. The positive relationship of LC and CY with factors related to eutrophication also has been reported in the literature. Vijverberg and Boersma (1997) indicated that LC (Daphnia) have a better response to the increase in detritus and filaments of Cyanobacteria than do SC, but are more vulnerable to fish predation. Our study wetlands are fishless ecosystems, which may reinforce the tendency for LC to increase as eutrophication increases. The tendency of CY to increase with eutrophication also is well known (Marques and Boavida 1997, Parra et al. 2009). Last, a shift in the body-size distribution toward smaller individuals as eutrophication progresses is in accordance with the general pattern of reduced size in stressed communities described by Kerr (1974). The 2\textsuperscript{nd} interesting idea that can be extracted from environmental variables associated with CCA1 obtained with species matrix and CCA3 obtained with coarse-taxa and size-class matrices is related primarily to DWI and secondarily to light limitation associated with turbidity and P concentration in shallow ecosystems. Thus, these axes, which are associated with 13 species, 2 coarse-level taxa (LC and SC) and 1 size class (S1), are indirectly related to the eutrophication process. DWI or length of the aquatic phase is one of the most important variables that influence the biota of temporary ponds (Williams 1997). Our results suggest that it is a key variable for zooplankton assemblage composition (correlation with CCA1; Table 2), but is less important for coarse-taxa or size-class composition. Rewetting induces sediment resuspension, but the initial turbidity decreases with time since initiation of inundation (Scheffer 1998). Sediment desiccation drastically affects nutrient cycling in Mediterranean wetlands. Rewetting of dry surface sediment increases P concentration in the water column, thereby affecting the trophic state of the system (Gilbert et al. 2014b). The correlation between CCA1 and the 13 zooplankton species is in accord with the pattern of occurrence of those species in the water column from the start of the inundation period. The relationship with LC is explained by the prevalence of this group in temporary waters (Williams 1997). In contrast, SC and C have longer generation times (Allan 1976), and their occurrence in wetlands is later in the period of inundation. The relationship obtained with S1 is related to the idea that invertebrates of temporary ponds exhibit traits of r-selected species (sensu MacArthur and Wilson 1967), especially rapid growth, short life span, and small size (Williams 1997). The combined use of taxon- and body-size approaches allowed us to identify successional phases, according to the Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis (Connell 1978). High diversity of species and body-size classes is achieved after inundation. Water inputs cause an input of nutrients to the ecosystem (Brucet et al. 2006), thereby increasing resource availability to a large number of species (Denslow 1985). As soon as water input ceases, resource scarcity begins and the assemblage moves to a competitive equilibrium characterized by low taxonomic and body-size diversity.
